entries.meaning: The object form of the archaic singular you: the person spoken to, when that person is the object of a verb or a preposition.
examples: "How do I love thee? Let me count the ways." (Elizabeth Barrett Browning)
"Get thee to a nunnery." (Hamlet)
"The Lord bless thee, and keep thee." (Numbers 6:24, King James Version)
I shall not tell thee twice, knave.
Fare thee well — we sail at dawn.
Friend, has thee signed the minute yet? (Quaker plain speech, with thee as subject and a third-person verb)
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form in modern recitation; in Quaker plain speech, unstressed /ði/ or /ðɪ/
entries.русский: тебя, тебе — устар. объектная форма thou, 2 л. ед. ч.
entries.case: object (but the subject in Quaker plain speech)
entries.register: archaic, literary, and religious; still living inside some Quaker families
entries.type: personal pronoun, archaic
entries.person / number: second person singular only. There is no plural thee — the plural object form is you.
entries.refers to: one addressee: a person, God, or a personified thing (Donne's Death, be not proud addresses Death itself throughout as thou). Never two or more people. Never a thing you are talking about rather than to.
entries.agreement: as an object it triggers no verb agreement at all. In Quaker plain speech, where thee took over the subject slot from thou, it takes the ordinary third-person singular verb — thee is, thee has, thee knows, thee was — and never ✗thee art or ✗thee knowest. That mismatch is the single most reliable way to tell genuine Quaker usage from Renaissance-fair pastiche.
entries.pattern: [verb] thee · [preposition] thee (unto thee, with thee, of thee) · [verb] thee [object] (I give thee my word) · get thee [directional] · (Quaker) thee [third-person singular verb]
entries.contrast: thou and thee divide exactly as I/me and he/him do — thou is the subject, thee the object: Thou lovest me / I love thee. The test here is substitution, not deletion: drop he or him into the slot and see which one fits — he loves me → thou lovest me; I love him → I love thee. (The deletion test is the tool for coordinated phrases — between you and me, Bob and I went — and it is set out under Other nonstandard forms.) Against ye/you, the difference is not case but number and politeness: thou/thee to one intimate or inferior, ye/you to several people or to one superior. And thee is not a fancier you — it is a smaller, warmer, more familiar one.
entries.see also: thou, thine, thyself, ye, thee (personal), thy

entries.meaning: Stands alone for "the thing or things belonging to thee" — the archaic equivalent of yours.
examples: "For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory." (the Lord's Prayer)
A friend of thine waits at the gate. (after a preposition, the double genitive)
My sword is thine, my lord.
Take what is thine and go.
Is this purse thine or the innkeeper's?
What is mine is thine.
The fault was thine, and thou knowest it.
entries.русский: твоё, твой — устар. самостоятельное притяжательное местоимение (ср. mine)
entries.register: archaic, literary, religious
entries.type: possessive pronoun, archaic — this entry covers the standalone pronoun only; the determiner thine that stands before a vowel (thine eyes) is a separate entry in the determiner dictionary
entries.person / number: second person singular only, invariant; it does not change for the number of the thing possessed (the kingdom is thine, these are thine).
entries.refers to: what belongs to the single person addressed. The possessor is always that one addressee; the thing possessed may be anything at all, count or mass, singular or plural, human or not.
entries.agreement: as a subject complement it takes no agreement of its own; as a subject, the verb agrees with what thine stands for — thine is the kingdom (singular), thine are the greater sins (plural).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] is thine · thine is [noun phrase] · of thine (a friend of thine) · what is thine · [verb] thine (take thine and go) · [preposition] thine (with thine)
entries.contrast: thy and thine split the way my and mine do — with one extra wrinkle. Thy is the determiner before a consonant (thy name), thine the independent pronoun (it is thine), and thine is also the determiner before a vowel or h, exactly as older English wrote mine eyes and mine host. So thine covers two of the three jobs, and which one it is doing depends on whether a noun follows it. A noun follows → determiner, and that is a determiner entry, not a pronoun one: thine eyes, thine heart, and To thine own self be true are all covered in the determiner dictionary. No noun follows → the pronoun entry you are reading, and every example below is that. Modern yours replaces the pronoun, and never takes an apostrophe — ✗your's is as wrong as ✗thine's.
entries.see also: thou, thee, thyself, yourn, thine (possessive), yours, thy

entries.respell: THOW (rhymes with now, not with toe)
entries.meaning: The subject form of the archaic singular you: the one person being addressed, as the subject of a verb.
examples: "Thou shalt not steal." (Exodus 20:15, King James Version)
"Thou art the man." (2 Samuel 12:7)
"Thou art more lovely and more temperate." (Shakespeare, Sonnet 18 — thou to a beloved, the intimate use)
What sayest thou to that, sir?
Where art thou going with that lantern?
Thou knowest well enough what I meant.
entries.русский: ты — устар. 2 л. ед. ч., подлежащее; форма близости или к низшему, а не почтения
entries.register: archaic, literary, religious
entries.type: personal pronoun, archaic
entries.person / number: second person singular only — one addressee, never more. Marked for intimacy or for the addressee's lower rank, not for reverence.
entries.refers to: the single person, deity, or personified thing being spoken to. It cannot refer to a group, and it cannot refer to anyone not present in the discourse as an addressee.
entries.agreement: takes the special second-person singular verb ending -(e)st or -t: thou art, thou hast, thou dost, thou wilt, thou shalt, thou canst, thou knowest, thou goest, thou lovest; past thou wast/wert, thou hadst, thou didst. Pairing thou with a modern verb (✗thou know, ✗thou are) is the commonest mistake in imitation-archaic English.
entries.pattern: thou [verb+est] · thou art [complement] · [verb] thou (inversion in questions: knowest thou?, art thou?) · thou [modal+t] [verb] (thou shalt not steal)
entries.contrast: thou is the subject, thee the object — thou seest me, I see thee. Against ye/you, thou is the intimate singular and ye/you the plural or polite singular, which is the reverse of what the King James Bible leads Americans to assume. Because the KJV addresses God as thou, the form now sounds solemn; historically, addressing a stranger as thou was rude enough to be actionable, and Shakespeare's characters use the switch as a weapon. Modern you descends from the polite plural, which is why the language keeps growing new plurals (y'all, youse, yinz) to fill the gap thou left.
entries.see also: thee, thine, thyself, ye, y'all, thou (personal), you, the personal pronoun paradigm

entries.meaning: The archaic singular reflexive: the addressee, when the addressee is both the subject and the object of the same clause. Also intensive, adding emphasis to thou.
examples: "Physician, heal thyself." (Luke 4:23, King James Version)
Know thyself. (the Delphic maxim, in its standard English form)
Thou hast said it thyself, and in front of witnesses.
Trouble not thyself over so small a matter.
Help thyself to the bread; there is plenty.
Thou wilt only injure thyself by arguing further.
entries.русский: себя, сам — устар. возвратное и усилительное к thou: know thyself «познай себя»
entries.register: archaic, literary, religious; survives in two frozen sayings
entries.type: reflexive and intensive pronoun, archaic
entries.person / number: second person singular only. The plural is yourselves; the archaic singular has no plural of its own.
entries.refers to: the single addressee, and only when that addressee is already the subject of the same clause. Like every reflexive, it needs an antecedent inside its own clause — know thyself works because the understood subject of know is thou.
entries.agreement: none of its own. The clause's verb agrees with its subject, which for an imperative is the understood thou (heal thyself), and for a stated subject takes the -est ending (thou deceivest thyself).
entries.pattern: [verb] thyself (reflexive object) · [preposition] thyself (to thyself, of thyself) · thou [verb] thyself (intensive: thou thyself hast said it) · imperative + thyself (know thyself, help thyself)
entries.contrast: thyself is to thou/thee what yourself is to you. It is built on the possessive thy + self, following the first- and second-person pattern (myself, thyself, ourselves, yourselves), while the third person builds on the object form (himself, themselves) — which is exactly the inconsistency that produces nonstandard hisself and theirselves by analogy. Do not use thyself for more than one person; that is yourselves.
entries.see also: thou, thee, thine, ourself, hisself, yourself, yourselves, reflexive formation

entries.meaning: The subject form of the archaic plural you: the group being addressed.
examples: "Gather ye rosebuds while ye may." (Robert Herrick)
"O ye of little faith." (Matthew 8:26, King James Version)
"Judge not, that ye be not judged." (Matthew 7:1)
Hear ye, hear ye — this court is now in session.
Come, all ye faithful, and bring the rest with you.
Ye have heard the charges; how say ye?
entries.pronunciation note: unstressed /jɪ/. Not the ye of Ye Olde Shoppe — see the contrast below, where the spelling is a printer's accident and the pronunciation is /ðə/, "the."
entries.русский: вы — устар. подлежащная форма 2 л. мн. ч.; также вежливое «вы» к одному
entries.case: subject (the matching object form is you)
entries.register: archaic, literary, religious; also mock-archaic and jocular
entries.type: personal pronoun, archaic
entries.person / number: second person plural — and, in polite address, second person singular to one superior. Historically the vous of English.
entries.refers to: two or more addressees taken together (O ye of little faith, addressed to a crowd), or one addressee treated with deference. It is always addressed, never third person.
entries.agreement: plural verb throughout: ye are, ye have, ye do, ye were, ye know — never the -est ending, which belongs to thou alone. ✗Ye art and ✗ye knowest are the standard giveaway of fake archaism.
entries.pattern: ye [plural verb] · [verb] ye (imperative with the pronoun expressed: hear ye, gather ye) · O ye [noun phrase] (vocative: O ye of little faith) · ye [modal] (ye shall know)
entries.contrast: ye is the subject and you the object of the same plural pronoun — ye see them / they see you — though by Shakespeare's day the two were already being swapped freely, and the KJV itself is inconsistent. Against thou/thee, the split is number and politeness, not case. Now the trap: the ye of Ye Olde Curiosity Shop is not this word at all. Early printers had no letter for the Old English thorn þ (the "th" sound) and substituted the visually similar y, so þe came out as ye — it was always the word the, and the sign should be read the old curiosity shop. Pronouncing it /ji/ is a modern misreading so entrenched that it has become the joke.
entries.see also: thou, thee, y'all, you all, youse, yinz, ye (personal), you

entries.meaning: Anything at all — the archaic ancestor of anything, now confined to a handful of set phrases.
examples: For aught I know, she left the country years ago.
For aught I care, they can settle it in court.
If aught should befall me, the letter explains everything.
He would not say aught against his brother.
Is there aught here worth carrying home?
She never took aught from anyone without paying for it.

senses.head: Anything whatever (pronoun, archaic)
body: In negatives, questions, and conditionals: if aught should happen, he would not say aught against her. This is the pronoun proper, and it is dead outside quotation and the phrase for aught I know.

senses.head: Zero (numeral noun, not a pronoun)
body: From a naught misheard as an aught: nineteen aught six for 1906, a thirty-aught-six, the aughts for the decade 2000–2009. Listed here only so the two are not confused; a numeral is not a pronoun.
examples: For aught I know, she left the country years ago.
For aught I care, they can settle it in court.
If aught should befall me, the letter explains everything.
He would not say aught against his brother.
Is there aught here worth carrying home?
She never took aught from anyone without paying for it.

entries.pronunciation note: /ɑt/ for the majority of Americans, whose cot and caught have merged. Homophone of ought — which is a different word entirely.
entries.русский: что-либо, что-нибудь — устар.; живёт в обороте for aught I know
entries.case: none — one invariant form in every position
entries.register: archaic; survives only in the fixed phrase for aught I know
entries.type: indefinite pronoun, archaic
entries.person / number: third person, singular, invariant. No plural, no possessive, no gender.
entries.refers to: anything at all — a thing, an event, a fact, or a whole state of affairs. Non-human and inanimate by default; for people, older English used any or any man. Like modern anything, it lives in negatives, questions, and conditionals rather than in plain statements: if aught should happen, not ✗aught happened.
entries.agreement: singular verb: if aught remains, should aught go wrong, aught that is worth saving is already gone.
entries.pattern: for aught [subject] [verb] (for aught I know, for aught I care) · if aught [verb] · [verb] aught (know aught of it) · aught of [noun] (aught of value) · aught but [noun] (= anything but)
entries.contrast: aught is "anything," naught is "nothing" — one letter and a complete reversal of polarity, which is why the two are worth learning as a pair. Do not confuse aught with its homophone ought (the modal of obligation: you ought to go); they sound identical and are unrelated. And keep the pronoun apart from the numeral aught meaning zero — nineteen aught six for 1906, a thirty-aught-six rifle, the aughts for 2000–2009 — which arose when a naught was misheard as an aught. That numeral is a noun, not a pronoun, and it is the only aught most Americans under forty have ever used.
entries.see also: naught, nought, somewhat, whatsoever

entries.meaning: Several; sundry ones; an unspecified few of a larger number. The archaic plural indefinite that several replaced.
examples: "And divers of them came from far." (Mark 8:3, King James Version)
Divers of the witnesses gave the same account, though none of them had spoken to the others.
The estate was charged with divers of the debts recited in the schedule annexed hereto. (legal boilerplate; divers debts, with the noun following, would be the determiner)
He had tried divers of the remedies advertised in the back of the paper, and not one had helped.
Divers were called before the committee that spring, and divers declined to answer.
Standard: Several of the witnesses gave the same account.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on the first syllable, which is the whole difference between this word and the modern adjective diverse /dɪˈvɚs/ · dih-VURSS
entries.русский: некоторые, несколько — устар. и юр.; неопределённое множество; не путать с diverse
entries.case: none — one invariant form in every position
entries.register: archaic and literary; still faintly productive in old-fashioned legal drafting and in deliberate period flavor
entries.type: indefinite quantifying pronoun, archaic and legal — this entry covers the standalone pronoun only; divers standing in front of a noun (divers reasons, divers persons) is a determiner and belongs to the determiner dictionary
entries.person / number: third person plural, invariant. No singular, no possessive, no gender.
entries.refers to: an unspecified handful of the members of a group already named or understood — people or things alike (divers of the witnesses, divers of these instruments). Its vagueness is the point: it says "more than two or three, and I am not going to count them."
entries.agreement: plural verb throughout: divers were present, divers of them have complained, divers have since died. ✗Divers was called is an error, not a period touch.
entries.pattern: divers of [noun phrase] (divers of them, divers of the company) · divers [plural verb] (divers were called) · and divers others · divers and sundry (the frozen legal doublet, where the second word carries the same meaning)
entries.contrast: the living word is several, and that is what a modern writer should put on the page: several of the witnesses said the same thing. Two confusions are worth heading off. Divers is not a spelling of diverse: they are the same Latin word split into two English ones, and they now mean different things — divers is "several, sundry," a matter of number, while diverse is "varied, of many kinds," a matter of variety, and they are not even stressed alike. And divers here is not the plural of diver; the identical spelling of the swimmers is an accident that has helped kill the word. In front of a noun it is a determiner, not a pronoun (divers reasons), and the frozen doublet divers and sundry is the last place most Americans meet it.
entries.see also: many another, aught, several, some, divers (determiner), sundry

entries.meaning: A great many people, taken one at a time. The archaic indefinite that keeps a singular verb while meaning a crowd.
examples: Many a one has gone up that mountain and never come down again.
Many a one of them would have given a year's wages for the chance.
She had buried many a one she loved before that winter was out. (object of the verb)
There is many a one in this town who remembers your father. (the existential, with the singular is)
Many a one was lost that September whose name is on no stone.
Modern English: A lot of people have gone up that mountain and never come down.
entries.pronunciation note: the main stress falls on one; many reduces to /mɛni/ and the article to /ə/, so at speed the whole phrase runs together as /mɛniəˈwʌn/ and the a disappears entirely
entries.русский: многие, не один — книжн., устар.; глагол при нём в ед. ч.
entries.case: none — the same form serves as subject and object
entries.register: archaic and literary; ballads, hymns, sermons, and prose written for a formal cadence
entries.type: indefinite pronoun phrase, archaic and literary — this entry covers the standalone pronoun only; many a in front of a singular noun (many a man, many a summer) is a determiner phrase and belongs to the determiner dictionary
entries.person / number: third person singular in form and in agreement, plural in sense — the same split that makes many a man was killed singular.
entries.refers to: a great many individual people, counted one at a time rather than gathered into a group; things are possible (many a one of these old clocks still runs) but people are the ordinary case. It never refers to a clause or a stretch of text.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always: many a one has tried, many a one was lost, ✗ many a one have tried. The singular is not a quirk but the point of the construction — it lets a writer say "a great many" one at a time, which is why the phrase belongs to elegy and sermon.
entries.pattern: many a one [singular verb] · [verb] many a one (object: she buried many a one) · many a one of [plural noun phrase] (many a one of them) · there is many a one [relative clause] (the existential, with the singular is) · many a one and many another
entries.contrast: its nearest neighbor is many another, and the two are not interchangeable: many another means "one more of the same kind" and needs the kind already named (the recipe calls for saffron; many another would do), while many a one is free-standing and simply means "a great many people." Both keep the singular verb that many a forces. Modern American English says a lot of people, plenty of them, or many; reaching for many a one in ordinary prose reads as pulpit costume. And keep the pronoun apart from the determiner: put a noun after many a and the dictionary line has been crossed.
entries.see also: many another, such a one, a body, divers, twain, many, one, many a

entries.meaning: One more of many; many others, counted one at a time. The singular-shaped literary pronoun that means a plural thing.
examples: He gave up in the second year, as many another has before him.
The recipe calls for saffron, but many another would do at a tenth the price.
She lived through the flood of '27, and many another after it.
Many another would have quit on the spot, and would have been right to.
The store closed the way many another has closed — quietly, over a holiday weekend.
Standard and far commoner: Many others have tried; or, with the noun expressed, many another man has tried.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress sits on -noth-; many reduces to /mɛni/ and never carries the main beat
entries.русский: многие другие, не один другой — книжн., устар.; глагол в ед. ч.
entries.register: literary and old-fashioned; alive in edited prose only where the writer wants a formal cadence
entries.type: indefinite pronoun, literary and archaic — this entry covers the standalone pronoun only; many another in front of a singular noun (many another summer, many another man) is a determiner phrase and belongs with many a in the determiner dictionary
entries.person / number: third person singular in form and in agreement, plural in sense — the same split that makes many a man was killed singular.
entries.refers to: one further unnamed member of a large class, offered as a stand-in for all the rest of them. People or things; whatever noun has just been named is what it stands for (the recipe calls for saffron; many another would do).
entries.agreement: singular verb, always: many another has tried, many another was lost, ✗many another have tried. This is the same rule as many a, and it is the whole reason the construction survives: it lets a writer say "a great many" while keeping the singular's weight.
entries.pattern: many another [singular verb] · as many another has [past participle] · and many another [after a named example] · many another standing for a noun just mentioned
entries.contrast: the ordinary modern equivalent is many others, and it is plural: many others have tried. Many another keeps the singular verb and the older rhythm, and it is one of the last living members of the many a family, alongside full many a and many's the. Do not mix the two patterns: ✗many another have takes the plural verb of many others and glues it to the singular phrase. And note the split that decides which dictionary you want — a noun after it (many another winter) makes it a determiner, while nothing after it (many another has said so) makes it the pronoun described here.
entries.see also: divers, a body, another, others, many, many a

entries.meaning: Nothing at all — the archaic ancestor of nothing, surviving mainly in the phrase for naught.
examples: Three years of work, and it was all for naught.
Their whole scheme came to naught within a month.
Naught remained of the barn but the foundation.
He gained naught but a reputation for stubbornness.
The court set his objections at naught.
She said naught to anyone about the letter.
entries.pronunciation note: /nɑt/ in cot–caught merged accents, making it a homophone of not and knot
entries.русский: ничто, ноль — устар.; all for naught «всё впустую», come to naught «сойти на нет»
entries.register: archaic and literary; alive in all for naught, come to naught, set at naught
entries.type: indefinite pronoun, archaic (also a noun meaning zero)
entries.person / number: third person, singular, invariant.
entries.refers to: nothing at all — no thing, no amount, no result. Non-human. It can stand for an outcome or a whole effort (the whole campaign came to naught), which is its commonest modern job.
entries.agreement: singular verb: naught remains, naught was said, naught but trouble comes of it.
entries.pattern: all for naught · come to naught / bring to naught · set at naught (= treat as worthless) · naught but [noun] (= nothing but) · naught [verb] (naught remains of the house)
entries.contrast: naught is "nothing," aught is "anything." Naught also names the digit zero — noughts and crosses is the British name for tic-tac-toe, and naught survives in American speech in a thirty-aught-six and nineteen aught nine, where the same zero has drifted into the aught spelling. The two spellings naught and nought are the same word: American English keeps naught for the pronoun and leaves nought to the British for the digit. Do not confuse it with the adjective naughty, which descends from it (originally "having nothing," then "worthless," then "badly behaved").
entries.see also: aught, nought, somewhat

entries.meaning: Nothing; zero. A spelling variant of naught, and the one an American is most likely to meet in British writing or in older mathematics.
examples: All their careful planning went for nought.
Nought but the wind answered him.
The experiment yielded nought of any value.
Write nought point five, not one half. (British arithmetic teaching)
He reduced my objections to nought in a single sentence.
The children were playing noughts and crosses on the back of the menu. (British; American tic-tac-toe)
entries.pronunciation note: identical to naught — the two spellings are one word
entries.русский: ничто, ноль — устар.; вариант написания naught, в брит. языке — цифра «ноль»
entries.register: archaic and literary in American English; standard British spelling for the digit zero
entries.type: indefinite pronoun, archaic (chiefly a noun meaning zero in British usage)
entries.person / number: third person, singular, invariant.
entries.refers to: nothing; no amount; zero. Non-human, inanimate.
entries.agreement: singular verb: nought remains, nought was gained.
entries.pattern: all for nought · come to nought · nought but [noun] · noughts and crosses (British, the game)
entries.contrast: nought and naught are the same word in two spellings, and the split is national rather than semantic: American editors write naught for the pronoun (all for naught) and reserve nought for quotation, poetry, and British contexts. A conservative American copy editor will change nought to naught on sight. Neither should be confused with not, with which both are homophones for most Americans, nor with aught, which means the opposite.
entries.see also: naught, aught

entries.meaning: Something; some amount or degree of a thing. The archaic pronoun, now alive only inside the phrase somewhat of a.
examples: "Simon, I have somewhat to say unto thee." (Luke 7:40, King James Version)
There is somewhat in his account that does not add up.
He has become somewhat of a legend in the department.
The delay was somewhat of a blessing, given the weather.
She told him somewhat of what had passed, but not all.
I found it somewhat of a relief when the offer fell through.
entries.pronunciation note: also /ˈsʌmˌhwʌt/ for speakers who keep the wh-
entries.русский: нечто, кое-что — устар. как местоимение; современное somewhat — наречие «отчасти»
entries.register: archaic as a pronoun; the surviving somewhat of a is informal-to-neutral American English and mildly contested
entries.type: indefinite pronoun, archaic (the modern word is an adverb of degree, which this entry does not cover)
entries.person / number: third person, singular, invariant.
entries.refers to: some thing, some amount, or some quality — non-human and typically abstract (somewhat to say, somewhat of the truth). Never a person.
entries.agreement: singular verb: there is somewhat in what he says.
entries.pattern: have somewhat to [verb] (I have somewhat to say) · somewhat of [noun phrase] (somewhat of the truth) · there is somewhat in [noun phrase] · the modern survival, somewhat of a [noun] (somewhat of a legend)
entries.contrast: the pronoun somewhat has been fully replaced by something: I have something to tell you, not ✗I have somewhat to tell you. What survives in American English is the quantifying idiom somewhat of a, which competes with something of a — He's somewhat of an expert vs He's something of an expert. Both are current in the United States; something of a is the older and safer choice, and conservative editors prefer it, but somewhat of a is common enough in edited American prose that calling it an error overstates the case. Keep all of this apart from the ordinary modern adverb somewhat (somewhat tired, somewhat better), which is standard, neutral, and not a pronoun at all.
entries.see also: aught, naught, whatsoever

entries.meaning: The two of them. The archaic pronoun for a pair, kept alive by one line of Kipling and one verse of Matthew.
examples: "Oh, East is East, and West is West, and never the twain shall meet." (Kipling, The Ballad of East and West)
"…and they twain shall be one flesh." (Matthew 19:5, King James Version)
The brothers quarreled in 1868, and the twain were never reconciled.
He would walk a mile or twain before breakfast, whatever the weather. (the old postpositive numeral)
"Mark twain!" — the leadsman's cry for two fathoms, and the pen name Samuel Clemens took from it.
"And the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom." (Mark 15:38 — the adverb, not the pronoun)
Modern English: the two of them never spoke again; the curtain was torn in two.
entries.pronunciation note: one syllable, rhyming with rain; no weak form at all — twain is always fully stressed, which is one reason it survived only inside set phrases. The article in the twain reduces normally to /ðə/
entries.русский: двое — устар. форма two; жива в обороте never the twain shall meet
entries.variants: the twain, the definite form, which is how nearly every American meets the word (never the twain shall meet); they twain, the biblical form, where twain sits in apposition to a pronoun
entries.case: none — the same form serves as subject and object
entries.register: archaic and literary; alive for Americans in two quotations, one frozen phrase, and one pen name
entries.type: fused-head numeral pronoun, archaic — the old form of two standing alone
entries.person / number: third person plural — two of something, always exactly two. There is no singular and no possessive.
entries.refers to: the two people or things already named, taken as a pair — East and West in Kipling, husband and wife in Matthew. People or things, never a clause. In the adverbial in twain it refers instead to the two pieces something is broken into, which is a different job and is noted in the contrast below.
entries.agreement: plural verb: never the twain shall meet, the twain were never reconciled, ✗ the twain is. This is worth stating because the phrase sounds singular to a modern ear — twain has no -s — and the twain is turns up in imitation-archaic writing.
entries.pattern: the twain [plural verb] · never the twain shall meet (the frozen Kipling line) · they twain (biblical apposition: they twain shall be one flesh) · in twain (adverbial: rent in twain, cut in twain) · a mile or twain (the old postpositive numeral, in verse)
entries.contrast: the living word is two, and the living pronoun for exactly two is both or the two of them. Three boundaries. In twain is an adverb, not a pronoun — it means "into two pieces," and the veil was rent in twain has no pronoun in it at all; it is listed here only so the two uses are not confused. Twain standing after a noun (days twain, brethren twain) is the archaic postpositive numeral and belongs to the determiner dictionary. And Mark Twain is neither: it is the Mississippi leadsman's call for a sounding of two fathoms, which Samuel Clemens took as a pen name.
entries.see also: t'other, many a one, divers, the same, both, other, twain (determiner)

entries.meaning: Whatever; anything at all that. The oldest and shortest member of the what- family, alive now only in quotation and deliberate pastiche.
examples: Whatso thou askest of me, that will I give thee. (Middle English pattern, with the thou verb endings intact)
Whatso remains after the debts are paid falls to the younger son.
Take whatso pleases thee and leave the rest upon the table.
Whatso is done in haste is commonly done twice.
He swore to obey, whatso the order might be.
Modern English: Take whatever you like — or, with the emphatic weight, whatsoever you like.
entries.pronunciation note: also /ˈhwʌtsoʊ/ for speakers who keep the wh-; stress on the first syllable, unlike whatsoever, and there is no weak form — the word is only ever recited
entries.русский: что бы ни, всё что — устар. (среднеангл.) краткая форма whatsoever
entries.case: none — the same form serves as subject and object
entries.register: archaic; Middle English and Early Modern English only, and dead in American English outside quotation and pastiche
entries.type: fused relative pronoun, archaic
entries.person / number: third person, singular in agreement however broad the reference.
entries.refers to: things, actions, and states of affairs — anything at all that satisfies the clause. Never people; the person word is whoso.
entries.agreement: singular verb inside its own clause: whatso remains is thine, whatso he asks shall be given. ✗Whatso remain is wrong even in imitation.
entries.pattern: whatso [singular verb] (subject of its own clause) · [verb] whatso [subject] [verb] (object: take whatso thou wilt) · whatso [subject] [verb], [main clause]
entries.contrast: whatso, whatsoever, and modern whatever are one word at three lengths, exactly as whoso, whosoever, and whoever are. Whatso is the oldest and shortest, and it is a full step deader than whatsoever: even Shakespeare preferred the longer form. Like every fused relative it swallows its own antecedent, so nothing may precede it (✗the thing whatso he asks) — that is what "fused" means. If you want the meaning today, write whatever; if you want the sound of 1400, this is the word, and the elided verse form is whatsoe'er.
entries.see also: whatsoever, whomso, whoso, whoe'er, whate'er, whosoe'er, whatsoe'er, whatever, what (fused relative)

entries.meaning: Whatever; anything at all that. The archaic fused relative, and — in negative contexts — a fully modern intensifier.
examples: "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might." (Ecclesiastes 9:10, King James Version)
"Whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them." (Matthew 7:12)
There is no evidence whatsoever that the file was ever opened.
She had nothing whatsoever to do with the decision.
I have no objection whatsoever to the schedule as written.
The tenant shall make no alterations whatsoever without written consent.

senses.head: Fused relative pronoun (archaic)
body: "Anything at all that," heading its own clause and needing no antecedent: whatsoever ye do, whatsoever remains. Modern English writes whatever.

senses.head: Emphatic postmodifier after a negative (standard modern English)
body: Attaches behind a negated noun phrase and intensifies the negation: no evidence whatsoever, nothing whatsoever, none whatsoever. This is ordinary American English at every level of formality, and it is the only living use of the word.
examples: "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might." (Ecclesiastes 9:10, King James Version)
"Whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them." (Matthew 7:12)
There is no evidence whatsoever that the file was ever opened.
She had nothing whatsoever to do with the decision.
I have no objection whatsoever to the schedule as written.
The tenant shall make no alterations whatsoever without written consent.

entries.pronunciation note: the -so- reduces to /sə/ in speech: /ˌwʌtsəˈɛvɚ/
entries.русский: что бы ни — устар. относительное; в совр. языке усилитель отрицания «вообще никакой»
entries.case: none — the same form serves as subject and object
entries.register: archaic as a pronoun; the negative-emphasis use is ordinary modern English at every level
entries.type: fused relative pronoun, archaic (also a modern emphatic postmodifier)
entries.variants: whatsoe'er, the metrically elided verse form (see whoe'er, whate'er, whosoe'er, whatsoe'er); the shorter and older whatso has its own entry
entries.person / number: third person, singular in agreement even when the reference is broad.
entries.refers to: things, actions, and states of affairs — never people. For people the corresponding form is whosoever. It can also take a whole clause as its reference (whatsoever befalls us).
entries.agreement: singular verb inside its own clause: whatsoever remains is yours, whatsoever thy hand findeth to do.
entries.pattern: whatsoever [verb] (subject of its clause) · [verb] whatsoever (object) · whatsoever [subject] [verb] (whatsoever ye do) · the modern use, [negative noun phrase] + whatsoever (no evidence whatsoever, none whatsoever, nothing whatsoever)
entries.contrast: as a pronoun, whatsoever is simply an emphatic whatever, and modern English uses whatever: Take whatever you need, not ✗Take whatsoever you need. What lives on is the postposed emphatic, which attaches to a negative and intensifies it — no reason whatsoever, none whatsoever, nothing whatsoever to do with me. That use is neither archaic nor formal; it is everyday American English, and it must follow the negative rather than precede it (✗whatsoever no reason). Whatsoever before a noun (whatsoever reason) is the determiner, covered in the determiner dictionary; whichsoever is the same construction on which and is rarer still.
entries.see also: whosoever, whomsoever, whoso, aught, whatever, whichsoever, whatsoever (determiner)

entries.meaning: From wherever; from whatever source or cause. The emphatic archaic form of whence.
examples: The trustee shall pay over the income, whencesoever derived, to the beneficiary for life.
Whencesoever the rumor came, it was all over the county by Sunday.
He would take good advice whencesoever it came, and from whosoever offered it. (whosoever, not ✗whomsoever: it is the subject of offered)
The claim, whencesoever arising, is barred six years after the breach.
Whencesoever that money reached him, it did not come out of this office.
Modern English: from wherever it came; income from whatever source derived.
entries.pronunciation note: also /ˌhwɛnsoʊˈɛvɚ/ for speakers who keep the wh-; five syllables with the main stress on ev, and the doubled s of whence + soever degeminates to one. No weak form — the word is only ever read aloud
entries.русский: откуда бы ни — устар., юр.; «из какого бы места, источника или причины»
entries.register: archaic; survives only in legal-ceremonial drafting and in deliberately grand English
entries.type: fused relative pro-adverb, archaic — whence with -soever welded on, "from whatever place, source, or cause"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: the origin of something, left deliberately open — a place, a source of money, a cause. It refers to a thing or a source, never to a person, and never to a whole clause.
entries.agreement: none of its own; the verb inside its clause agrees with that clause's own subject (whencesoever it comes, whencesoever they came). In the participial legal formula there is no verb at all (income, whencesoever derived).
entries.pattern: whencesoever [subject] [verb] · whencesoever derived / whencesoever arising (the drafting formula, on the model of from whatever source derived) · from whencesoever (the redundant from, exactly as in from whence) · [noun] whencesoever [clause]
entries.contrast: it is whence with the emphatic tail added, and it means no more than whence does — -soever buys emphasis and length, nothing else, exactly as whosoever buys nothing over whoever. Its mates are wheresoever, whithersoever, whensoever: whencesoever is "from wherever," whithersoever "to wherever," wheresoever "at wherever." Like whence it already contains from, so from whencesoever is redundant; like from whence, it is four hundred years old and nobody serious calls it an error. Modern American English writes from wherever or from whatever source, and the tax code's from whatever source derived is the living descendant of the formula.
entries.see also: whence, wheresoever, whithersoever, whensoever, whosoever, whatsoever, thence, therefrom

entries.meaning: Wherever; to wherever; whenever. The -soever forms of where, whither, and when, emphatic in the same way whosoever is emphatic.
examples: "Whithersoever thou goest, I will go." (the pattern of Ruth 1:16, in the emphatic form)
The policy covers the insured property wheresoever located and howsoever stored.
Whensoever the note falls due, payment shall be made in lawful money.
He vowed to follow her whithersoever fortune might carry her.
Wheresoever two or three are gathered, there is a committee waiting to be formed. (jocular)
Modern English: wherever it is stored, whenever the note comes due, wherever she goes.
entries.pronunciation note: the -so- reduces to /sə/ at speed (/ˌwɛrsəˈɛvɚ/), and speakers who keep the wh- say /ˌhwɛr-/, /ˌhwɛn-/; the main stress is on -ev- in all three
entries.русский: где бы ни, куда бы ни, когда бы ни — устар., библ. и юр.
entries.register: archaic, biblical, and legal; wheresoever still turns up in insurance policies and jurisdiction clauses
entries.type: fused relative pro-adverbs, archaic — they stand in for a whole prepositional phrase of place, direction, or time rather than for a noun phrase
entries.person / number: third person, invariant. No plural, no possessive.
entries.refers to: wheresoever → any place at all in which (position); whithersoever → any place at all to which (direction); whensoever → any time at all at which. Places and times, never people or things.
entries.agreement: none of their own; the verb inside the clause agrees with that clause's own subject — wheresoever the goods are stored, whensoever the tenant fails to pay.
entries.pattern: wheresoever [subject] [verb] · whithersoever [subject] [verb] (whithersoever thou goest) · whensoever [subject] [verb] · and wheresoever situate (the frozen conveyancing tag, with situate as an adjective)
entries.contrast: these are the -soever forms of the old place-and-time trio, and they line up exactly with it: wheresoever is emphatic whence's stay-put cousin where, whithersoever is emphatic whither ("to where"), whensoever is emphatic when. The distinction they preserve is the one modern English threw away — where for position, whither for motion toward — so ✗whithersoever it is kept is a misuse for wheresoever, and wheresoever thou goest loses the motion the King James translators were marking. Modern English writes wherever, wherever … to, and whenever; the only one still earning its keep is wheresoever in legal drafting, where goods wheresoever located is doing real work by refusing to let a place be argued about.
entries.see also: whosoever, whatsoever, whence, whither, wherein, whatever, anywhere

entries.meaning: Whomever; whatever person, as the object of a verb or a preposition. The object mate of whoso.
examples: He would serve whomso the abbot appointed over him.
Let the ring pass to whomso she chooses, and let none dispute it.
Whomso the council summons must appear within the fortnight.
She would speak of it to whomso she trusted, and there were few enough of those.
Reward whomso thou findest faithful in a little thing.
Modern English: the ring passes to whomever she chooses — and in ordinary American writing, to whoever she chooses.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on the first syllable, unlike whomsoever; the wh- is /h/ for every speaker, as in who
entries.русский: кого бы ни — устар., книжн.; объектная форма whoso, только о людях
entries.register: archaic and literary; even deader than whoso, and essentially confined to Middle English and to poetry imitating it
entries.type: fused relative pronoun, archaic
entries.person / number: third person; people only, open in number.
entries.refers to: human beings only — whatever person the clause picks out. For things, whatso.
entries.agreement: as an object it triggers no agreement of its own; the verb in its clause agrees with that clause's own subject (whomso the king favors — king is the subject, so favors).
entries.pattern: [verb] whomso [subject] [verb] (serve whomso thou wilt) · [preposition] whomso [subject] [verb] (to whomso he names) · whomso [subject] [verb], [main clause]
entries.contrast: whoso is the subject form and whomso the object form, and — as with whosoever and whomsoever — the choice is decided inside the pronoun's own clause, never by a preposition sitting in front of it. Give it to whomso the steward names is right because whomso is the object of names; give it to whoso comes first is right because whoso is the subject of comes. Substitute he or him to test it. Modern English has retired the whole set: write whoever and whomever, and note that even whomever is receding in American usage, exactly as plain whom has receded to the one position after a preposition.
entries.see also: whoso, whomsoever, whatso, whosoever, whom, whomever

entries.meaning: Whomever; whatever person, as the object of a verb or preposition.
examples: The proceeds shall be paid to whomsoever the trustee designates.
Deliver the summons to whomsoever you find at the residence.
He would defend whomsoever the court assigned him.
Give the seat to whomsoever you please; it makes no difference to me.
To whomsoever these presents shall come, greeting. (the opening formula of an old deed)
She invited whomsoever she had met at the conference.
entries.pronunciation note: reduced /ˌhumsəˈɛvɚ/
entries.русский: кого бы ни, кому бы ни — устар. и юр.; объектная форма whosoever
entries.register: archaic; still productive in legal drafting
entries.type: fused relative pronoun, archaic and legal
entries.person / number: any person, singular or plural in reference; people only.
entries.refers to: human beings only — an unnamed or not-yet-determined person or persons. For things, use whatsoever.
entries.agreement: as an object it triggers no agreement of its own; the verb in its clause agrees with that clause's own subject (whomsoever the board appoints — board is the subject, so appoints).
entries.pattern: [preposition] whomsoever [subject] [verb] (to whomsoever the court appoints) · [verb] whomsoever [subject] [verb] (hire whomsoever you please) · whomsoever [subject] [verb], [main clause]
entries.contrast: this is the entry where case actually matters, and where careful writers still go wrong. The case of whosoever/whomsoever is set by its job inside its own clause, not by anything before it. Compare: The estate passes to whomsoever the testator names — whomsoever is the object of names, so the object form is right. But The estate passes to whosoever survives him — here the pronoun is the subject of survives, so the subject form is right, even though a preposition sits immediately in front of it. The test: replace the clause with he or him. The testator names him → whomsoever. He survives him → whosoever. Writing ✗to whomsoever survives him is a hypercorrection, the same error as ✗whom shall I say is calling. Modern English writes whoever/whomever, and outside legal boilerplate even whomever is receding. Plain whom has made the same retreat: in present-day American English it survives mainly right after a preposition — to whom it may concern, for whom the bell tolls, the tenant with whom we spoke — while at the head of a clause or a question almost everyone now writes who (Who did you invite?, Who were you talking to?), and no American editor will stop them. Reaching for whom outside its one safe position is where the hypercorrections come from.
entries.see also: whosoever, whoso, whatsoever, whom, whomever

entries.meaning: Whoever; anyone who. The oldest and shortest of the three, alive now only in quotation.
examples: "Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein." (Proverbs 26:27, King James Version)
"Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing." (Proverbs 18:22)
Whoso enters here does so at his own peril.
Whoso keeps this covenant shall not be forsaken.
Whoso has ears to hear, let him hear.
Whoso would be a man must be a nonconformist. (Emerson, Self-Reliance)
entries.pronunciation note: stress on the first syllable, unlike whosoever
entries.русский: кто бы ни — устар., книжн.; «всякий, кто», глагол в ед. ч.
entries.register: archaic and literary; effectively confined to scripture and older poetry
entries.type: fused relative pronoun, archaic
entries.person / number: third person; singular in agreement, though its reference is open-ended ("anyone who").
entries.refers to: people only — any person who satisfies the condition in the clause. Never things.
entries.agreement: singular verb in both clauses: whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein. Treating it as plural (✗whoso believe) is wrong even in imitation.
entries.pattern: whoso [singular verb] [rest of clause], [main clause with singular verb] · whoso is [complement]
entries.contrast: whoso, whosoever, and modern whoever are the same word at three degrees of length and archaism, and all three are subject forms that fuse the head and the relative — whoso finds it means "the person who finds it," so no separate antecedent is needed or possible (✗the man whoso finds it). Whoso is a full step older than whosoever and is essentially dead outside quotation; if you need the meaning, write whoever.
entries.see also: whosoever, whomsoever, whatsoever, whoever

entries.meaning: Whoever; any person who. The emphatic archaic form, familiar to most Americans from a single famous verse.
examples: "That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life." (John 3:16, King James Version)
"Whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also." (Matthew 5:39)
Whosoever enters this hall shall leave his weapons at the door.
Let whosoever is without sin cast the first stone.
The reward goes to whosoever brings him in alive.
Whosoever will may come.
entries.pronunciation note: reduced /ˌhusəˈɛvɚ/
entries.русский: кто бы ни — устар., книжн., юр.; «всякий, кто», подлежащная форма
entries.register: archaic and religious; also legal, and jokingly grand
entries.type: fused relative pronoun, archaic
entries.variants: whosoe'er, the metrically elided verse form (see whoe'er, whate'er, whosoe'er, whatsoe'er); the object form is whomsoever
entries.person / number: third person; singular in agreement, however many people it may end up covering.
entries.refers to: people only — any person at all who meets the description. For things, whatsoever.
entries.agreement: singular verb in its own clause and in the main clause: whosoever believeth in him should not perish, whosoever is found guilty shall be fined. This is the same rule that gives everyone is, somebody was, nobody knows, and anybody who wants a ticket has to line up, and it runs through the neighboring families too: each of them is, either of them is, and neither of them is are all singular, while both, several, and a few are plural, and all, some, and most take their number from what they refer to (all of the water is gone, all of the seats are taken). Only none goes either way. A wrong plural here (✗whosoever believe) is a real error, not a stylistic slip.
entries.pattern: whosoever [singular verb] [rest of clause] + [main clause] · [preposition] whosoever [verb] (to whosoever asks) · whosoever will (elliptical: "anyone who is willing")
entries.contrast: whosoever is the subject form and whomsoever the object form, and the choice depends on the pronoun's role in its own clause, not on a preceding preposition — give it to whosoever asks is correct because whosoever is the subject of asks. Against the modern forms: whosoever : whoever :: whomsoever : whomever, with the long forms adding weight and age and nothing else. In present-day American writing, use whoever; reserve whosoever for quotation, liturgy, and deliberate grandeur.
entries.see also: whoso, whomsoever, whatsoever, whoever

entries.meaning: It is; it was; it were. The old front-contracted forms of dummy it plus its verb, kept alive by poetry, carols, and one famous Christmas poem.
examples: "'Twas the night before Christmas, when all through the house…" (Clement Clarke Moore, A Visit from St. Nicholas)
"'Tis better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all." (Tennyson, In Memoriam)
"If it were done when 'tis done, then 'twere well it were done quickly." (Macbeth — all three forms in one sentence, and 'twere the subjunctive)
"'Tis but thy name that is my enemy." (Romeo and Juliet)
'Tis a pity the letter arrived a day too late.
'Twere folly to sail with the glass falling like that. (subjunctive: "it would be folly")
Modern English: It's a pity the letter came late; it would be foolish to sail.
entries.pronunciation note: weak forms /twəz/ and /twɚ/ in the middle of a line, where the whole point of the contraction is that the syllable is light; 'twill is /twɪl/ and 'twould /twʊd/
entries.русский: это есть, это было — устар., поэт. стяжения it is, it was, it were
entries.case: subject (the it is the subject of its clause)
entries.register: archaic, poetic, and liturgical; in living American English, quotation, carols, and jokey elevated tone
entries.type: frozen contractions of the dummy pronoun it with a following verb — pronoun plus verb welded into one word
entries.person / number: third person singular throughout, invariant. 'Tis is present, 'twas past, and 'twere the past subjunctive ('twere well = "it would be well").
entries.refers to: whatever dummy it refers to — usually nothing at all. This is the empty it of weather, time, and general states of affairs ('tis cold, 'tis a pity, 'twas the night before Christmas), not a pointing pronoun with an antecedent.
entries.agreement: the verb is already fused in and cannot change: 'tis carries is, 'twas carries was, 'twere carries the subjunctive were. ✗'Tis were and ✗'twas be are impossible. Nothing can be inserted between the two halves, and the contraction cannot be negated inside itself — the negative is 'tis not, never ✗'tisn't in careful verse, though 'tisn't does turn up in nineteenth-century dialect writing.
entries.pattern: 'tis [complement] ('tis a pity, 'tis true) · 'twas [noun phrase] ('twas the night before Christmas) · 'twere [complement] (subjunctive: 'twere well it were done quickly) · 'tis [comparative] to [verb] ('tis better to have loved)
entries.contrast: modern English contracts from the back — it's, it'll, it'd — and these contract from the front, which is the single fastest way to date a line of English. They are not the same words spelled differently: ✗it's the night before Christmas is grammatical but flattens the meter Moore wrote, and 'tis in a business email is a costume, not a register. Keep 'twere apart from 'twas: 'twas is a plain past ('twas cold that night), while 'twere is the past subjunctive used for hypotheticals ('twere better said in private), the same were that survives in if I were you. And keep the whole family apart from the possessive: there is no ✗'ts, and its never takes an apostrophe.
entries.see also: whoe'er, whate'er, whosoe'er, whatsoe'er, methinks, thou, it, it (weather, time, and distance), it's (not a possessive pronoun)

entries.meaning: Whoever, whatever, whosoever, whatsoever — each with the v of -ever knocked out to save a syllable of meter.
examples: "Whate'er is best administer'd is best." (Pope, An Essay on Man)
Whoe'er thou art that readest this, remember me.
Whatsoe'er befall, we shall be found at our posts.
Whosoe'er shall keep this trust shall want for nothing.
She sang of a love that would follow him whate'er the cost.
Full forms: whatever is best administered is best; whoever you are; whatever befalls.
entries.pronunciation note: each is exactly one syllable shorter than the word it replaces, which is the entire reason it exists; no weak forms, since they occur only in recited verse
entries.русский: кто бы ни, что бы ни — устар., поэт. стяжённые формы ради стихотворного размера
entries.case: whoe'er and whosoe'er are subject forms, matched by the rare objects whome'er and whomsoe'er; whate'er and whatsoe'er have no case at all
entries.register: archaic and poetic; hymns, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century verse, and pastiche
entries.type: fused relative pronouns, archaic — metrically elided forms of whoever, whatever, whosoever, and whatsoever
entries.person / number: third person, singular in agreement. Whoe'er and whosoe'er are people only; whate'er and whatsoe'er are things only.
entries.refers to: whatever person (whoe'er, whosoe'er) or whatever thing, act, or state of affairs (whate'er, whatsoe'er) satisfies the clause. Like all fused relatives they carry their own antecedent inside them, so nothing may precede them.
entries.agreement: singular verb in the pronoun's own clause: whoe'er believes, whate'er befalls, ✗whoe'er believe. The elision changes the meter and nothing else — agreement, case, and meaning are identical to the full forms.
entries.pattern: whoe'er [singular verb] [rest of clause] + [main clause] · whate'er [subject] [verb] (whate'er thou dost) · [verb] whate'er (object) · whatsoe'er after a negative, exactly as whatsoever is used
entries.contrast: these are not separate words and they carry no separate meaning: whoe'er is whoever with a syllable removed, and swapping one for the other changes only the scansion. The apostrophe marks the missing v of -ever, and it belongs where that v stood — ✗whoe're and ✗who'er misplace it. The same elision gives the adverbs e'er ("ever"), ne'er ("never"), and o'er ("over"), which are not pronouns and are not covered here. In present-day American writing, use the full forms; the elided ones are for singing and quoting, and reaching for them in prose reads as costume in exactly the way methinks does.
entries.see also: 'tis, 'twas, 'twere, whatsoever, whosoever, whatso, whoso, whoever, whatever

entries.meaning: One; a person; anyone at all. The archaic and dialectal generic pronoun that modern English replaced with one and with generic you.
examples: "If a body meet a body, comin' thro' the rye." (Robert Burns — the line behind the title of The Catcher in the Rye)
A body can't get a moment's peace around here. (subject)
What's a body to do with a boy like that? (subject of an infinitive)
It would try a body's patience to sit through that twice. (possessive)
That road is hard on a body and harder on a truck. (object of a preposition)
They worked him till there was nothing left of a body at all. (object of a preposition, with the noun sense playing against the pronoun)
Standard: One never knows — or, far more naturally in American English, you never know.
entries.pronunciation note: the d taps to [ɾ], so it comes out /ə ˈbɑɾi/; in the Scots song it is /ə ˈbʌdɪ/ · unstressed a is /ə/ and never /eɪ/
entries.русский: человек, всякий — устар., диал. обобщённое «любой, и я в том числе» (ср. one)
entries.case: none — the same form serves as subject and object; the possessive is a body's
entries.register: archaic and literary; still heard in older rural American speech, and preserved for everyone in one Burns song
entries.type: generic indefinite pronoun, archaic and dialectal
entries.person / number: third person singular, invariant. It has no plural — for more than one, English says folks or people.
entries.refers to: any person at all, with the speaker quietly included — the same generic human that modern English calls one or generic you. People only, never a thing; and never a specific, identified person.
entries.agreement: singular verb, exactly like generic one and like everyone, somebody, and nobody: a body gets tired, a body never knows, a body has to eat somewhere. ✗A body get tired is an error, not a dialect feature.
entries.pattern: a body [singular verb] · [verb] a body (it would tire a body out) · [preposition] a body (hard on a body) · a body's [noun] (possessive: a body's own kin) · if a body [verb] · what's a body to do?
entries.contrast: English has four ways to be generic and this is the oldest one still recognizable. Formal writing uses one (one never knows); ordinary speech uses generic you (you never know); the indefinite compounds cover the rest (everybody knows); and a body is the dialect member of the set. It is also the parent of the others: the -body in anybody, everybody, nobody, and somebody is this same noun body meaning "person," with a quantifier welded onto the front. Its reflexive is the phrasal a body's self, never ✗abodyself. Do not confuse the pronoun with the ordinary count noun a body meaning a corpse or a torso (they found a body in the creek) — that is not a pronoun at all, and it is the only sense most Americans under sixty still have.
entries.see also: oneself, we'uns, one (generic), somebody, everybody, nobody

entries.meaning: And the sections following. The citation abbreviation that stands in for the run of text after the one named.
examples: The Fair Labor Standards Act, 29 U.S.C. § 201 et seq., sets the federal minimum wage.
Plaintiff's claims arise under Chapter 93A, §§ 2 et seq., of the Massachusetts General Laws.
The committee's discussion of the amendment begins at page 45 et seq. of the report.
See Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 152 et seq. on mutual mistake.
Rule 26 et seq. — the discovery rules and everything that follows them — was rewritten in 2015.
Humanities style prefers ff.: see pp. 45ff., meaning the same thing.
Careful modern drafting names the endpoint instead: 29 U.S.C. §§ 201–219.
entries.pronunciation note: two syllables, stress on seq; lawyers who expand it say /ɛt sɪˈkwɛnʃə/ · et si-KWEN-sha for et sequentia. There is no weak form — the phrase belongs to the page, and even in court it is read out at full value
entries.русский: и след. — юр. и науч., лат. et sequentes «и последующие» (статьи, страницы)
entries.register: legal and scholarly; standard and unremarkable inside a citation, and out of place in any running sentence
entries.type: abbreviated Latin anaphoric phrase — et sequentes / et sequentia, "and the following ones"; a pro-form that stands in for the unnamed run of sections, pages, or verses after the one just cited
entries.person / number: third person plural — "and the ones after it." There is no singular; a single following item is et seq. only by courtesy, and older style wrote et sequens for it.
entries.refers to: the units of text that follow the one cited — sections of a statute, pages of a report, paragraphs of a treatise, verses of scripture. Things, never people, and never a whole clause. It is strictly anaphoric on the citation immediately in front of it and cannot stand without one.
entries.agreement: it heads no clause and takes no verb of its own. When the whole citation is the subject, the verb agrees with what the writer means by it — 29 U.S.C. § 201 et seq. governs overtime (the statute, singular), sections 201 et seq. are the operative provisions (the sections, plural). Both are correct, and the choice is a choice of referent.
entries.pattern: [citation] et seq. (§ 201 et seq., pp. 45 et seq.) · §§ [number] et seq. (the doubled section mark for a run) · et seqq. (the older doubled q, for more than one following item) · ff. (the humanities equivalent: pp. 45ff.)
entries.contrast: the everyday equivalent is and following, or a stated range — and a stated range is what a careful modern drafter writes, because et seq. has no endpoint and a reader cannot tell where the cited run stops. Keep it apart from the other Latin abbreviations of the footnote: et al. is "and others" and points at people (co-authors, co-defendants); ibid. points at the work cited immediately above; id. at the same authority again; supra and infra at a place earlier or later in the text, and those two are adverbs with no pronoun in them at all. Note the period, which is not optional — et is a whole Latin word but seq. is an abbreviation — and note that American style now sets the phrase in roman rather than italic type.
entries.see also: the aforesaid, the aforementioned, the foregoing, the premises, hereinafter, hereinbelow, thereinafter, thereinbefore

entries.meaning: It seems to me. A frozen Middle English impersonal, now used only for comic or literary effect.
examples: "The lady doth protest too much, methinks." (Hamlet — the line is Gertrude's, and it is regularly misquoted as methinks the lady doth protest too much)
Methinks someone has been reading the minutes rather closely.
Methinks not, sir.
This, methinks, is the third excuse we have heard this week.
Methought I heard the gate latch at midnight.
Methinks the committee has already decided and is merely being polite.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on the verb; the me is unstressed /mi/ and never reduces to /mɪ/ the way an ordinary object me can
entries.русский: мне думается, сдаётся мне — устар.; в совр. языке только шутливо-иронически
entries.case: object (the me is an old dative, not a subject)
entries.register: archaic; in living American English, purely jocular or ironic
entries.type: frozen impersonal construction — an object pronoun plus a fixed verb, functioning as a whole parenthetical
entries.person / number: first person singular, frozen. There is no ✗theethinks, ✗usthinks, or ✗himthinks; the only inflected relative is the past tense methought.
entries.refers to: the speaker, as the person to whom something seems the case. What follows is a whole clause — the thing that seems true.
entries.agreement: the verb is permanently third-person singular thinks, agreeing with an unexpressed impersonal "it," not with me. ✗Methink is impossible. The construction takes no auxiliary and cannot be negated internally: not ✗me doesn't think, but methinks not.
entries.pattern: methinks [clause] (methinks he protests too much) · [clause], methinks (parenthetical, at the end) · methinks not · past: methought [clause]
entries.contrast: methinks is not a compressed I think. The verb inside it descends from Old English þyncan "to seem," a different word from þencan "to think," so the literal sense is "it seems to me" — and the me is the object of that seeming, which is why the pronoun is me and not I (✗Ithinks). The same dative survives in woe is me and in if it please you. Related frozen forms: methought (past), meseems (rarer and fully dead), mehearty (not related — that is me for my in stage-pirate speech). Every modern use is a costume: a writer reaching for mock-Elizabethan tone, usually attached to the misquotation below.
entries.see also: oneself, thou, me (nonstandard as subject), me, it (weather, time, and distance)

entries.meaning: The reflexive of the generic pronoun one: any person at all, when that person is both subject and object of the same clause.
examples: One should never send an angry email without giving oneself a night to think it over.
It is difficult to see oneself as others do.
One can easily talk oneself into a bad decision.
Living by oneself is not the same as being lonely.
One does oneself no favors by arguing with the referee.
To dress well is to present oneself honestly, not expensively.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on self; the one does not reduce
entries.русский: себя, сам — обобщённо-возвратное к one; книжн., но вполне литературное
entries.register: formal but fully standard — one of the handful of entries in this file a careful writer can put in edited prose without hedging (the others being whereby, which is ordinary formal English, the modern postposed whatsoever, the quantifier you all, and, inside legal drafting, herein, thereof, and their relatives)
entries.type: reflexive and intensive pronoun
entries.person / number: generic third person, singular, gender-neutral. It has no plural: the generic one has no plural of its own.
entries.refers to: the generic person — anyone at all, people in general — and only when that generic one is already the subject of the same clause. It cannot refer to a specific named person; for that you need himself, herself, or themselves.
entries.agreement: no agreement of its own. The clause's verb agrees with generic one, which is singular: one does oneself no favors, one finds oneself wondering — never ✗one do.
entries.pattern: one [verb] oneself · [preposition] oneself (by oneself, to oneself, for oneself) · to [verb] oneself in an infinitive with generic reference (to see oneself as others do) · intensive: one must do it oneself
entries.contrast: the rule is consistency: once a sentence starts with generic one, it stays with one, one's, and oneself — One should watch one's step, not the mixed ✗One should watch your step. Older American style permitted One should watch his step, and you will meet it in mid-century prose, but it now reads as both dated and needlessly gendered; the modern American solution is usually to abandon one altogether and write you (You should watch your step), which is why oneself sounds formal. Spelled as two words, one's self means something different — the self as a thing, in psychological or philosophical writing (the discovery of one's self). And do not use oneself for a specific person: ✗Karen finished the report oneself → herself.
entries.see also: thyself, ourself, hisself, oneself (reflexive), one (generic), one's

entries.meaning: Someone or something of that kind. The archaic pronoun phrase that modern English replaces with someone like that.
examples: "I knew a man in Christ… such an one caught up to the third heaven." (2 Corinthians 12:2, King James Version)
"Restore such an one in the spirit of meekness." (Galatians 6:1)
Such a one is not to be trusted with money, whatever his references say.
He wanted a horse, and such a one as would carry him forty miles before noon.
If any man be idle, let such a one be set to work or sent away.
She had never met such a one before, and never met his like again.
Modern English: Someone like that is not to be trusted with money.
entries.pronunciation note: the article reduces to /ə/ and the main stress lands on one; at speed the whole phrase runs to /sʌtʃəˈwʌn/
entries.русский: такой человек, таковой — устар., книжн. «человек подобного рода»
entries.variants: such an one, the older spelling, standard in the King James Bible and in prose down to about 1800 — see the contrast below, where the an turns out not to be an error
entries.case: none — the same form serves as subject and object
entries.register: archaic and literary; survives in formal, sermonic, and legal English, and in the fixed such a one as
entries.type: anaphoric indefinite pronoun phrase, archaic and formal
entries.person / number: third person singular. The plural is such ones or, far more idiomatically, plain such (such are the risks).
entries.refers to: a person or thing of the kind just described — the reference is backward, to a description already on the page, and the phrase substitutes for the whole of it. Most often human (such a one is not to be trusted), but things qualify too (a knife, and such a one as would frighten a butcher).
entries.agreement: singular verb: such a one is rare, such a one was found, ✗such a one are. When it heads a comparison the verb belongs to the following clause instead (such a one as has never been seen).
entries.pattern: such a one [singular verb] · [verb] such a one (object) · such a one as [clause] (the fixed comparative: such a one as I had never met) · no such a one · some such a one
entries.contrast: modern English says someone like that, anyone of that kind, or simply such: such are the risks, no such thing. Two points repay attention. The archaic spelling such an one is not an error and not a typo: one was once pronounced without the /w/ that begins it today, so it took an the way an hour still does, and the King James translators wrote restore such an one in the spirit of meekness (Galatians 6:1) on ordinary phonetic grounds. And note where the dictionary line falls — such a standing in front of a noun (such a fool, such an idea) is a determiner, covered in the determiner dictionary; the entry you are reading is the phrase standing alone with one as its head, which makes it a pronoun.
entries.see also: a body, the same, such, such, one, ones, such a, such an

entries.meaning: The person or thing already named in this document. The legal anaphors that stand where an ordinary writer would put it, they, or the noun again.
examples: The aforesaid shall appear before the magistrate on the first Tuesday of the month.
The buyer agrees to indemnify the aforementioned against any claim arising from the sale.
Rent, utilities, and insurance: the aforesaid are payable on the first of each month.
Nothing in this section limits the obligations of the aforementioned under Article IV.
The aforesaid having been duly notified, the hearing proceeded in his absence.
Plain-language rewrite: The tenant must appear before the magistrate; the buyer will indemnify the seller.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is /ði/ before both, since both begin with a vowel; aforementioned also has a first-syllable-stressed variant /əˈfɔrˌmɛnʃənd/ · uh-FOR-men-shund
entries.русский: вышеупомянутый, вышеназванный — юр., канц.; отсылка к уже названному
entries.case: none — the same form serves as subject and object
entries.register: legal, official, and bureaucratic; outside those documents they read as parody, and plain-language drafting deletes them
entries.type: anaphoric pronoun phrases of legal and bureaucratic style — the plus a participle, standing in for a full noun phrase
entries.person / number: third person; singular or plural according to what has been named (the aforesaid is liable, the aforesaid are jointly liable).
entries.refers to: whatever was named earlier in the same document — a person, a company, a vehicle, a parcel, a sum, a date. Unlike the same, these can and routinely do refer to people (the aforesaid shall appear at the hearing), which is the one job they do that same cannot do without sounding grotesque.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the referent, never with the phrase: the aforesaid (Mr. Alvarez) is hereby notified; the aforementioned (the three tenants) are in default.
entries.pattern: the aforesaid [verb] (as subject) · [verb] the aforesaid (as object) · [preposition] the aforementioned (with respect to the aforementioned) · all of the aforesaid · the aforesaid, together with [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: the everyday equivalents are it, they, that, and those — and in a well-drafted document, the repeated noun (the Tenant, the Vehicle), which is what a modern drafting manual will tell you to write. Keep the standalone pronoun apart from the determiner: the aforesaid vehicle and the aforementioned tenants put a noun after the word, and those are determiner entries, covered as aforesaid and aforementioned alongside said. The two words are near-perfect synonyms; aforesaid is the older and more purely legal of them, aforementioned the one that leaks into ordinary officialese. And distinguish them from the foregoing, which points at a passage of text rather than at a thing the text named.
entries.see also: the same, the foregoing, the premises, the undersigned, herein, thereof, aforesaid, aforementioned, said

entries.meaning: Everything said above. The formal pro-form that gathers up a stretch of preceding text and refers to it as one thing.
examples: Notwithstanding the foregoing, the Landlord may enter the premises without notice in an emergency.
The foregoing is a summary only and does not modify the terms of the policy.
Subject to the foregoing, the parties agree to bear their own costs.
The foregoing are the only exceptions the committee is prepared to allow.
In view of the foregoing, the court denies the motion.
Plain-English rewrite: Even so, the landlord may enter without notice in an emergency.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on go; a first-syllable-stressed /ˈfɔrˌɡoʊɪŋ/ · FOR-go-ing is also heard, and the article reduces to /ðə/
entries.русский: вышеизложенное, вышесказанное — книжн., юр.; отсылка к предыдущему тексту
entries.case: none — the same form serves as subject and object
entries.register: formal, legal, and academic; standard within those registers and stiff outside them
entries.type: anaphoric pronoun phrase of formal and legal style — the plus a participle, standing in for a stretch of text
entries.person / number: third person; singular or plural depending on what it gathers up — one clause or a list of twelve.
entries.refers to: the text immediately above — the preceding sentence, paragraph, list, or section, taken as a lump. This is what separates it from every other entry in this group: it points at words on the page rather than at a thing those words named. It cannot point forward (for that, the following), and it cannot point outside the document.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with what the phrase covers: the foregoing is a summary (one passage), the foregoing are the only exceptions (a list of them). Both are correct, and the choice is a matter of what you mean.
entries.pattern: notwithstanding the foregoing (by far the commonest, and a full sentence-opener in contracts) · the foregoing [verb] · subject to the foregoing · in view of the foregoing · all of the foregoing · the foregoing shall not apply to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Notwithstanding the foregoing is the phrase to learn, because it does real work: it announces that the sentence about to be written overrides everything just said, and in a contract that reversal can be the most important thing on the page. The everyday equivalents are the above, this, and all of that — and in American editing, the above is perfectly respectable while the foregoing is a register choice, not an error. Its opposite is the following, which points down the page. Keep it apart from the aforesaid, which points at a thing already named rather than at the naming; from the premises, which is the legal noun for the recitals of an instrument; and from the verb forgo ("to do without"), spelled without the e and unrelated.
entries.see also: the aforesaid, the aforementioned, the premises, the same, herein, hereinbefore, heretofore, this, that

entries.meaning: The matters aforesaid; the things already set out. The legal pronoun that turned into the ordinary word for a building.
examples: Now therefore, in consideration of the premises and of the mutual covenants set forth herein, the parties agree as follows. (the standard recital)
The premises considered, the court finds for the plaintiff.
The affiant states that the premises set out above are true to the best of his knowledge.
Upon the premises aforesaid, the petitioner prays for relief.
The modern sense, and the only one most Americans use: the tenant agreed to vacate the premises by the first of the month.
Also modern: there is no smoking anywhere on the premises.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on the first syllable; the singular premise /ˈprɛmɪs/ belongs to logic and to storytelling, and the legal word is plural only
entries.русский: вышеизложенное — устар., юр. «упомянутые обстоятельства»; отсюда совр. «помещение»
entries.register: legal and archaic; frozen in a handful of drafting formulas, and the source of the ordinary modern word for a building
entries.type: anaphoric pronoun phrase, legal and archaic — the premises meaning "the matters aforesaid"
