entries.person / number: third person plural, invariant. There is no singular in this sense.
entries.refers to: the matters already set out in the same instrument — the recitals, the facts stated, the things previously described. It refers to statements, not to people. In a deed it originally covered the opening portion that described the property, which is exactly how the word came to mean the property itself.
entries.agreement: plural verb when it is the subject: the premises are true and correct, the premises being considered. ✗The premises is is wrong in either sense of the word — the building sense is plural too (the premises are closed).
entries.pattern: in consideration of the premises (the old recital formula) · the premises considered / the premises being considered · upon the premises aforesaid · may it please the court, upon the premises · the modern survival: the premises = a building or grounds (vacate the premises, no smoking on the premises)
entries.contrast: this is the entry where an ordinary American word turns out to be a fossil pronoun. A deed's opening section — the part that recited the parties, the consideration, and the description of the land — was called the premises, "the things set out before"; lawyers then used the premises to point back at all of it, and finally the phrase slid from the description onto the thing described, which is why the premises now means a building. All three senses are alive: the pronominal one (in consideration of the premises, archaic and formulaic), the property one (vacate the premises, ordinary modern English), and the logic one (the premises of the argument, where a single premise is a proposition an argument starts from). Only the first is a pronoun. Do not confuse the legal plural with the logical plural, and note that both are plural: the premises are, never ✗the premises is.
entries.see also: the foregoing, the aforesaid, the aforementioned, the same, herein, thereof, the within

entries.meaning: It; them. The referring pronoun of legal and commercial boilerplate, standing for whatever was last named.
examples: Please sign the enclosed agreement and return same to our office by Friday.
The invoice was received on the third, and payment for same was issued the following week.
The vehicle was recovered, and same was released to its registered owner.
Any deposit shall be held in escrow until the closing, at which time the same shall be applied to the purchase price.
We acknowledge receipt of your letter and will respond to same in due course.
The tenant shall keep the premises in good repair and shall surrender the same at the end of the term.
entries.pronunciation note: the article reduces to /ðə/; bare same /seɪm/ in the legal idiom
entries.русский: оное, таковое — юр. и дел.; отсылка к уже названному (sign and return same)
entries.case: none — the same form serves as subject and object
entries.register: legal, commercial, and bureaucratic; widely criticized as jargon
entries.type: anaphoric pronoun of legal and commercial style
entries.variants: bare same, with no article — the form that actually turns up in invoices and police reports (please sign and return same, payment for same). It is the same pronoun; dropping the is what marks the register as commercial rather than merely formal
entries.person / number: third person; singular or plural depending entirely on what it stands for.
entries.refers to: a noun phrase already named in the document — goods, a sum, a vehicle, a document, a right. Things and abstractions, not people (✗we interviewed the witness and dismissed same is grotesque even by the standards of the register).
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the referent, not with the word same: the goods were delivered and same were inspected on arrival; the payment was late and same was returned.
entries.pattern: [verb] same (please sign and return same) · [preposition] same (payment for same) · the same as subject (the same shall be forfeited) · the same being [complement] (the same being due and payable on the first)
entries.contrast: ordinary English uses it or them here, and any editor outside a law office will change same to one of those: please sign and return it. The pronominal same is a genuine survival, not an error — it is standard inside contracts, invoices, insurance claims, and police reports — but it is exactly the kind of writing that plain-language statutes were passed to stamp out. Keep it apart from ordinary the same meaning "identical" (we ordered the same), which is everyday English and takes a following as (the same as yours). And keep it apart from the determiner said (said vehicle, said defendant), which does the same anaphoric job in front of a noun instead of standing alone.
entries.see also: thereof, herein, the same (demonstrative), said, selfsame

entries.meaning: I; we — the writer, referred to in the third person as the person who signs below.
examples: The undersigned hereby certifies that the foregoing statement is true and correct.
The undersigned, being duly sworn, deposes and says that he is over eighteen years of age. (the affidavit formula)
The undersigned have reviewed the audit and accept its findings. (several signers, plural verb)
Please direct any further correspondence to the undersigned at the address above.
The undersigned respectfully requests an extension of thirty days.
Plain-language rewrite: I certify that the statement above is true; please write to me at the address above.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is /ði/ before the vowel of un-; the main stress falls on signed, and the whole phrase has no reduced form because it appears in writing far more often than in speech
entries.русский: нижеподписавшийся — юр., офиц.; автор документа о самом себе
entries.case: none — the same form serves as subject and object
entries.register: legal, official, and military; standard in affidavits, certifications, and formal letters, and pompous anywhere else
entries.type: anaphoric pronoun phrase, legal and official — the plus a participle, used by writers to refer to themselves
entries.person / number: grammatically third person, but referentially first — it means I or we. Singular or plural according to how many people sign (the undersigned certifies / the undersigned parties agree).
entries.refers to: the person or persons who have signed, or are about to sign, the document in which the phrase appears — that is, the writer. It is self-reference in the third person, and it is the only entry in this file that lets a writer avoid saying I while still meaning it.
entries.agreement: the verb follows the number of the signers, and the document has to tell you which: the undersigned hereby certifies that… (one signer), the undersigned have reviewed the report (several). Getting this wrong is the standard slip in form letters that were drafted for one signature and then signed by three.
entries.pattern: the undersigned hereby [verb] (hereby certifies, hereby acknowledges, hereby resigns) · the undersigned, being duly sworn, deposes and says (the affidavit formula) · the undersigned [verb] (as subject) · [preposition] the undersigned (to the undersigned, by the undersigned)
entries.contrast: the word it replaces is I — or we — and in almost all present-day American writing that is what to put. The undersigned hereby certifies is I certify, three words shorter and no less binding; federal plain-language guidance says so outright, and no court has ever held that a signature meant less because the signer wrote I. Two related forms are worth knowing: the below-signed (rarer, and the same thing), and the older your obedient servant, which did the same self-effacing job in letters. Distinguish it from the aforesaid, which points at somebody else already named, and from the same, which points at a thing.
entries.see also: the aforesaid, the aforementioned, the same, the foregoing, hereby, hereunto, herein, I, we

entries.meaning: At this; at this point. The occasion-marking member of the here- family, and the rarest of them.
examples: Hereat the whole company fell silent, and the fiddler put down his bow.
She named her price, and hereat the buyer rose and left the room without another word.
The bill was read a second time; hereat the Speaker adjourned the House until Tuesday.
He confessed the whole business, and hereat his lawyer asked the court for a recess.
Hereat I must beg the reader's patience for a short digression. (the essayist's aside)
Modern English: At this, the whole room fell silent.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on at, which keeps its full /æ/; the here- never takes the beat, and there is no weak form — the whole family is read rather than spoken
entries.русский: при сём, тут же — устар.; «в ответ на это, вслед за этим» (о только что сказанном)
entries.case: object (governed by the fused preposition at)
entries.register: archaic and literary in the narrative sense, formal-legal in the drafting sense; the rarest member of the here- family and the one a drafter is least likely to have seen
entries.type: pronominal adverb — at + this, where "this" is the thing just said or done, taken as the occasion of what follows
entries.person / number: third person, invariant. No plural, no possessive.
entries.refers to: the statement or event immediately preceding — what has just been said, read, or done — treated as the point at which the next thing happens. It points at an event or an utterance, not at a person and not at a physical place.
entries.agreement: none of its own; it is adverbial, and the clause it opens takes its own subject and verb (hereat the company fell silent).
entries.pattern: hereat [subject] [verb] (the narrative opener: hereat the fiddler stopped) · [clause], and hereat [clause] · hereat [subject] must [verb] (the essayist's aside: hereat I must beg the reader's patience)
entries.contrast: the family splits by deixis and hereat is the this member: hereat is "at this," thereat is "at that," and whereat is "at which," the only one of the three with any real life left in it. Against hereupon — which English barely built at all, preferring whereupon and thereupon — the difference is that upon carries a sense of immediate sequence and at carries only occasion. Against hereby, the difference is the whole distinction that organizes this section: hereby performs the act the sentence names, while hereat merely says when something happened. Modern American English writes at this, at this point, or at that, and there is no reason to write anything else.
entries.see also: thereat, whereat, hereby, herein, thereupon, whereupon

entries.meaning: By this act; by these words. The performative member of the here- family — it does not point at anything, it does the thing.
examples: I hereby resign my position on the board, effective at the close of business Friday.
You are hereby notified that the lease will not be renewed.
The Company hereby grants the Employee an option to purchase one thousand shares.
The parties hereby agree to submit any dispute to binding arbitration.
The motion is hereby denied, and the hearing is adjourned.
Not performative, and therefore impossible: ✗ I hereby believe the report is finished.
Plain-language rewrite: I resign from the board effective Friday.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on by, which keeps its full diphthong; the here- never takes the beat
entries.русский: настоящим — юр., офиц.; «этим самым документом или действием»
entries.case: object (governed by the fused preposition by)
entries.register: legal, official, and ceremonial; standard within those registers
entries.type: pronominal adverb — by + this, where "this" is the present document or utterance taken as an act; performative rather than referential
entries.person / number: third person, invariant. No plural, no possessive.
entries.refers to: the very sentence it stands in, understood as the deed that sentence performs — I hereby resign means "by these words, I resign." It is the only member of the here- family that points at the speech act rather than at a text.
entries.agreement: none of its own; it is adverbial and the clause's own subject controls the verb (the Company hereby grants — singular; the parties hereby agree — plural).
entries.pattern: [subject] hereby [performative verb] (hereby certify, hereby resign, hereby grant, hereby declare) · [subject] is hereby [past participle] (you are hereby notified, the motion is hereby denied) · I hereby swear / affirm
entries.contrast: the family splits three ways and hereby is the odd member. Whereby is by which and takes an antecedent; thereby is by that means and points back at something already done; hereby points at nothing — it announces that the sentence you are reading is itself the act. That is why it only attaches to performative verbs, the ones a person can do by saying them: resign, certify, grant, declare, notify, appoint, agree, waive. Bolt it to any other verb and the sentence collapses (✗I hereby believe the report, ✗I hereby went to the meeting). It is also the one member you can almost always delete without changing the legal effect — I resign ends the job just as surely — which is why plain-language drafting cuts it, and why hereby survives mostly as a signal of formality. Do not confuse it with hereby in the sense "near here," which is not English; that is hereabouts.
entries.see also: herein, hereof, hereto, hereunto, thereby, whereby, the undersigned

entries.meaning: In this document; in this agreement. The self-referential pro-form of legal drafting.
examples: The terms defined herein apply to every schedule and exhibit.
Nothing herein shall be construed as a waiver of either party's rights.
Except as otherwise provided herein, notice must be given in writing.
The parties agree to the covenants contained herein.
The rates set forth herein are effective as of January 1.
Capitalized terms not defined herein have the meanings given in the Master Agreement.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on in
entries.русский: в настоящем документе — юр.; «здесь, в этом тексте», не вне его
entries.case: object (the pronoun element is governed by the fused preposition in)
entries.register: legal and formal; standard within that register
entries.type: pronominal adverb — in + this, a pro-form for "in this document"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant. No plural, no possessive.
entries.refers to: the present document or the present passage of it — the contract, the statute, the policy, the letter in which the word appears. It is self-referential: it never points at anything outside the text.
entries.agreement: none — it is adverbial and takes no verb of its own.
entries.pattern: [noun] defined herein · set forth herein · contained herein · except as otherwise provided herein · nothing herein shall [verb]
entries.contrast: herein is "in this document"; therein is "in that thing just mentioned." Swapping them is the standard drafting error: the Premises and all fixtures therein means inside the premises, while all fixtures herein would absurdly mean fixtures inside the lease. Also distinguish herein from hereinafter ("later in this document," as in hereinafter referred to as the Buyer) and from hereby, which performs an act rather than pointing anywhere (I hereby resign).
entries.see also: hereof, hereto, therein, wherein, the same

entries.meaning: Later in this document; below. The forward-pointing member of the here- family.
examples: Acme Industries, Inc., hereinafter referred to as the Seller, warrants clear title to the goods.
The rates set out hereinafter supersede those in the previous schedule.
Except as hereinafter provided, no notice is required.
The property, hereinafter called the Premises, is described in Exhibit A.
This obligation is subject to the exceptions hereinafter enumerated in Section 12.
Modern drafting: Acme Industries, Inc. (the "Seller") warrants clear title.
entries.pronunciation note: four syllables, stress on af; the older /ˌhɪrɪnˈɑftɚ/ turns up in British-influenced drafting
entries.русский: далее по тексту, в дальнейшем — юр.; «ниже в настоящем документе»
entries.register: legal and formal; standard within legal drafting and out of place anywhere else
entries.type: pronominal adverb — after + herein, a pro-form for "later in this document"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: the remainder of the present document — the text that follows the point where the word appears. It points at text, never at time, and never outside the document.
entries.agreement: none of its own.
entries.pattern: hereinafter referred to as [defined term] · hereinafter called [name] · (hereinafter, the "Buyer") · as hereinafter provided · the terms hereinafter set forth
entries.contrast: the trap here is one letter of difference in meaning and a lawsuit's worth of difference in effect: hereinafter means "later in this document," while hereafter means "after now, from this time forward." A will that says the trustee shall hereafter distribute the income is talking about the future; one that says hereinafter is pointing at a later clause. Its mirror is hereinbefore ("earlier in this document"), and its time-facing mirror is heretofore ("until now"). The single commonest use is the defined-term parenthesis — Acme Industries, Inc. (hereinafter "Acme") — which modern drafting shortens to (the "Buyer") or just ("Acme"), since the word adds nothing a reader could misunderstand.
entries.see also: herein, hereinbefore, heretofore, hereof, the foregoing

entries.meaning: Earlier in this document; above. The backward-pointing member of the here- family.
examples: Except as hereinbefore provided, all notices must be sent by certified mail.
The party hereinbefore named as Trustee shall serve without bond.
The capitalized terms used in this Article have the meanings hereinabove assigned to them.
The property hereinabove described is conveyed subject to the easement of record.
Nothing hereinbefore stated limits the Buyer's remedies at law.
Plain-language rewrite: Except as stated above, all notices must be sent by certified mail.
entries.pronunciation note: four syllables, stress on for
entries.русский: выше по тексту — юр.; «ранее в настоящем документе» (вариант hereinabove)
entries.variants: hereinabove /ˌhɪrɪnəˈbʌv/ · heer-in-uh-BUV, the same word with above in place of before, and the commoner of the two in American drafting; hereinbefore is older and slightly more British
entries.register: legal and formal
entries.type: pronominal adverb — before + herein, a pro-form for "earlier in this document"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: the part of the present document that comes before the point where the word appears — a definition, a recital, a numbered section already passed.
entries.agreement: none of its own.
entries.pattern: as hereinbefore provided · the term hereinbefore defined · the party hereinbefore named · except as hereinabove set forth · hereinabove described
entries.contrast: the four-way grid is worth memorizing, because two of the four are about text and two are about time: hereinafter = later in this document; hereinbefore / hereinabove = earlier in this document; hereafter = after now; heretofore = before now. Drafters slip between the pairs constantly, and in an instrument the slip is substantive. Against the foregoing, the difference is grammatical rather than semantic: the foregoing is a noun phrase that can be the subject of a sentence (the foregoing is a summary), while hereinbefore is an adverb that can only modify (as hereinbefore stated). Plain-language drafting replaces both with above — as stated above, the term defined above — which no reader has ever misunderstood.
entries.see also: hereinafter, heretofore, herein, the foregoing, hereof

entries.meaning: Later in this document; below. The younger twin of hereinafter, built to match hereinabove.
examples: Except as hereinbelow provided, the Tenant shall pay all utilities charged to the premises.
The parcels hereinbelow described are conveyed subject to the easement of record.
The schedule of payments is set out hereinbelow in Section 9.
Nothing hereinabove or hereinbelow limits the Buyer's remedies at law. (the matched pair, which is why the word exists)
The warranties hereinbelow stated are the only warranties the Seller gives.
Plain-language rewrite: Except as stated below, the tenant pays all utilities.
entries.pronunciation note: four syllables, stress on low; the middle two syllables reduce to /ɪn/ and /bɪ/ and carry no beat at all
entries.русский: ниже по тексту — юр., амер. драфтинг; «далее в настоящем документе»
entries.register: legal; American drafting almost exclusively, and a comparative newcomer, built on the pattern of hereinabove because drafters like matched pairs
entries.type: pronominal adverb — below + herein, a pro-form for "later in this document"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: the part of the present document that comes after the point where the word appears — a schedule, an exhibit, a numbered section further down. It points at text, never at time, and never at anything outside the instrument.
entries.agreement: none of its own.
entries.pattern: as hereinbelow provided · except as hereinbelow set forth · the terms hereinbelow defined · hereinbelow described · the schedule hereinbelow
entries.contrast: it means exactly what hereinafter means, and hereinafter is older, commoner, and the safer choice in any document that will be read by a court. Hereinbelow exists because hereinbefore has the variant hereinabove, and once a drafter has written hereinabove the pull toward a matching hereinbelow is hard to resist. Fit it into the four-way grid that organizes this family, two members about text and two about time: hereinafter and hereinbelow = later in this document; hereinbefore and hereinabove = earlier in this document; hereafter = after now; heretofore = before now. Its there- counterpart, pointing at some other document, is thereinafter. Plain-language drafting replaces all of them with below and above.
entries.see also: hereinafter, hereinbefore, herein, heretofore, thereinafter, thereinbefore, the foregoing

entries.meaning: Of this document; of this agreement.
examples: All representations are true and correct as of the date hereof.
Section 9 hereof governs the resolution of disputes.
The obligations described in Article III hereof survive termination.
This exhibit forms an integral part hereof.
The schedule attached to and made a part hereof lists every covered device.
The term hereof begins on the first day of the month following execution.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on of, which keeps its full /ʌv/ rather than reducing to /əv/
entries.русский: настоящего документа — юр., род. п.: Section 5 hereof, the date hereof
entries.register: legal and formal
entries.type: pronominal adverb — of + this, a pro-form for "of this document"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: the present document, or a numbered part of it. Almost always used to cross-reference a section or to date the instrument itself.
entries.agreement: none.
entries.pattern: Section [number] hereof · the date hereof · as of the date hereof · Article [number] hereof
entries.contrast: hereof points at this document, thereof at the thing just named: Section 4 hereof is a section of this contract, while the term thereof is the term of whatever was last mentioned. The commonest live phrase is the date hereof, meaning the date of this agreement — which is not the same as the date thereof, the date of some other document already named. Modern plain-language drafting replaces both with a repeated noun: the date of this Agreement.
entries.see also: herein, hereto, thereof, whereof

entries.meaning: To this document; to this agreement.
examples: The parties hereto agree to submit any dispute to binding arbitration.
A copy of the policy is attached hereto as Exhibit B.
The signatories hereto warrant that they are authorized to sign.
The schedules annexed hereto are incorporated by reference.
Neither party hereto may assign its rights without written consent.
The floor plan attached hereto controls in the event of any inconsistency.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on to
entries.русский: к настоящему документу — юр.; the parties hereto «стороны настоящего договора»
entries.register: legal and formal
entries.type: pronominal adverb — to + this, a pro-form for "to this document"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: the present document, most often in naming its signatories or its attachments.
entries.agreement: none of its own; when it modifies a subject, that subject controls the verb — the parties hereto agree (plural parties), the exhibit attached hereto is incorporated (singular exhibit).
entries.pattern: the parties hereto · attached hereto as Exhibit [letter] · annexed hereto · the signatories hereto
entries.contrast: hereto attaches things to this document; thereto attaches them to something already named — the lease and all amendments thereto. The single most common phrase in American contract drafting, the parties hereto, means simply "the parties to this agreement," and plain-language drafters delete hereto as adding nothing. Do not confuse it with the adverb heretofore, which means "until now" and points at time rather than at the document.
entries.see also: herein, hereof, thereto, the same

entries.meaning: Until now; up to this time. The time-pointing member of the here- family, and the one an ordinary writer can still use.
examples: The parties have heretofore operated without a written agreement.
The dig turned up a burial practice heretofore unknown in the region.
Nothing in this policy affects any claim heretofore filed and accepted.
Heretofore the committee has met twice a year; beginning in January it will meet quarterly.
The manuscript contains three letters heretofore unpublished.
Plain English: Until now, the parties have worked without a written agreement.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on for; also /ˌhɪrtuˈfɔr/ with the middle syllable unreduced in careful reading
entries.русский: до сих пор, ранее — книжн., юр.; о времени до настоящего момента
entries.register: formal and legal; the least jargon-ish member of the family, and usable in ordinary formal prose
entries.type: pronominal adverb of time — before + this, where "this" is the present moment rather than the present document
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: all the time up to now. Unlike every other here- form, it points at a period, not at a text, which is why it is at home in a history book as well as in a contract.
entries.agreement: none of its own; it sits happily with a perfect tense, which is the tense its meaning implies (the parties have heretofore operated without a written agreement).
entries.pattern: [subject] has/have heretofore [past participle] · heretofore unknown / unavailable / unpublished (before an adjective) · as heretofore · the practice heretofore followed
entries.contrast: heretofore is "until now"; hereinbefore is "earlier in this document." The pair is easy to keep straight once you see that -tofore contains before in its temporal sense while -inbefore contains herein, the document. Its forward mate is hereafter ("from now on"), not hereinafter. The everyday equivalents are until now, up to now, and previously, and unlike most of this family heretofore survives in respectable non-legal prose — a species heretofore unknown to science is the kind of sentence a magazine will still print. Do not stretch it to mean "therefore"; the two are unrelated, and ✗heretofore, the motion is denied is a malapropism.
entries.see also: hereinbefore, hereinafter, herein, the foregoing, thereupon

entries.meaning: Under this agreement; under this instrument.
examples: The Contractor's obligations hereunder survive the termination of this Agreement.
Any amount due hereunder and not paid within thirty days bears interest at nine percent.
Notices given hereunder must be in writing and sent to the addresses in Section 14.
A failure to perform hereunder is not excused by a shortage of labor.
Nothing hereunder requires either party to violate applicable law.
Plain-language rewrite: The Contractor's obligations under this Agreement survive termination.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on un
entries.русский: по настоящему договору — юр.; «в силу этого документа»; также «ниже по тексту»
entries.register: legal and formal; one of the workhorses of American contract drafting
entries.type: pronominal adverb — under + this, a pro-form for "under this agreement"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: the present agreement, statute, or instrument, treated as the authority that creates a right or duty — rights hereunder are the rights this contract gives you. A secondary and rarer sense points at position on the page ("below," as in the schedule set out hereunder), which American drafters usually write as below instead.
entries.agreement: none of its own; the noun it modifies keeps its own agreement (the obligations hereunder are several, any payment due hereunder is payable in dollars).
entries.pattern: rights and obligations hereunder · any amount due hereunder · performance hereunder · a default hereunder · notices given hereunder · nothing hereunder shall [verb]
entries.contrast: hereunder means "under this instrument"; thereunder means "under that one," the agreement or statute just named. In a document that incorporates another one by reference — a master agreement with work orders under it — the difference decides which contract a right comes from, and swapping them is a real drafting error rather than a stylistic one. Distinguish it also from hereto ("to this document," used of parties and attachments) and from thereunder in its physical sense (the deck and the crawlspace thereunder), which is ordinary spatial English. The plain rewrite is under this Agreement, which costs two words and removes all doubt.
entries.see also: herein, hereof, hereto, thereunder, thereof

entries.meaning: To this document; to this instrument. The ceremonial twin of hereto, alive inside one formula.
examples: In witness whereof, the parties have hereunto set their hands and seals the day and year first above written.
I have hereunto subscribed my name and affixed the seal of the Court.
The exhibits hereunto annexed form part of this deed.
The plan hereunto attached shows the boundary as agreed by the surveyors.
In testimony whereof, the Secretary of State has hereunto caused the Great Seal to be affixed.
Ordinary modern drafting: the parties have signed this Agreement as of the date first written above.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on to; the middle syllable is full /ʌn/, not reduced, because the word survives only in a formula that is read slowly
entries.русский: к сему — устар., юр.; в формуле подписания hereunto set my hand
entries.register: archaic and legal; effectively confined to the attestation clause at the foot of a signed instrument
entries.type: pronominal adverb — unto + this, a ceremonial pro-form for "to this document"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: the document being signed, as the thing a signature is applied to.
entries.agreement: none of its own; the subject of the attestation clause controls the verb (the parties have hereunto set their hands).
entries.pattern: IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the parties have hereunto set their hands and seals (the whole living use of the word) · hereunto affixed · hereunto annexed · the schedule hereunto attached
entries.contrast: hereto is the living form and does all the ordinary work — the parties hereto, attached hereto as Exhibit B. Hereunto is the same meaning in ceremonial dress, built on unto rather than to, and it appears in modern American documents almost exclusively inside the closing formula that pairs it with whereof: In witness whereof, the parties have hereunto set their hands. Outside that sentence it is dead, and writing attached hereunto instead of attached hereto marks a drafter as reaching for an antique. Note that hereunto is not hereunder: unto is direction, under is authority.
entries.see also: hereto, hereunder, whereof, hereby, thereunto, the undersigned

entries.meaning: With this letter; with this document.
examples: Enclosed herewith is the executed counterpart of the lease.
We submit herewith the annual report of the trustees for the year ended June 30.
Transmitted herewith are the six exhibits identified in our letter of the fourth.
Please find herewith a check in the amount of four hundred dollars.
Herewith the draft you asked for; I have marked the two clauses that still worry me.
Plain English: I've attached the signed lease — and never ✗enclosed herewith please find.
entries.pronunciation note: also /hɪrˈwɪð/ with the voiced th, exactly as ordinary with varies; stress on with
entries.русский: при сём, настоящим направляется — офиц., дел.; «вместе с этим письмом»
entries.register: formal, commercial, and legal; the most letter-flavored member of the family and the one most often criticized as padding
entries.type: pronominal adverb — with + this, a pro-form for "with this letter" or "with this document"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: the present letter, email, or filing, as the thing something is sent along with. Its natural home is a transmittal sentence — the sentence that says what is in the envelope.
entries.agreement: none of its own.
entries.pattern: enclosed herewith · transmitted herewith · we submit herewith · please find herewith · herewith the report you requested (verbless, in a cover note)
entries.contrast: herewith means "with this letter"; therewith means "with that thing already named." The reason herewith has a bad reputation is redundancy: in enclosed herewith please find, every one of the four words is doing the work of the other three, and it is the standard example in every guide to plain business writing. Enclosed is the report says it, and I've attached the report says it in an email, where nothing is "enclosed" at all. Keep the pro-form apart from the adverb herewith meaning "hereby, by this act" (I herewith resign), which is an old and now stilted alternative to hereby.
entries.see also: herein, hereto, hereby, therewith, hereunto

entries.meaning: At that; at that place. The vaguest of the there- compounds, displaced by thereon in deeds and by thereupon in narrative.
examples: The Landlord shall insure the premises and all fixtures thereat.
The mill, together with the machinery thereat, passed to the younger son.
The parcel and the improvements thereat are assessed as a single unit.
He accused her of forging the letter, and thereat she left the house. (the narrative sense)
The clerk read the verdict; thereat a shout went up in the gallery.
Modern English: at it, at that point, or simply on the property.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on at; the there- is unstressed /ðɛr/ and never reduces to the /ðɚ/ of there in there's a man here, because the compound is a written word before it is a spoken one
entries.русский: там; при этом — устар.; «в том месте» (юр.) или «после чего» (книжн. повеств.)
entries.case: object (governed by the fused preposition at)
entries.register: archaic in the narrative sense and legal in the locative one; rare in both, and rare even in drafting
entries.type: pronominal adverb — at + that, with two distinct jobs: locative ("at that place or thing," in a deed) and narrative ("at that; upon that," in older prose)
entries.person / number: third person, invariant. No plural, no possessive.
entries.refers to: in the locative sense, the place or thing most recently named — a parcel, a mill, a building; in the narrative sense, the event or statement just reported, taken as the occasion of what follows. Never a person.
entries.agreement: none of its own. In the narrative use it opens a clause whose own subject controls the verb (thereat she left the house).
entries.pattern: [noun] + thereat (the locative postmodifier: the mill and the machinery thereat) · the premises and all improvements thereat · thereat [subject] [verb] (the narrative opener: thereat he rose) · [clause]; thereat [clause]
entries.contrast: the neighbors are close and the differences are prepositional: therein is "in that," thereon "on that," thereto "to that," and thereat "at that" — vaguer than any of them, which is why drafters reach for the others and why thereat has all but disappeared from modern instruments. In the narrative sense thereupon took the word's place entirely, and thereupon is what an American actually meets. Its deictic mates are hereat ("at this") and whereat ("at which"). Modern English writes at it, at that point, or names the place again.
entries.see also: hereat, whereat, thereon, therein, thereto, thereupon

entries.meaning: Between them; through it. The patent-claim compounds, built on demand from there- and any preposition that is needed.
examples: The two plates are spaced apart, defining a channel therebetween.
The housing includes a bore extending therethrough to receive the drive shaft.
A gasket is seated therebetween to prevent leakage at the joint.
The frame carries a lens, and light passing therethrough is focused on the sensor.
The first and second rollers are journaled in the frame, with the web traveling therebetween.
The same rule on demand: a rail therealong, a bracket thereacross.
Plain English: a channel between them; a bore through it.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on the preposition in both, as everywhere in this family; therethrough keeps the voiceless th of thin in its second half and the voiced th of this in its first, which is why it is awkward to say and almost never said
entries.русский: между ними; сквозь него — юр. и патент.; «между тем» и «через то»
entries.variants: the same rule builds thereacross, therealong, therearound, thereabove, and therebeneath on demand; a drafter who needs one simply makes it
entries.register: legal and technical, and effectively confined to patent claims and older engineering specifications; outside a patent an American will never meet either word
entries.type: pronominal adverbs — between + those, through + that; a small productive set rather than two learned words
entries.person / number: third person, invariant. Therebetween requires two or more antecedents; therethrough takes one.
entries.refers to: the components named earlier in the same claim — the two plates a gap sits between, the housing a bore runs through. Things only, never people, and never a clause. In a patent claim the antecedent must be an element already recited, which is the whole reason the compound is preferred to between them: the pronoun them could point anywhere, while therebetween points at the last-recited pair.
entries.agreement: none of their own; both are adverbial and attach to a participle or a verb (a gap formed therebetween, a shaft extending therethrough).
entries.pattern: [noun] formed therebetween · the space therebetween · a bore extending therethrough · a conduit passing therethrough · [two elements recited] + participle + therebetween
entries.contrast: plain English says between them and through it, and outside patent practice that is what to write. Inside it, the compound survives for a reason worth knowing: a claim must have unambiguous antecedent basis for every reference, and therebetween is read as pointing at the elements just recited, while a bare them invites an examiner's rejection for indefiniteness. That is a drafting convention rather than a rule of grammar, and modern claim-drafting guides increasingly recommend the plain forms anyway. Note that therebetween needs a pair: ✗ a bore formed therebetween with one element recited is meaningless. Its relatives in this file are the ordinary compounds therein, thereon, and thereunder, which are built by the same rule and are simply commoner.
entries.see also: therein, thereon, thereto, thereunder, thereof, thereat, wherein

entries.meaning: By that means; as a result of that.
examples: "And thereby hangs a tale." (The Taming of the Shrew; Shakespeare uses the phrase more than once)
She filed the amended complaint within the window and thereby preserved the claim.
The statute exempts small estates from probate, thereby saving families several months.
He signed the release without reading it and thereby gave up the right to sue.
The company moved the servers offshore, thereby placing them outside the court's reach.
Compare therefore: the release was signed; therefore no suit lies. (reason, not means)
entries.pronunciation note: stress on by, which keeps its full diphthong; unlike therefore it is never stressed on the first syllable
entries.русский: тем самым, посредством этого — книжн., юр.; вполне живое в деловом языке
entries.case: object (governed by the fused preposition by)
entries.register: formal, legal, and academic — and, alongside whereby, one of the two members of this family that ordinary careful American writing still uses without irony
entries.type: pronominal adverb — by + that, a pro-form for "by that means"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: the action or means just described, not a thing — what precedes it is normally a whole clause (she paid the filing fee, thereby preserving the claim). It cannot point at a person, and it cannot point forward.
entries.agreement: none of its own.
entries.pattern: [clause], thereby [present participle] (thereby avoiding the penalty) · [subject] thereby [verb] · and thereby [verb] · thereby hangs a tale (frozen)
entries.contrast: the pair to keep straight is thereby against therefore. Thereby is by that means — it names the mechanism (he signed the waiver, thereby giving up the appeal). Therefore is for that reason — it names the consequence (the waiver was signed; therefore no appeal lies). Substitute the long forms to test which you want. Against the rest of its family, thereby points back at an act, hereby performs one, and whereby introduces a relative clause about a means. One caution of style: because thereby so often attaches to a participle, it collects dangling modifiers — the fee was paid, thereby preserving the claim leaves the participle with nothing to hang on, and a careful writer recasts it as paying the fee preserved the claim. Finally, the fixed thereby hangs a tale, Shakespeare's phrase, means "there is a story attached to that," and is the only place most Americans use the word in speech.
entries.see also: whereby, hereby, thereof, therewith, thereupon

entries.meaning: For it; for that; in exchange for that.
examples: The Seller shall deliver the goods, and the Buyer shall pay the price therefor within thirty days.
The application must be filed with the fee therefor in the amount of ninety dollars.
Any officer who exceeds this authority is personally liable therefor.
The board denied the request and stated its reasons therefor in writing.
The lot was conveyed for ten dollars and other good and valuable consideration, receipt therefor acknowledged.
Not the same word: the fee was not paid; therefore the application was rejected.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on the second syllable — which is the entire difference in speech between this word and therefore /ˈðɛrfɔr/ · THAIR-for
entries.русский: за это, взамен этого — юр.; не путать с therefore «поэтому» (ударение на 2-м слоге)
entries.register: legal; outside legal drafting it is read as a typo for therefore, and copy editors "correct" it constantly
entries.type: pronominal adverb — for + it/that, a pro-form for "for it" or "in exchange for that"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant; stands for singular or plural alike.
entries.refers to: a thing, sum, service, or right already named, as the thing something is given for — most often in exchange (the goods and the price therefor) or in purpose (the application and the fee therefor).
entries.agreement: none of its own; the noun it modifies keeps its own (the consideration therefor is ten dollars).
entries.pattern: the price therefor · the consideration therefor · the fee therefor · in payment therefor · and shall be liable therefor · the reasons therefor
entries.contrast: this is the one entry in the family where a missing letter changes the word. Therefor (no final e, stressed on the second syllable) means "for it" or "for that." Therefore (with the e, stressed on the first) means "consequently." The Buyer shall pay the price therefor is the amount owed for the goods; the Buyer shall therefore pay is a conclusion drawn from something above. American legal drafting keeps both, ordinary writing keeps only therefore, and because the shorter spelling looks like an error, a drafter who wants therefor should expect to defend it — which is a good reason to write for them instead. The parallel members are thereof ("of it") and therewith ("with it").
entries.see also: thereof, therewith, therefrom, thereby, whereof

entries.meaning: From it; from that; out of that.
examples: The trustee shall hold the fund and pay the income therefrom to the beneficiary quarterly.
Excepting therefrom the westerly twenty feet conveyed to the county for road purposes. (deed language)
Any claim arising therefrom must be brought within one year.
The company sold the division and applied the proceeds therefrom to its debt.
The report and the conclusions drawn therefrom were published in the same week.
Plain English: the trustee pays the income from it to the beneficiary.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on from, which keeps its full vowel instead of reducing to /frəm/
entries.русский: из этого, оттуда — юр., книжн.; «от того, из названного источника»
entries.register: legal and formal; heavy even by the standards of this family
entries.type: pronominal adverb — from + it/that, a pro-form for "from it"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant; stands for singular or plural.
entries.refers to: the source-like noun phrase most recently named — a fund, a property, a sale, a trust, a document — as the thing something comes out of. Things and abstractions, not people.
entries.agreement: none of its own; the noun it modifies keeps its own (the proceeds therefrom are taxable, the income therefrom is payable quarterly).
entries.pattern: the income therefrom · the proceeds derived therefrom · any rents and profits therefrom · excepting therefrom (the conveyancing formula that carves a piece out of a described parcel) · arising therefrom
entries.contrast: the everyday equivalent is from it or from them, and therefrom is worth knowing mainly because of one formula: excepting therefrom, which in a deed removes a described strip from a described parcel and is therefore the sentence that decides where your property line is. Distinguish it from thereof ("of it"), which marks possession or portion rather than origin — the proceeds thereof and the proceeds therefrom are both used, but thereof attaches the proceeds to the thing while therefrom traces them out of it. And do not use it for people: ✗the witness and the statement therefrom should be her statement.
entries.see also: thereof, thereto, therein, therefor, whence

entries.meaning: In it; in that place or thing.
examples: "Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein." (Proverbs 26:27, King James Version)
The house and everything contained therein passed to his daughter.
Therein lies the difficulty: nobody wants to pay for the survey.
The report is attached, and the figures cited therein have been audited.
The tenant may use the parking structure and the spaces designated therein.
She bought the old bookshop and every volume therein.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on in
entries.русский: в нём, там — юр., книжн.; «внутри того, что названо» (о вещах, не о людях)
entries.register: legal, formal, and literary
entries.type: pronominal adverb — in + it/that, a pro-form for "in that thing"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant; the thing it stands for may be singular or plural.
entries.refers to: the container-like noun phrase most recently named — a place, a building, a document, a pit, a fund. Things, not people.
entries.agreement: none of its own.
entries.pattern: [noun] and everything contained therein · the property and the improvements therein · therein lies [noun phrase] · described therein
entries.contrast: therein is "in that," herein is "in this document," wherein is "in which." The idiom therein lies the problem is the one place the word survives in ordinary American speech, and it is fixed in that inverted order — therein lies, not ✗therein the problem lies. In a lease, watch the pair carefully: the premises and all fixtures therein means the fixtures inside the building; all fixtures herein would mean fixtures inside the lease document.
entries.see also: thereof, thereon, thereto, herein, wherein

entries.meaning: Later in that document; earlier in that document. The there- mates of hereinafter and hereinbefore, pointing at some other instrument.
examples: The 1974 trust deed, and the amendments thereinafter set out, govern the distribution.
The court quoted the policy and the exclusions thereinbefore recited.
The lease refers to a schedule of fixtures, described thereinafter in Part III.
The residuary clause revoked the gift to the beneficiary thereinbefore named.
The statute defines "vehicle" in section 2 and uses the term thereinafter without qualification.
The error to avoid: a contract that says as thereinafter provided about itself, where it means hereinafter.
Plain-language rewrite: later in that deed; earlier in the policy.
entries.pronunciation note: four syllables each, stress on af and on for; the older /ˌðɛrɪnˈɑftɚ/ turns up in British-influenced drafting, exactly as it does in hereinafter
entries.русский: далее / ранее в том документе — юр.; о тексте другого, уже названного документа
entries.variants: thereinabove and thereinbelow are built on the same pattern and are rarer still; they mean what thereinbefore and thereinafter mean
entries.register: legal; rare, and correct only where the writer is pointing at a document other than the one in hand — most often a judge construing an instrument quoted in the opinion
entries.type: pronominal adverbs — after and before welded onto therein, pro-forms for "later in" and "earlier in that document"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: a part of a document already named — a will, a deed, a policy, a statute under construction — before or after the point already discussed. It points at text in another instrument, never at time, and never at the document the writer is drafting. That last restriction is the entire content of the entry.
entries.agreement: none of their own.
entries.pattern: the beneficiary thereinbefore named · as thereinafter provided · the covenants thereinbefore recited · the schedule thereinafter set out · the trust deed and the amendments thereinafter described
entries.contrast: the here- / there- split is the whole point and it is substantive, not stylistic: hereinafter means "later in this instrument," thereinafter means "later in that one." A drafter who writes thereinafter about the contract being drafted has pointed at nothing, and a court reading the clause has to guess. The word an American is far likelier to meet is thereafter, which is about time ("after that moment") and is ordinary English; the one-syllable difference between thereafter and thereinafter is the same trap that separates hereafter from hereinafter, and in an instrument the slip changes the meaning. Against the foregoing, the difference is grammatical: the foregoing is a noun phrase that can be a subject, while these are adverbs that can only modify. Plain-language drafting writes earlier in the deed and later in the policy.
entries.see also: hereinafter, hereinbefore, hereinbelow, therein, thereof, thereupon, the foregoing

entries.meaning: Of it; of them; of that.
examples: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof." (First Amendment)
The lease may be terminated upon breach of any provision thereof.
The lot and any structures erected on any portion thereof are covered.
We discussed her qualifications, or the lack thereof, for most of the meeting.
The committee reviewed the proposal and rejected the greater part thereof.
Each shareholder shall be notified of the meeting and of the purpose thereof.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on of, with a full vowel
entries.русский: этого, его, их — юр.; род. п. к названному: the terms thereof «его условия»
entries.register: legal and formal; the commonest member of the family
entries.type: pronominal adverb — of + it/that, a pro-form for "of it," "of them," "of that"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant; stands for singular or plural alike (the parts thereof = of it or of them).
entries.refers to: the noun phrase most recently named — a right, a term, a property, a law, a sum. Things and abstractions; not people.
entries.agreement: none of its own; the verb agrees with whatever noun thereof modifies (any portion thereof is forfeited, all copies thereof are destroyed).
entries.pattern: any part thereof · the whole thereof · the term thereof · the exercise thereof · or any portion thereof · and the like thereof
entries.contrast: thereof replaces of it or of them and points backward to a noun already in the text, while hereof points at this document. The everyday equivalent is simply its or of it: the free exercise thereof = its free exercise. It is not archaic in the way thou is — it is fully productive in legal English today — but outside that register it is pure jargon, and the fixed joke or lack thereof is the only form most Americans use in speech.
entries.see also: therein, thereto, thereon, hereof, whereof, the same

entries.meaning: On it; on that.
examples: The deed conveys the land and all improvements thereon.
Interest accrues on the principal balance and on any late charges assessed thereon.
The parcel and the barn standing thereon were sold as one lot.
The buyer accepts the lot and any encumbrances recorded thereon.
He set the tray down and arranged the glasses thereon.
The note is due in full, together with all interest earned thereon.
entries.pronunciation note: also /ðɛrˈɔn/; stress on on
entries.русский: на нём, на это — юр.; о земле, участке, основной сумме, поверхности
entries.register: legal and formal, chiefly in real-estate and lending documents; the variant thereupon is more literary
entries.type: pronominal adverb — on + it/that, a pro-form for "on it"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: a surface-like or base-like noun phrase already named — land, a parcel, a principal sum, a structure. Things only.
entries.agreement: none of its own.
entries.pattern: the land and all improvements thereon · the principal and interest thereon · the building erected thereon · the note and all sums due thereon
entries.contrast: thereon is "on it," therein is "in it," thereto is "to it" — the family differs only in which preposition got fused, and choosing the wrong one produces nonsense rather than mere clumsiness. Thereupon is the same word with the heavier preposition, and it has drifted: as a pro-form it still means "on that" (the table and the lamp thereupon), but its ordinary modern sense is temporal, "immediately after that" (he read the letter and thereupon resigned), which is an adverb of time, not a pronominal.
entries.see also: thereof, therein, thereto

entries.meaning: To it; to that.
examples: The Master Agreement and all amendments thereto remain in force.
The policy, together with any endorsements thereto, must be produced on request.
The parties thereto have already performed most of their obligations.
Any exhibits thereto are incorporated by this reference.
She reviewed the complaint and every document related thereto.
The proposal, and any objections thereto, will be heard on Tuesday.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on to
entries.русский: к нему, к этому — юр.; о приложениях, дополнениях, сторонах договора
entries.register: legal and formal
entries.type: pronominal adverb — to + it/that, a pro-form for "to it"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: a document, agreement, or thing already named, as the target of attaching, amending, adding, or being a party.
entries.agreement: none of its own; a subject it modifies keeps its own agreement (the amendments thereto are attached).
entries.pattern: and all amendments thereto · the parties thereto · exhibits thereto · any supplement thereto · related thereto
entries.contrast: hereto attaches to this document, thereto to one already mentioned: the Master Agreement and all amendments thereto. Confusing the two reverses the reference and, in a contract, changes what is actually being incorporated. In everyday English the phrase is simply to it, and the plain-language rewrite of the parties thereto is the parties to that agreement.
entries.see also: hereto, thereof, therein, thereon

entries.meaning: Under that agreement; under that statute; underneath that thing.
examples: The Clean Air Act and the regulations promulgated thereunder govern the permit.
The Master Agreement remains in force, and each work order issued thereunder is a separate contract.
A default thereunder is a default under this Agreement as well.
The patent and every license granted thereunder passed to the acquiring company.
They inspected the deck and the crawlspace thereunder. (the spatial sense)
Plain-language rewrite: the regulations issued under that Act govern the permit.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on un
entries.русский: по нему, на основании его — юр.; о договоре или законе как источнике прав
entries.register: legal and formal, chiefly where one document or statute sits beneath another
entries.type: pronominal adverb — under + it/that, a pro-form for "under that"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: in its main sense, the agreement, statute, or regulation just named, treated as the authority under which a right or duty arises (the Act and the regulations promulgated thereunder). In a secondary and much rarer sense it is spatial — the thing physically beneath what was just mentioned (the deck and the crawlspace thereunder).
entries.agreement: none of its own; the noun it modifies keeps its own (the rights thereunder are assignable).
entries.pattern: the Act and the rules thereunder · rights and obligations thereunder · any default thereunder · licensed thereunder · the Master Agreement and each order thereunder
entries.contrast: hereunder is "under this agreement," thereunder is "under that one," and in a layered deal — a master agreement with work orders beneath it, a statute with regulations beneath it — the choice decides which instrument a right comes from. That is a substantive error, not a stylistic one. Distinguish the authority sense from the spatial sense, which is ordinary English and which thereon mirrors from above (the land and the barn thereon / the deck and the crawlspace thereunder). The plain rewrite names the instrument: under the Master Agreement.
entries.see also: hereunder, thereon, thereof, thereto, therein

entries.meaning: To that; belonging to that. The ceremonial twin of thereto, surviving in two formulas.
examples: Together with all the tenements, hereditaments, and appurtenances thereunto belonging.
The office, and the salary thereunto attached, passed to his successor in January.
Executed by the Company by its officer thereunto duly authorized.
He was called thereunto and did not refuse.
The easement, and the rights of way thereunto appertaining, run with the land.
Ordinary modern drafting: together with everything that belongs to the property.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on to; the middle syllable keeps its full /ʌn/, since the word survives only inside slowly read formulas
entries.русский: к тому, к сему — устар., юр.; в формулах о принадлежностях имущества
entries.register: archaic and legal; effectively confined to conveyancing formulas and to scriptural style
entries.type: pronominal adverb — unto + that, a ceremonial pro-form for "to that"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: the property, right, or office just named, as the thing something belongs to or is attached to.
entries.agreement: none of its own; the noun it modifies keeps its own (the rights thereunto belonging are conveyed).
entries.pattern: together with the appurtenances thereunto belonging (the deed formula) · the rights and privileges thereunto appertaining · called thereunto · thereunto authorized (in a signature block: by its officer thereunto duly authorized)
entries.contrast: thereto is the ordinary working form — the lease and all amendments thereto — and thereunto is the same meaning in ceremonial dress, built on unto. It survives in two places an American may actually encounter: the deed phrase together with all and singular the tenements, hereditaments, and appurtenances thereunto belonging, and the corporate signature block by its officer thereunto duly authorized, which means nothing more than "authorized to do this." Its here- twin is hereunto, and the two are just as easy to swap as hereto and thereto: hereunto attaches to this document, thereunto to something already named.
entries.see also: thereto, hereunto, thereof, thereon, whereof

entries.meaning: Immediately after that; on that. The there- compound that drifted out of place and into time, and now nearly always says when rather than where.
examples: He read the letter through twice and thereupon resigned.
The court found the notice defective and thereupon dismissed the petition.
The clerk called the case; the parties thereupon came forward.
She learned that the buyer had withdrawn and thereupon relisted the house.
The altar, and the offering laid thereupon, were consumed. (the older spatial sense)
Compare: the land and the buildings thereon — the everyday legal form for "on it."

senses.head: Immediately after that; at once (adverb of time — the living sense)
body: He read the letter and thereupon resigned. Ordinary formal English, common in narrative and in judicial opinions.

senses.head: On that; upon that thing (pronominal, archaic)
body: The table and the lamp thereupon. The job thereon took over, and rare in modern text.
examples: He read the letter through twice and thereupon resigned.
The court found the notice defective and thereupon dismissed the petition.
The clerk called the case; the parties thereupon came forward.
She learned that the buyer had withdrawn and thereupon relisted the house.
The altar, and the offering laid thereupon, were consumed. (the older spatial sense)
Compare: the land and the buildings thereon — the everyday legal form for "on it."

entries.pronunciation note: also /ˌðɛrəˈpɔn/; stress on the last syllable, and the middle vowel reduces to /ə/
entries.русский: тотчас после этого; на том — книжн.; чаще временное «вслед за тем»
entries.register: formal, legal, and narrative; the temporal sense is at home in ordinary formal prose
entries.type: pronominal adverb — upon + that, with two jobs: a pro-form for "on that" and, far more commonly, an adverb of time meaning "immediately after that"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: in the spatial sense, a surface-like noun phrase already named (the table and the lamp thereupon); in the temporal sense, the event just narrated — what it points at is a moment, not a thing.
entries.agreement: none of its own.
entries.pattern: [clause]; thereupon [clause] (temporal: he read the letter and thereupon resigned) · [noun] thereupon (spatial, rare) · whereupon is its relative counterpart — see whereupon
entries.contrast: thereon is the everyday legal form for "on it" — the land and all improvements thereon — and thereupon is the heavier word that has drifted away from that job into time. In present-day American writing, thereupon nearly always means "at once, right after that," and reading it as "on that" in a modern text will usually be wrong. Its relative counterpart is whereupon ("immediately after which"), which does the same work inside a relative clause, and its here- mate would be hereupon, which is dead. Do not confuse the temporal thereupon with thereby: thereupon says when, thereby says how.
entries.see also: thereon, whereupon, thereby, therewith, heretofore

entries.meaning: With it; with that; along with that.
examples: The Company shall pay all filing fees and any expenses incurred in connection therewith.
The deed, and the survey delivered therewith, were both recorded on Tuesday.
He handed her the key and therewith the deed to the cabin.
The approved site plan, and the permit issued therewith, must both be posted on the fence.
Therewith he turned on his heel and left the room. (the narrative use, shading into thereupon)
Plain English: the Company pays the filing fees and any related expenses.
entries.pronunciation note: also /ðɛrˈwɪð/ with the voiced th; stress on with
entries.русский: с этим, посредством этого — юр., книжн.; «вместе с тем, что названо»
entries.register: legal, formal, and literary
entries.type: pronominal adverb — with + it/that, a pro-form for "with it" or "with that"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant; stands for singular or plural.
entries.refers to: the thing just named, as the thing something goes along with or is done by means of — a document, a payment, an instrument, a tool. Things and abstractions, not people.
entries.agreement: none of its own.
entries.pattern: and all rights connected therewith · in connection therewith · together therewith · dealt therewith · therewithal (the reinforced literary form)
entries.contrast: herewith is "with this letter," therewith is "with that thing already named," and the swap turns a transmittal sentence into a reference to something else entirely. The commonest living phrase is in connection therewith, which every plain-language guide rewrites as in connection with it or, better, by naming the thing. The literary form therewithal adds nothing but weight, and therewith in narrative can also carry a faint temporal sense — "with that, and at that moment" (therewith he turned and left), where it shades into thereupon. Keep all of it apart from thereof ("of it"), which marks portion or possession rather than accompaniment.
entries.see also: herewith, thereof, thereupon, therefor, wherewith

entries.meaning: At which; at what. The reaction-marking member of the where- family.
examples: He named a price three times the estimate, whereat she laughed out loud.
The judge read the verdict, whereat the gallery erupted.
She let slip that the money had already been spent, whereat the meeting fell silent.
He was passed over a second time, whereat he began to look for another job.
Whereat do you marvel — that the train was late, or that it came at all? (the bookish question use)
Modern English: He named a price three times the estimate, at which point she laughed.
entries.pronunciation note: also /hwɛrˈæt/ for speakers who keep the wh-; stress on at
entries.русский: на что, после чего — устар., книжн.; вводит реакцию на сказанное или увиденное
entries.register: archaic and literary; the rarest of the surviving where- forms
entries.type: relative and interrogative pronominal adverb — at + which/what
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: an antecedent naming an event, sight, or statement that provokes a reaction — whereat introduces the reaction (he named the price, whereat she laughed). Things and happenings, never people (for people, at whom).
entries.agreement: none of its own; the verb in the relative clause agrees with that clause's own subject.
entries.pattern: [clause], whereat [subject] [verb] (whereat the crowd cheered) · [noun] whereat [clause] · whereat as a question word (whereat do you marvel?, thoroughly bookish)
entries.contrast: whereat and whereupon both hang a reaction onto what came before, and they are not quite the same. Whereupon is about sequence — "immediately after which," and it reports what happened next. Whereat is about cause or provocation — "at which," and it reports a response to a stimulus, which is why it so often precedes verbs of emotion: whereat she laughed, whereat the crowd jeered, whereat he took offense. In present-day American English both are formal and whereat is genuinely archaic; the plain versions are at which point, and then, and simply and. Do not confuse it with the dialectal question where at? (where's he at?), two separate words, which is a different construction entirely.
entries.see also: whereupon, whereby, wherein, whereof, thereupon, by which, in which, on which

entries.meaning: By which; by means of which.
examples: The contract sets up an arrangement whereby the tenant pays the property taxes directly.
They proposed a system whereby every claim is reviewed by two adjusters before payment.
There is no mechanism whereby a member can be expelled without a hearing. (after a negated noun phrase)
The statute created a procedure whereby small estates skip probate entirely.
She explained the method whereby the samples are kept sterile in transit.
Standard plain-English rewrite: a system in which every claim is reviewed twice — or simply a system that reviews every claim twice.
entries.pronunciation note: also /hwɛrˈbaɪ/ for speakers who keep the wh-; stress on by, which keeps its full diphthong
entries.русский: посредством чего, согласно которому — книжн. и офиц.; вполне живое
entries.case: object (governed by the fused preposition by)
entries.register: formal and legal — and, alone in this family, fully standard in ordinary careful American writing
entries.type: relative pronominal adverb — by + which
entries.person / number: third person, invariant. No plural, no possessive.
entries.refers to: an antecedent noun phrase naming a means or mechanism — a system, an arrangement, a procedure, a method, a rule, a device. Things and abstractions only; for people the phrase is by whom (the clerk by whom the form was filed), never ✗the clerk whereby.
entries.agreement: none of its own; the verb inside the relative clause agrees with that clause's own subject — an arrangement whereby the tenant pays the taxes (singular tenant), rules whereby claims are settled in thirty days (plural claims).
entries.pattern: [noun] whereby [clause] · a system whereby · an arrangement whereby · a procedure whereby · a means whereby · no mechanism whereby [clause]
entries.contrast: whereby = by which, the relative counterpart of thereby ("by that means") and hereby ("by this act"). It is the one member of the where- family a present-day American writer can use without sounding like a deed: a system whereby every claim is reviewed twice is ordinary formal English and no editor will touch it, while wherein and whereof in the same sentence would read as costume. Two limits are worth holding onto. It takes inanimate antecedents only, as above. And it means by which and nothing else — ✗the year whereby the company failed is a misuse for in which (wherein) or plain when, and ✗the fund whereby the money was taken should be from which. The plainest rewrite is usually to drop the pro-form altogether: a system that reviews every claim twice.
entries.see also: wherein, whereof, thereof, by which, in which, on which, which

entries.meaning: In which; in what.
examples: He described a system wherein every vote is counted twice before certification.
The paragraph wherein the warranty is disclaimed appears in capital letters.
Wherein lies the difference between the two proposals?
That was the year wherein the company nearly failed.
She wrote a memoir wherein almost nobody is named directly.
The court identified the respect wherein the statute is unconstitutional.
entries.pronunciation note: also /hwɛrˈɪn/ for speakers who keep the wh-; stress on in
entries.русский: в чём, в котором — книжн., юр.; о месте, документе, положении дел, не о людях
entries.register: formal, legal, and literary
entries.type: relative and interrogative pronominal adverb — in + which/what
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: an antecedent noun phrase that can contain something — a place, a document, a situation, a state of affairs. Things and abstractions, not people (for people, in whom).
entries.agreement: none of its own; the verb inside the relative clause agrees with that clause's own subject (a system wherein every vote counts).
entries.pattern: [noun] wherein [clause] (relative) · wherein lies [noun phrase] · Wherein [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? (interrogative: wherein does the difference lie?)
entries.contrast: wherein = in which, so it is the relative counterpart of therein (in that) and herein (in this). Modern English writes in which, and the plainest version often drops the preposition entirely: a system in which every vote counts, or a system where every vote counts. As a question word, wherein means "in what respect" and is now thoroughly bookish — wherein does the difference lie? for what exactly is the difference?
entries.see also: whereof, therein, herein, which, by which, in which, on which

entries.meaning: Of which; of what.
examples: In witness whereof, the parties have executed this Agreement as of the date first written above.
He worked on the assembly line for thirty years, so he knows whereof he speaks.
The charges whereof the defendant stands accused are set out in the indictment.
She spoke of a shortage whereof the rest of us had heard nothing.
Whereof do you accuse him, exactly?
This is the treaty whereof the ambassador made so much in his speech.
entries.pronunciation note: also /hwɛrˈʌv/; stress on of
entries.русский: о чём, чего — юр., книжн.; in witness whereof «в удостоверение чего»
entries.register: legal, literary, and archaic
entries.type: relative and interrogative pronominal adverb — of + which/what
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: an antecedent noun phrase — a fact, a matter, a document, a subject of knowledge. Things and abstractions.
entries.agreement: none of its own.
entries.pattern: In witness whereof [clause] · know whereof [subject] [verb] (he knows whereof he speaks) · [noun] whereof [clause] · the matter whereof he complains
entries.contrast: whereof = of which, the relative counterpart of thereof (of it) and hereof (of this). Two idioms keep it alive in American English: In witness whereof, the closing formula of nearly every executed contract, and to know whereof one speaks, meaning to speak from real knowledge — which is fixed in that order and cannot be modernized inside the idiom (✗he knows of which he speaks). Everywhere else, write of which, or recast: a matter he knows nothing about.
entries.see also: wherein, thereof, hereof, whose, of which

entries.meaning: To which; to what.
examples: The trust names the charitable purposes whereto the income is dedicated.
The office whereto she was appointed carries no salary.
This is the agreement whereto the amendments of last spring were attached.
He never disclosed the account whereto the funds were transferred.
Whereto does this road lead, if not to the river? (the archaic question use)
Modern English: the purposes to which the income is dedicated.
entries.pronunciation note: also /hwɛrˈtu/ for speakers who keep the wh-; stress on to
entries.русский: к чему, куда — устар., юр.; о цели или назначении
entries.register: archaic and legal; rare even in contracts, where to which has almost entirely replaced it
entries.type: relative and interrogative pronominal adverb — to + which/what
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: an antecedent noun phrase treated as a destination or an end — a purpose, a fund, an office, a place. Things and abstractions; for people, to whom.
entries.agreement: none of its own; the verb inside the relative clause agrees with that clause's own subject (the purposes whereto the fund is dedicated).
entries.pattern: [noun] whereto [clause] · the purposes whereto · the office whereto he was appointed · Whereto? (archaic question: "to what place?")
entries.contrast: whereto = to which, and it is the relative counterpart of hereto ("to this") and thereto ("to that"). Two neighbors are easy to confuse with it. Whither also means "to where," but it is about physical motion — whither goest thou — while whereto is about attachment, purpose, and destination in the abstract. And whereto is not whereat: one is direction, the other is reaction. In present-day American English write to which, or recast to lose the pro-form entirely: the fund's purposes, the office he was appointed to.
entries.see also: hereto, thereto, whereof, wherein, whither, to whom, for whom, with whom

entries.meaning: Immediately after which; at which point. Also, archaically, on which.
examples: The clerk read out the verdict, whereupon the gallery emptied in about a minute.
She asked whether anyone objected, whereupon three hands went up.
The engine coughed twice, whereupon the pilot turned back toward the field.
He was told the shop had closed at six, whereupon he sat down on the curb to wait for morning.
This is the stone whereupon the first oath was sworn. (the archaic spatial use)
Plain English: the clerk read the verdict, and then the gallery emptied.
entries.pronunciation note: also /ˌwɛrəˈpɔn/ and /ˌhwɛr-/; stress on the last syllable, with the middle vowel reduced to /ə/
entries.русский: после чего, вслед за чем — книжн., повеств.; вполне живое
entries.register: formal and narrative; the sequence use is ordinary formal American English and needs no apology
entries.type: relative pronominal adverb with two jobs — an adverb of sequence meaning "immediately after which," and, archaically, a pro-form for "on which"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: the event or statement just narrated, taken as the moment the next thing follows. It never points at a person, and in the modern sense it does not point at a surface either — its antecedent is a whole clause.
entries.agreement: none of its own; the clause it introduces keeps its own subject and verb (whereupon the crowd dispersed).
entries.pattern: [clause], whereupon [subject] [verb] · [clause], whereupon [clause] (always second, never first in its sentence) · the archaic spatial use, [noun] whereupon (the stone whereupon he sat)
entries.contrast: whereupon says what happened next; whereat says what it provoked; whereby says by what means. All three attach a clause to what precedes, and only the first is common today. Its there- counterpart is thereupon, which does the same job without a relative clause — he read the letter and thereupon resigned / he read the letter, whereupon he resigned — and the choice between them is the ordinary choice between an adverb and a relative. The plainest rewrites are and then, at which point, and simply and. Note that whereupon must follow the clause it attaches to; it cannot open a sentence on its own, and it takes a comma before it rather than after.
entries.see also: whereat, whereby, thereupon, thereon, wherein

entries.meaning: With which; with what. The instrument-naming member of the where- family, alive today mainly through the noun wherewithal.
examples: "Wherewith shall I come before the Lord?" (Micah 6:6, King James Version)
