"If the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted?" (Matthew 5:13)
The estate left him a name and a title, but nothing wherewith to keep either up.
She had neither the tools wherewith to repair it nor anyone to ask.
The fund out of which the claims are paid, and wherewith the reserve is maintained, is described in Article VI.
The living descendant: he simply did not have the wherewithal to fight it in court.
entries.pronunciation note: also /wɛrˈwɪð/ and /hwɛr-/; stress on with
entries.русский: чем, посредством чего — устар., библ.; о средстве (ср. живое wherewithal)
entries.register: archaic, biblical, and literary; dead in modern American prose, but its derived noun wherewithal is fully alive
entries.type: relative and interrogative pronominal adverb — with + which/what
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: an antecedent naming a means or instrument — money, a tool, a substance, an argument. Things only; for people, with whom.
entries.agreement: none of its own; the verb inside the clause agrees with that clause's own subject (the salt wherewith the meat is cured).
entries.pattern: [noun] wherewith [subject] [verb] (the means wherewith he lived) · wherewith as a question word (wherewith shall I come before the Lord?) · wherewith to [verb] (nothing wherewith to pay) · the derived noun, the wherewithal
entries.contrast: wherewith = with which, the relative mate of herewith ("with this") and therewith ("with that"), and it overlaps heavily with whereby — the difference is that whereby names a method (a system whereby claims are reviewed) while wherewith names an instrument or resource (the money wherewith the claims are paid). Modern English writes with which, or recasts. The word that survives is the noun wherewithal, meaning the means — usually the money — to do something: he lacked the wherewithal to fight it in court. That noun is ordinary American English at every level, and it is the only reason most Americans recognize the root at all.
entries.see also: herewith, therewith, whereby, whereof, wherein

entries.meaning: From this place; from this time; therefore. The three-way pro-adverb whose only living American sense is the third, hence the delay.
examples: "Get thee hence, Satan." (Matthew 4:10, King James Version — the place sense)
The option expires three years hence, on the anniversary of closing. (time)
The parts were held at customs; hence the delay. (inference, verbless — the ordinary modern use)
The rules changed in March, and hence the forms you were given last year are worthless.
He was ordered hence and did not set foot in the city again. (archaic place sense)
Henceforth the office will close at four on Fridays. (the surviving compound)

senses.head: From this place (archaic)
body: Get thee hence. Dead outside quotation, though henceforth keeps the shape alive.

senses.head: From this time; from now (formal)
body: Three years hence, a week hence. Alive in formal and literary writing, always after the time expression.

senses.head: Therefore; for that reason (standard modern English)
body: Hence the delay. The living sense, and the only one an American writes on purpose.
examples: "Get thee hence, Satan." (Matthew 4:10, King James Version — the place sense)
The option expires three years hence, on the anniversary of closing. (time)
The parts were held at customs; hence the delay. (inference, verbless — the ordinary modern use)
The rules changed in March, and hence the forms you were given last year are worthless.
He was ordered hence and did not set foot in the city again. (archaic place sense)
Henceforth the office will close at four on Fridays. (the surviving compound)

entries.pronunciation note: one syllable, rhyming with fence; no weak form
entries.русский: отсюда; отныне; следовательно — «поэтому» живо, «отсюда» устар., «через (год)» книжн.
entries.register: the inferential sense is ordinary formal American English; the place sense is archaic; the time sense is formal and slightly literary
entries.type: pro-adverb with three jobs — motion from here (archaic), from now (formal), and therefore (a conjunctive adverb, and the only living use)
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: in the place sense, the location of the speaker ("from this place"); in the time sense, the moment of speaking ("from now"); in the inferential sense, the statement just made, which is the sense in which it still stands in for something — hence the delay means "because of what I have just told you, the delay."
entries.agreement: none of its own. In the inferential use it very often heads a verbless phrase — hence the confusion, hence the new forms — which is standard and not an error, though a following clause needs its own verb (hence we were late).
entries.pattern: get thee hence (archaic, place) · [number] [time noun] hence (three years hence) · hence [noun phrase] (verbless inference: hence the delay) · hence [clause] (hence the committee met twice) · henceforth, henceforward (from now on)
entries.contrast: the three senses are one word only historically, and only the third is live: hence = therefore is what an American writes today, and it is fully standard. Against its neighbors, hence is "from here," thence is "from there," and whence is "from where" — and all three already contain from, which is why from hence is strictly redundant, even though the King James Bible and Shakespeare both use it. Do not confuse hence with whence: ✗the country hence he came should be whence he came. And keep the inferential hence apart from thus and therefore, which are its ordinary synonyms; hence is the shortest and the most comfortable in front of a bare noun phrase.
entries.see also: thence, whence, hither, thereby, heretofore, herein

entries.meaning: To this place; to here. The archaic directional mate of here, alive inside come-hither.
examples: Come hither, boy, and let me look at you.
Bring the lamp hither — I can't read a word of this.
They were driven hither by the storm and stayed the winter.
She sent messengers hither and thither, and none of them came back with anything.
He gave her a come-hither look over the top of the menu. (the living compound)
Modern English: Come here; bring the lamp over here.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on the first syllable, voiced th as in this; no weak form
entries.русский: сюда — устар., книжн.; движение к говорящему; hither and yon «туда-сюда»
entries.register: archaic and literary; survives for everyone inside two fixed phrases, come-hither and hither and yon
entries.type: pro-adverb of motion toward the speaker — "to this place"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: the place where the speaker is, as a destination. It is the directional mate of here, and it can only be used with verbs of motion — come hither, bring it hither, never ✗stand hither.
entries.agreement: none of its own.
entries.pattern: come hither · [verb of motion] hither (bring hither, send hither, drew hither) · hither and yon / hither and thither (the fixed pairs, meaning "in every direction") · come-hither as a compound adjective (a come-hither look)
entries.contrast: hither is "to here" and here is "at here," and modern English uses here for both — come here does the whole job, because come already supplies the direction. That redundancy is what killed the word. Its mates are thither ("to there") and whither ("to where"); its opposite in direction is hence ("from here"). The one place it is genuinely alive is the compound adjective come-hither, describing a look or a manner that invites — a phrase most Americans use without ever noticing that they are speaking Middle English. In hither and yon and hither and thither, the pair has stopped meaning direction at all and simply means "all over the place."
entries.see also: thither, whither, hence, yonder, yon

entries.meaning: From that place; from there. The one member of the trio that ordinary documents still use.
examples: Thence north forty degrees east, one hundred feet, to an iron pin. (metes and bounds, the live legal use)
We flew to Reykjavik and thence to Oslo on the morning flight.
The river rises in the hills above the town and runs thence to the sea.
He went first to Paris, and thence, after two hard years, to New York.
The evidence went to the sheriff's office and thence to the state laboratory.
Thenceforth the family never spoke of it again. (the time compound)
entries.pronunciation note: one syllable, voiced th as in this, rhyming with fence
entries.русский: оттуда — книжн., юр.; движение от названного места (описания границ, маршруты)
entries.register: formal and legal; genuinely alive in two places, land surveying and itineraries
entries.type: pro-adverb of motion from a place already named — "from there"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: the place, point, or state most recently named, as the point something moves away from. In a metes-and-bounds description each thence means "from the point I just described," and the chain of them walks the boundary all the way around.
entries.agreement: none of its own.
entries.pattern: and thence to [place] (to Reykjavik and thence to Oslo) · thence [compass bearing] [distance] (the surveyor's chain: thence north 40 degrees east, 100 feet) · thence forward · thenceforth, thenceforward (from that time on)
entries.contrast: hence is "from here," thence is "from there," whence is "from where" — and, like its two mates, thence already contains from, so from thence is redundant, however often the King James Bible writes it. The word an American is most likely to meet it beside is thenceforth, which shifts the meaning from place to time ("from that moment on"), exactly as henceforth does. In ordinary writing the phrase is and from there: we flew to Reykjavik and from there to Oslo. Where thence still earns its keep is a legal description of land, where the whole point is that each call starts precisely where the last one ended, and no plainer word does that job as compactly.
entries.see also: hence, whence, thither, therefrom, thereupon

entries.meaning: To that place; to there. The archaic directional mate of there.
examples: The road runs thither, past the mill and over the ridge.
He sent men hither and thither with messages, and heard nothing back for a week.
She looked thither, toward the smoke rising over the trees.
The whole household was carried thither in two wagons.
Papers blew hither and thither across the parking lot. (the fixed phrase, with no direction left in it)
Modern English: the road goes there; he sent men in every direction.
entries.pronunciation note: with the voiceless th of thin in most American mouths, though /ˈðɪðɚ/ with the voiced th of this is also standard; stress on the first syllable
entries.русский: туда — устар., книжн.; движение к названному месту; hither and thither «туда-сюда»
entries.register: archaic and literary; alive for everyone only inside hither and thither
entries.type: pro-adverb of motion toward a place already named — "to there"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: the place already named or pointed at, as a destination. Like hither, it goes only with verbs of motion.
entries.agreement: none of its own.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] thither (go thither, sent thither, carried thither) · hither and thither (the fixed pair: "in all directions") · thitherward (rarer still)
entries.contrast: thither is "to there" and there is "at there," and modern English uses there for both: go there is the whole of it. Its mates are hither ("to here") and whither ("to where"); its directional opposite is thence ("from there"). The pronunciation is worth a note of its own, because thither is one of a small set of English words — with thence and thistle on one side and this and those on the other — where American speakers genuinely differ on whether the th is voiced; both are correct, and dictionaries list both. In hither and thither the pair has lost its direction entirely and just means "scattered all over," which is how nearly every living American use of the word arrives.
entries.see also: hither, whither, thence, thereto, yonder

entries.meaning: From where; from which place, source, or cause.
examples: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." (Psalm 121:1, King James Version)
Return whence you came, and do not come back through this valley.
He never would say whence the money had come.
She showed us the village whence her grandparents emigrated in 1892.
Whence this sudden enthusiasm for committee work? (the verbless bookish question)
Modern English: the village her grandparents came from; where did the money come from?
entries.pronunciation note: also /hwɛns/ for speakers who keep the wh-; one syllable, rhyming with fence
entries.русский: откуда — устар., книжн.; о месте, источнике или причине происхождения
entries.register: archaic and literary; alive in one famous psalm, in the phrase return whence you came, and in bookish questions
entries.type: relative and interrogative pro-adverb — "from what place," "from which"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: the origin — the place, source, or condition something came out of. It can point at a physical place (the town whence her family emigrated), at an abstract source (whence the money came), and, in the question use, at a cause (whence this sudden enthusiasm?).
entries.agreement: none of its own; the verb in its clause agrees with that clause's own subject (the hills, whence cometh my help).
entries.pattern: [noun] whence [clause] (relative: the country whence he came) · return whence [subject] [verb] (return whence you came) · Whence [verb] [subject]? (question: whence comes this rumor?) · whence [noun phrase]? (verbless: whence this enthusiasm?) · from whence (redundant but four hundred years old)
entries.contrast: whence is "from where," whither is "to where," and where is neither — it is position only. The distinction English lost is exactly the one whence preserves, which is why the word survives at all. On from whence: the from is redundant, since whence already contains it, and generations of usage guides have called it an error — but the King James translators wrote from whence cometh my help, Shakespeare wrote it, and no modern authority treats it as wrong. Use it if you like the sound; nobody who knows the history will object. Do not confuse whence with hence: they point in the same direction from different places (from where / from here), and swapping them produces nonsense. And whence is not when; the resemblance is an accident of spelling.
entries.see also: whither, hence, thence, wherein, therefrom, of which

entries.meaning: To where; to which place. The direction-marking question word English replaced with plain where.
examples: "Whither thou goest, I will go." (Ruth 1:16, King James Version — the wedding reading)
"None of you asketh me, Whither goest thou?" (John 16:5)
Whither the euro? (the magazine headline formula: "what is going to become of it?")
He asked whither the road led, and nobody could tell him.
The country whither she was posted had no embassy of its own.
Modern English: Where are you going?; where does this road go?
entries.pronunciation note: also /ˈhwɪðɚ/ for speakers who keep the wh-; for everyone else it is an exact homophone of wither, "to dry up," which is the trap below
entries.русский: куда — устар., книжн.; о цели движения; омофон wither «вянуть»
entries.register: archaic and literary; alive in one biblical passage, and in a headline formula that news magazines still use
entries.type: relative and interrogative pro-adverb — "to what place," "to which"
entries.person / number: third person, invariant.
entries.refers to: the destination — the place, state, or future something is moving toward. In the headline use (Whither the euro?) the destination is figurative: the question is what will become of the thing.
entries.agreement: none of its own; the verb in the clause agrees with that clause's own subject (whither thou goest, with the archaic thou ending).
entries.pattern: whither [subject] [verb] (whither thou goest) · Whither [verb] [subject]? (question with inversion: whither goest thou?) · Whither [noun phrase]? (the verbless headline: Whither the party?) · [noun] whither [clause] (relative: the country whither he was sent)
entries.contrast: whither is "to where," whence is "from where," and where alone is position — the same three-way split as hither / thence / here. Modern English says where … to, or just where: where are you going? does the job that whither goest thou? once did. Two traps. First, the homophone: for the great majority of Americans whither and wither sound exactly alike, and the spelling is the only thing keeping Whither the republic? from reading as a prediction of its collapse — which headline writers have exploited more than once. Second, do not use whither for position: ✗the town whither he lives should be where he lives, or wherein in formal prose.
entries.see also: whence, hither, thither, whereto, wheresoever, whithersoever, whensoever, wherein

entries.meaning: Every last one of the group being addressed — the emphatic, exhaustive plural.
examples: I need all y'all in the van by six, not just the drivers.
All y'all are going to hear me out before anybody says a word.
This applies to all y'all, including the folks in the back.
Coach said he was tired of all y'all showing up late.
Happy Thanksgiving to all y'all and all y'all's families.
If all y'all would quiet down, I could read the list.
entries.pronunciation note: /ɑl ˈjɑl/ in merged accents; the first word reduces to /əl/ in fast speech
entries.русский: вы все до одного — диал. (Юг США), разг.; усиленное y'all, весь адресат без исключения
entries.register: informal, spoken; Southern American English and African American English
entries.type: second-person plural pronoun, emphatic; regional
entries.person / number: second person plural, always plural, and specifically exhaustive — the entire group without exception.
entries.refers to: every member of the group addressed, human. It cannot address one person, and that is the whole point of it.
entries.agreement: plural verb: all y'all are late, all y'all were there, have all y'all eaten? Never ✗all y'all is.
entries.pattern: all y'all [plural verb] · [verb] all y'all · all y'all's [noun] (possessive) · every one of all y'all (heavier still)
entries.contrast: this form is the answer to the objection outsiders raise about y'all — that it has lost the ability to be emphatic because it is used so freely. Y'all addresses a group; all y'all insists on the whole of it, usually when part of the group has been assuming the remark is aimed at somebody else: I'm not talking to some of you, I'm talking to all y'all. Structurally it is all + y'all, the same predeterminer stacking that gives all of you and all of us, so it is not a doubled all despite the y'all < you all etymology — no speaker parses y'all as containing all any more.
entries.see also: y'all, you all, you guys, y'all's

entries.meaning: You, plural — the Southern and African American second-person plural, and the most successful of all the repairs to the missing plural you.
examples: Y'all are welcome to stay for dinner.
I'll see y'all at the game on Saturday.
Do y'all have any sweet tea?
Y'all's dog got out again last night.
Where are y'all parked?
Y'all come back now, you hear?
I didn't mean any of y'all in particular.
entries.pronunciation note: /jɑl/ for the cot–caught merged majority; weak form /jl̩/ or /jəl/, so y'all come back now runs together as /jl̩ˈkʌm/
entries.русский: вы (мн. ч.) — диал., разг.; южноамериканское «вы» к нескольким, стяжение you all
entries.case: none — the same form is subject and object
entries.register: informal and spoken; ordinary, unstigmatized standard usage within the American South and in African American English, and spreading nationally in informal writing
entries.type: second-person plural pronoun; regional
entries.person / number: second person plural. Contracted from you all, but a single word to its speakers — no one hears an all inside it.
entries.refers to: the people addressed, two or more; human only. In its associative use it can be spoken to one person while referring to that person's household, business, or group: asking a lone waiter Do y'all have sweet tea? means the restaurant, not the waiter.
entries.agreement: plural verb, always: y'all are, y'all were, y'all have, do y'all know. ✗Y'all is is not a Southern form; it is a caricature. The possessive is y'all's (y'all's car), and the reflexive is y'all's selves or plain yourselves.
entries.pattern: y'all [plural verb] · [verb] y'all (I'll see y'all Sunday) · [preposition] y'all (with y'all) · y'all's [noun] · all y'all (emphatic) · y'all come back now (the leave-taking formula)
entries.contrast: y'all against you guys is the sharpest regional line in American pronouns: y'all south of roughly the Ohio River and throughout African American English, you guys nearly everywhere else. The persistent Northern claim that Southerners use y'all for one person is mostly a misreading of the associative use above; most Southern speakers reject a truly singular y'all, though genuinely singular uses are attested in some communities and the point is honestly contested. Spelling matters more than it should: the apostrophe stands for the missing ou of you, so it goes after the y — y'all, never ✗ya'll, which is a very common misspelling and is treated as an error even by people who use the word constantly. Against modern you, y'all is simply the plural that you stopped being when it absorbed thou.
entries.see also: all y'all, you all, you guys, youse, yinz, who all, what all, ye, y'all (personal), y'all's

entries.meaning: You, plural — the Appalachian and Ohio Valley form, from you ones.
examples: Are y'uns going up to the cabin this weekend?
Y'uns better bring a jacket; it gets cold up there.
I told y'uns the road was washed out.
Do y'uns need help carrying that in?
Y'uns can park behind the church.
Which one of y'uns left the gate open?
entries.pronunciation note: also /jɪnz/, at which point it has become yinz
entries.русский: вы (мн. ч.) — диал., разг.; Аппалачи и Питтсбург, из you ones; вариант yinz
entries.register: informal and spoken; nonstandard outside its region
entries.type: second-person plural pronoun; regional
entries.person / number: second person plural.
entries.refers to: the people addressed, two or more; human only. Like y'all, it can be used associatively of a household (Are y'uns coming to the reunion?).
entries.agreement: plural verb: y'uns are, y'uns were, do y'uns want.
entries.pattern: y'uns [plural verb] · [verb] y'uns · y'uns's [noun] (possessive, rare in writing) · y'uns guys (reinforced)
entries.contrast: y'uns is a contracted spelling of you'uns — "you ones" — and the three-way set you'uns / y'uns / yinz is one word at three stages of erosion, moving west and north from Appalachia into the Ohio Valley and finally into Pittsburgh, where it lands as yinz. Region separates it from its rivals: y'uns belongs to Appalachia, western Pennsylvania, eastern Ohio, and West Virginia, while y'all belongs to the South proper. Speakers whose grandparents said you'uns often say yinz, and the spelling in print is unsettled — y'uns, yuns, younz, and yinz all occur.
entries.see also: you'uns, yinz, y'all, youse

entries.meaning: You, plural — the Pittsburgh form.
examples: Are yinz going dahntahn for the game?
Yinz want to split a pizza?
I'll meet yinz at the bridge around seven.
Did yinz hear about the water main on Liberty?
Yinz guys need to move that car before the street sweeper comes.
Yinz better redd up before your mother gets home.
entries.pronunciation note: also spelled yunz, yins
entries.русский: вы (мн. ч.) — диал., разг.; примета питтсбургской речи, вариант y'uns
entries.register: informal and spoken; a local identity marker as much as a pronoun
entries.type: second-person plural pronoun; regional
entries.person / number: second person plural.
entries.refers to: the people addressed, two or more; human only.
entries.agreement: plural verb: yinz are, yinz were, did yinz see.
entries.pattern: yinz [plural verb] · [verb] yinz · yinz guys (reinforced) · yinz'll (contracted with will)
entries.contrast: yinz is the Pittsburgh form, the tightest geographic marker of any pronoun in American English — western Pennsylvania and essentially nowhere else. It is the end of the erosion chain you ones → you'uns → y'uns → yinz, and it is so strongly identified with the city that a native speaker of the local dialect is called a yinzer, a label worn with pride, irony, or contempt depending on who is using it. Against y'all and you guys the difference is purely regional; the grammar is identical.
entries.see also: y'uns, you'uns, youse, y'all

entries.meaning: You, plural — the full form behind y'all, and the neutral way to address a group without picking a regional side.
examples: You all are welcome to bring a dish.
Thank you all for coming out in this weather.
Is this you all's first time at the fair?
I hope you all had a good drive down.
You all have already seen the numbers, so I'll be brief.
Would you all like coffee before we start?

senses.head: Second-person plural pronoun (Southern, informal)
body: You all as a single unit addressing a group, the uncontracted parent of y'all: You all are welcome, Is this you all's first time?

senses.head: You plus the floating quantifier all (standard everywhere)
body: Two words doing two jobs, meaning "all of you": I thank you all, You all failed the quiz. The proof that it is two words is that all can float away from you entirely — You have all seen the memo — which the Southern pronoun cannot do.
examples: You all are welcome to bring a dish.
Thank you all for coming out in this weather.
Is this you all's first time at the fair?
I hope you all had a good drive down.
You all have already seen the numbers, so I'll be brief.
Would you all like coffee before we start?

entries.pronunciation note: reduces toward /jəˈɔl/ and, in the South, all the way to y'all
entries.русский: вы все — разг. и нейтр.; полная форма y'all и обычное «вы все» повсеместно
entries.register: informal to neutral; the uncontracted Southern form, and also plain English everywhere
entries.type: second-person plural pronoun (regional), or ordinary you plus the quantifier all
entries.person / number: second person plural.
entries.refers to: the people addressed, two or more; human only.
entries.agreement: plural verb: you all are, you all were, have you all decided.
entries.pattern: you all [plural verb] · [verb] you all (thank you all) · you all's [noun] (Southern possessive) · quantifier float, you [verb] all (you have all seen the memo)
entries.contrast: this entry is two things wearing one spelling, and stress separates them. As a pronoun, you all is the uncontracted Southern plural, stressed on all as a unit with you (You all are invited), and it is the ancestor of y'all — many Southern speakers use both, with you all the more careful or emphatic choice. As ordinary quantification, you all is just the pronoun you with the floating quantifier all attached, and it means "all of you" in the arithmetic sense: You all failed the quiz (every one of you), I thank you all, You have all seen the memo — where all has floated away from you entirely, proving it is a separate word. That second use is standard everywhere in the country and is not regional at all. The determiner all is covered in the determiner dictionary.
entries.see also: y'all, all y'all, you guys, you all (personal), all

entries.meaning: You, plural — the informal plural you of most of the country, gender-neutral in use if not in form.
examples: Are you guys coming to the show tonight?
I told you guys the train leaves at 7:04.
Do you guys want to split an appetizer?
You guys were right about the shortcut.
Hey, you guys — the meeting moved to the third floor.
It was good seeing you guys again.
entries.pronunciation note: weak form /jəˈɡaɪz/, and in fast speech the whole phrase can run to /jəɡaɪz/
entries.русский: вы, ребята — разг.; общеамериканское «вы» к группе, независимо от пола
entries.register: informal, spoken; the default plural you for most of the United States outside the South
entries.type: second-person plural pronoun; general American informal
entries.person / number: second person plural.
entries.refers to: the people addressed, two or more, human — and, for most speakers, regardless of gender: a group of women is routinely addressed as you guys. That mismatch between the literal guys and the actual reference is exactly why many speakers and institutions are now retreating from it.
entries.agreement: plural verb: you guys are, you guys were, do you guys want. The possessive is you guys's /ˈɡaɪzɪz/, which is awkward enough that speakers usually rephrase (your car rather than you guys's car).
entries.pattern: you guys [plural verb] · [verb] you guys · you guys's [noun] (avoided in writing) · hey, you guys (vocative)
entries.contrast: you guys is to the North, West, and Midwest what y'all is to the South, and the two are in open competition. You guys is the more widespread; y'all is the one gaining ground, partly because it carries no gender. Many American workplaces and schools now discourage you guys for mixed or female groups and suggest y'all, everyone, folks, or all of you instead. Note that in this use guys is not the plural noun guys — it has bleached into part of the pronoun, which is why you guys can address a group of women while those guys cannot describe them. Regional relatives reinforce their pronoun the same way: youse guys, yinz guys, y'uns guys.
entries.see also: y'all, you all, youse, yinz, you lot, you guys (personal)

entries.meaning: You, plural — the British and Irish informal plural, with a built-in note of impatience. Listed here so an American recognizes it; not for American use.
examples: What have you lot done to the kitchen? (British)
You lot had better be ready when the coach arrives.
I'm not driving you lot anywhere until this car is cleaned out.
Are you lot coming to the pub or not?
You lot never listen to a word I say.
Right, you lot — books away.
entries.pronunciation note: British /juːˈlɒt/
entries.русский: вы там, вы все — разг., брит. и ирл. (не амер.), с оттенком досады
entries.register: informal, spoken, and mildly brusque or exasperated
entries.type: second-person plural pronoun; British and Irish, not American
entries.person / number: second person plural.
entries.refers to: the group addressed, human, usually with a faint edge of impatience or affectionate disparagement — a teacher to a class, a parent to children, a friend to a rowdy table.
entries.agreement: plural verb: you lot are, you lot were, have you lot finished?
entries.pattern: you lot [plural verb] · [verb] you lot · oi, you lot (vocative, British)
entries.contrast: flagged as not American. An American may read or hear you lot constantly in British television, novels, and football commentary, but producing it in American speech sounds like costume. Its American equivalents are you guys and y'all, neither of which carries the built-in note of exasperation that you lot does: What have you lot done now? is a complaint in a way that What have you guys done now? is not. British English also uses you two, you three, and this lot the same way.
entries.see also: you guys, y'all, youse

entries.meaning: You, plural — the Appalachian you ones, in its fullest spelling.
examples: Are you'uns headed to town this morning?
You'uns are more than welcome to stay for supper.
I reckon you'uns know the way from here.
Did you'uns get any rain over on your side of the ridge?
You'uns left the porch light on all night.
I'll ride down with you'uns if there's room.
entries.pronunciation note: also /ˈjuənz/ when said slowly; the apostrophe marks the swallowed o of ones
entries.русский: вы (мн. ч.) — диал., разг.; сельское, из you ones; за пределами региона просторечно
entries.register: informal and spoken; strongly rural and regional, and stigmatized outside its home ground
entries.type: second-person plural pronoun; regional
entries.person / number: second person plural.
entries.refers to: the people addressed, two or more; human only. Associative use of a household is common (Are you'uns coming for Christmas?).
entries.agreement: plural verb: you'uns are, you'uns were, do you'uns want.
entries.pattern: you'uns [plural verb] · [verb] you'uns · you'uns's [noun] (possessive, rare in writing)
entries.contrast: you'uns is transparently you ones — the same strategy as the Scots-Irish you ones that the settlers of Appalachia brought with them, and the same strategy that produced yinz at the far end of the erosion. Its territory is Appalachia, the Southern Midland, West Virginia, eastern Ohio, and western Pennsylvania, overlapping with but distinct from the y'all country to the south. It is the most rural-sounding of the American plurals and the one most likely to draw a reaction outside its region, which is worth knowing before imitating it.
entries.see also: y'uns, yinz, y'all, we'uns, yourn, you'uns (personal)

entries.meaning: You, plural — the Northeastern urban form, spelled without the e.
examples: Yous better get moving if you want a seat.
Are yous coming down the shore this weekend?
I already told yous twice.
Did yous two finish the job or not?
Yous guys never call anymore.
What do yous want on the pizza?
entries.pronunciation note: identical to use and to the plural of ewe
entries.русский: вы (мн. ч.) — прост., диал.; рабочие кварталы Северо-Востока США
entries.register: informal and spoken; working-class urban Northeast, and nonstandard everywhere
entries.type: second-person plural pronoun; regional
entries.person / number: second person plural.
entries.refers to: the people addressed, two or more; human only.
entries.agreement: plural verb: yous are, yous were, did yous hear.
entries.pattern: yous [plural verb] · [verb] yous · yous guys (reinforced) · yous two
entries.contrast: yous and youse are one word in two spellings, and nothing but the spelling separates them — yous is the more transparent (you + the regular plural -s), youse the more common in print. Its territory is New York City, northern New Jersey, Philadelphia, Boston, Chicago's older neighborhoods, and Irish-American communities generally, with parallel forms in Irish, Scouse, and Australian English. Unlike y'all, it has not spread and has not shed its class marking: it reads as working-class urban wherever it appears, and no editor will let it through outside quoted speech.
entries.see also: youse, y'all, yinz, you guys

entries.meaning: You, plural — the Northeastern urban form, in its usual spelling.
examples: Youse guys want anything from the deli?
Are youse going to the wake tomorrow?
I'll save seats for youse.
Youse have no idea what I put up with.
What are youse looking at?
Tell youse what — I'll drive.
entries.pronunciation note: the -e is silent; identical in sound to yous
entries.русский: вы (мн. ч.) — прост., диал.; тот же yous, другой вариант написания
entries.register: informal and spoken; working-class urban Northeast; nonstandard and class-marked
entries.type: second-person plural pronoun; regional
entries.person / number: second person plural.
entries.refers to: the people addressed, two or more; human only.
entries.agreement: plural verb: youse are, youse were, have youse eaten?
entries.pattern: youse [plural verb] · [verb] youse · youse guys (the commonest form of all) · [preposition] youse
entries.contrast: youse is yous with a fuller spelling and is the version most often written down, above all in the fixed phrase youse guys, which doubles the plural marking exactly as y'uns guys and yinz guys do. Against y'all, the difference is region and reputation: both are efficient repairs to the missing plural you, but y'all has drifted upward into general informal use while youse stayed put and stayed stigmatized — it is the American pronoun most likely to be used in fiction as a shorthand for a character's class and neighborhood. Recognize it; do not write it except in dialogue.
entries.see also: yous, you guys, y'all, yinz, youse (personal)

entries.meaning: Who, exhaustively; what, exhaustively. The Southern question words that ask for the whole list rather than one answer.
examples: Who all is coming to the reunion? (Southern; standard Who is coming?)
Who all did you invite to the wedding? (object of invite)
What all did she say about the offer? (object)
I don't know who all he told about the layoffs. (embedded relative)
Who all's truck is parked behind the barn? (possessive)
To who all did the letter go, exactly? (after a preposition)
Standard: Who came, and what did she tell them? — with all of them or everything added if the whole list is what you want.
entries.pronunciation note: /ɑl/ for the cot–caught merged majority; the stress falls on all, which is what marks the two words as a single pronoun rather than a question word with a stray quantifier after it
entries.русский: кто все, что всё — диал. (Юг США); вопрос об исчерпывающем составе
entries.case: who all takes the case of who — subject in who all came?, object in who all did you invite? and to who all did he send it?; the formal object whom all exists but is vanishingly rare, and whom is retreating from this position exactly as it is retreating everywhere else. What all is invariant, with no case at all
entries.register: informal and spoken; Southern American English, the South Midland, and Appalachia
entries.type: interrogative and relative pronouns, exhaustive; regional
entries.person / number: who all is human and open in number — grammatically it can take either verb, but it always expects a list. What all is third person, non-human, invariant.
entries.refers to: who all — the complete set of people who did, will do, or were affected by something. what all — the complete set of things, actions, or facts. Neither refers to a single known individual; asking who all came? when one guest was expected is odd.
entries.agreement: either number is standard within the dialect, and the singular is the more common: who all is coming? alongside who all are coming?; what all was in the box? alongside what all were in the box? Neither is an error. This is the same latitude that none has, and it is not shared by the compounds — everyone, somebody, and nobody take a singular verb only.
entries.pattern: who all [singular verb] (Who all is going?) · who all [auxiliary] [subject] [verb] (Who all did you tell?) · what all [auxiliary] [subject] [verb] (What all did you buy?) · embedded: [verb] who all / what all [clause] (I don't know who all he told) · who all's [noun] (possessive: whose all is not a form)
entries.contrast: the two words are a unit and cannot be pulled apart — ✗Who did all you tell? is not the same construction and is not English. Keep the pronoun apart from the ordinary floating quantifier, which is standard everywhere and looks similar on the page: in They all came, all has floated off they and can be moved (All of them came), while the all of who all cannot move at all. The nearest standard equivalents are clumsier by design: Who came — all of them?, Which people came?, What else did you buy? The relative use (I don't know who all he told) is the one that most often escapes the dialect, since it fills a real gap in the standard language. The set also runs to where all, when all, and how all in the same regions, though those are adverbs rather than pronouns.
entries.see also: y'all, all y'all, you all, who, what, whom, all

entries.meaning: A coined gender-neutral third-person singular pronoun: e, em, eir, eirs, emself.
examples: If a reader finds an error, e should write to the publisher at the address on the copyright page. (the generic use Spivak's manuals were written for)
Each student brings eir own laptop, and e is responsible for charging it. (determiner and subject in one sentence)
I asked Robin whether the package had reached em yet.
The blue notebook on the table is eirs, not mine.
E taught emself to solder from a library book. (reflexive)
The same sentences with singular they, and the agreement that comes with it: if a reader finds an error, they should write to the publisher; each student brings their own laptop.
entries.pronunciation note: the object em is /ɛm/, the possessive eir /ɛr/ (rhyming with air), eirs /ɛrz/, and the reflexive emself /ɛmˈsɛlf/ · in connected speech em is easily confused with the ordinary weak 'em of them, which is one practical reason some users prefer the spelling ey
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — гендерно-нейтральное 3 л. ед. ч.: e/em/eir/emself
entries.case: subject e; object em; possessive determiner eir; possessive pronoun eirs; reflexive emself
entries.register: neutral where it is used; unfamiliar to most American readers, so writing usually introduces it or glosses it
entries.type: personal pronoun, coined (gender-neutral third person singular)
entries.person / number: third person singular. There is no separate plural — for more than one person, ordinary they and them.
entries.refers to: one person, without specifying gender. It is used both generically (for an unknown or unspecified person, in the slot where a writer might otherwise use he or she) and specifically (for a particular person who uses these forms).
entries.agreement: takes the same third-person singular verb forms as he and she: e is, e has, e goes, e was. This is the practical difference from singular they, which takes are and were — e was late against they were late for the same one person.
entries.pattern: e [singular verb] · [verb] em · eir [noun] (determiner: eir coat) · eirs standing alone (the coat is eirs) · emself as reflexive (e taught emself)
entries.contrast: two closely related sets circulate under the name Spivak pronouns, and they differ in one letter. The set in this entry — e / em / eir / eirs / emself — is the one usually called "the original Spivak," from the mathematician Michael Spivak, who used it in his TeX manuals in the 1980s to write about a reader whose gender he did not know. The other set, ey / em / eir, was proposed by Christine Elverson in 1975 and is formed by knocking the th- off they / them / their; it is now the commoner of the two, largely because a written e is easy to miss and a spoken /i/ is easy to lose. Both were adopted in early text-based online worlds — LambdaMOO offered "Spivak" as a selectable option in the early 1990s — and both are still used. Against singular they, the practical differences are verb agreement (e is / they are) and familiarity: they needs no explanation to any reader, and e usually does. Against ze/hir, another widely used set, the difference is only which forms were coined.
entries.see also: thon, thonself, they, them, themself, they (generic), he (generic), Singular they

entries.meaning: A coined gender-neutral third-person singular pronoun, blended out of he and she, proposed repeatedly and never adopted.
examples: If a driver runs a red light, heesh will be photographed and mailed a citation. (the generic sentence the coinage was built for)
Whoever wrote the note did not sign it, and heesh has not come forward since.
The proposal was that a teacher should be free to write heesh rather than he or she on a form.
Each candidate is told the result as soon as heesh has finished the last section.
A subscriber may cancel at any time, and heesh will be refunded the unused balance.
What Americans write instead: if a driver runs a red light, they will be photographed.
entries.pronunciation note: one syllable, rhyming with leash; no weak form, because the word is written far more often than it is said, and most of the people who have written it have never heard it spoken
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — «он-она», слияние he и she, без полной парадигмы
entries.case: no settled paradigm. Heesh is a subject form; the object and possessive slots were never agreed on, and different proposers left the word invariant, paired it with hisher and himer, or simply fell back on his or her. Nothing standardized, because the word never got enough use to standardize anything
entries.register: coined and effectively dead. It belongs to the long list of failed epicene pronouns, and an American meets it only in an article or a dictionary note about that list
entries.type: personal pronoun, coined (gender-neutral third person singular) — a blend of he and she
entries.person / number: third person singular. There is no plural — for more than one person, ordinary they and them.
entries.refers to: one person, without specifying gender. In every recorded use it is generic — an unknown or unspecified person, in the slot where a writer might otherwise put he or she — rather than a form any particular person has asked to be called by.
entries.agreement: takes the same third-person singular verb as he and she: heesh is, heesh was, heesh has, heesh goes. This is the practical difference from singular they, which takes are and were for the same one person.
entries.pattern: heesh [singular verb] · heesh is / heesh was / heesh has · the other slots are unsettled, so a writer using it either leaves heesh invariant (I told heesh) or falls back on him or her and his or her
entries.contrast: heesh is a blend — the front of he welded to the back of she — so both source words stay visible in it. That transparency is the argument its proposers made for it and the objection its critics made against it, and the word got no measurable use either way. Compare hesh, the same idea worked out into a full three-case paradigm; thon, a blend of that one; and e, which is a subtraction from an existing word rather than a fusion of two. The written s/he does the same blending on the page and is the only member of this family with real currency, and even it is confined to writing. None of this is part of any traditional English paradigm, and no measurable number of American speakers uses it. The form that actually filled the gap is singular they, which is native, six hundred years old, and now recognized as standard by Chicago, AP, APA, MLA, and Merriam-Webster.
entries.see also: hesh, ou, thon, thonself, e, they, they (generic), he (generic), Singular they

entries.meaning: A coined gender-neutral set with a full case paradigm: hesh, himer, hizer, himerself.
examples: If a patient misses an appointment, hesh will be charged for the visit.
The committee asked each nominee to send hizer résumé by Friday. (the possessive determiner)
Nobody answered, so I left the message and hoped somebody would pass it to himer. (the object)
Whoever left that truck running should move it before hesh gets a ticket.
Every juror must decide the case for himerself, on the evidence and nothing else. (the reflexive)
The blue notebook is hizer, not mine. (the possessive standing alone)
What American writers use instead: if a patient misses an appointment, they will be charged.
entries.pronunciation note: one syllable, rhyming with mesh; the object himer is /ˈhɪmɚ/ · HIM-er and the possessive hizer /ˈhɪzɚ/ · HIZ-er, both stressed on the first syllable. The h drops in connected speech exactly as it does in him and his, so tell himer is /ˈtɛlɪmɚ/
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — гендерно-нейтральный набор hesh/himer/hizer
entries.case: a full three-way paradigm, which is what separates this set from heesh: subject hesh; object himer; possessive determiner and possessive pronoun hizer (hizer coat, the coat is hizer); reflexive himerself where a proposer supplied one
entries.register: coined; circulated in American discussions of sexist language in the 1970s, adopted by nobody, and obsolete in practice
entries.type: personal pronoun set, coined (gender-neutral third person singular) — three blends built by one rule
entries.person / number: third person singular. No plural of its own.
entries.refers to: one person, gender unspecified — used generically, for an unknown or unspecified person, in the slot a writer might otherwise fill with he or she.
entries.agreement: third-person singular verb, like he and she: hesh is, hesh has, hesh was, hesh goes. Not ✗ hesh are, which is singular they's pattern, not this one's.
entries.pattern: hesh [singular verb] · [verb] himer (object: tell himer) · hizer [noun] (determiner: hizer résumé) · hizer standing alone (the coat is hizer) · himerself (reflexive)
entries.contrast: every form in the set is a blend of the corresponding masculine and feminine pair — he + she → hesh, him + her → himer, his + her → hizer — so the whole paradigm is generated by one rule, which is more than most coinages manage and is the reason it is worth a separate entry from heesh. Against e, the difference is method: the Spivak set is made by subtraction (they minus th-), this one by fusion. Against thon, the difference is age and standing: thon spent sixty-six years in American dictionaries and hesh never entered one. Against singular they, the practical difference is agreement (hesh is against they are) and familiarity. These forms are not part of any traditional English paradigm and are not used by any appreciable number of speakers; whether to use any coined set for a particular person is settled the way a name is settled — by asking.
entries.see also: heesh, ou, thon, thonself, e, themself, they (generic), Singular they

entries.meaning: He, she, or it — one form for all three. The eighteenth-century English dialect pronoun that filled the gender-neutral gap by inheritance rather than by design.
examples: Ou will — the Gloucestershire form its recorder glossed as "he will, she will, or it will."
Ou is gone to market and will not be back before dark.
If anybody calls for me, tell them ou has left for the day.
Ou said nothing at all, and nobody could tell whether ou was pleased or not.
The dialect that kept ou had one third-person singular where the standard language had three.
Modern English: they — the native form that now does the same work, and the only one in general use.
entries.pronunciation note: recorded as an unstressed /ə/ in running speech — ou will came out roughly /ə ˈwɪl/ — and it has no stressed form at all, which is exactly how a pronoun this small gets lost
entries.русский: он, она — диал., устар.; унаследованное бесполое местоимение 3 л. ед. ч., подлежащее
entries.case: subject only. It is recorded in the subject slot and nowhere else; the ordinary him, her, and it did the object work in the same dialect, and his and her the possessive
entries.register: dialectal and obsolete. An eighteenth-century English West Country form, written down by an observer rather than by its speakers, and never carried to America
entries.type: personal pronoun, dialectal and epicene (gender-neutral third person singular) — an inherited form, not a coinage
entries.person / number: third person singular. It covered he, she, and it alike — one form for all three genders.
entries.refers to: one person or thing, without specifying gender. It is the only English pronoun on record that did this job as an ordinary inherited word rather than as somebody's proposal, and that is why it is in this section.
entries.agreement: ordinary third-person singular verb: ou is, ou has, ou will, ou was. Never the plural agreement that singular they takes.
entries.pattern: ou [singular verb] · ou will / ou is / ou has · subject position only — there is no recorded ✗ give it to ou and no recorded possessive
entries.contrast: everything else in this section was invented; ou was inherited. It is a worn-down descendant of Middle English a, itself a reduced form of he, heo, and hit — so the three genders collapsed into one unstressed syllable by ordinary sound change, with nobody deciding anything. That is why the word matters far out of proportion to its size: it is the standing evidence that English can grow a gender-neutral singular on its own, which is also what singular they shows on a much larger scale. It was reported in 1789 by the agricultural writer William Marshall, describing the speech of the Vale of Gloucester, and it is cited in nearly every modern discussion of epicene pronouns for that reason. Do not confuse it with the French où, with the digraph ou, or with the interjection ow.
entries.see also: heesh, hesh, thon, e, hit, a body, they, they (generic), Singular they

entries.meaning: A gender-neutral third-person singular pronoun coined in 1858 and carried by American dictionaries until 1964.
examples: If a subscriber wishes to cancel, thon must give thirty days' notice. (the kind of sentence Converse coined the word for)
Each candidate will be told the result as soon as thon has finished the last section.
I left a message, but nobody could tell me whether thon had received it.
Every driver is responsible for thon's own tolls. (the possessive, with its unusual apostrophe)
The applicant should sign the form thonself rather than send an agent. (the reflexive)
The same sentences today: if a subscriber wishes to cancel, they must give thirty days' notice.
entries.pronunciation note: voiced th as in this, rhyming with John; also /ðɔn/ where cot and caught are kept apart. The possessive is thon's /ðɑnz/ and the reflexive thonself /ðɑnˈsɛlf/
entries.русский: неологизм, эквивалента в русском нет — гендерно-нейтральное «он/она»; ныне не употребляется
entries.case: thon serves as both subject and object; the possessive is thon's; the reflexive is thonself
entries.register: coined and now obsolete in practice; historically it carried no informality of its own, and it was proposed for ordinary edited prose
entries.type: personal pronoun, coined (gender-neutral third person singular)
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. No plural.
entries.refers to: one person whose gender is unknown, unstated, or irrelevant — the slot filled today by singular they and formerly by generic he.
entries.agreement: third-person singular verb, like he and she: thon is, thon has, thon was, thon knows.
entries.pattern: thon [singular verb] · [verb] thon (object: tell thon) · thon's [noun] (possessive: thon's coat) · thonself (reflexive)
entries.contrast: thon is the most successful failure in the history of English pronoun coinage. It was proposed in 1858 by Charles Crozat Converse, an American lawyer and hymn composer, as a contraction of that one; it was entered in Funk & Wagnalls' Standard Dictionary in 1898 and stayed there until 1964, and it appeared in Webster's Second New International in 1934 — sixty-six years of dictionary standing without ever entering ordinary speech. Its case system is simpler than any other English pronoun's: one form for subject and object, and the ordinary apostrophe-s for the possessive, which no other personal pronoun takes (his, her, their, and its are all apostrophe-free). Against the modern coinages, thon is a blend (that + one), while e and ey are subtractions from existing words, which is part of why the newer sets are easier to learn. Against singular they, thon was designed to answer the objection that they is plural — an objection that has since lost most of its force. Do not confuse thon with the Scots and Ulster demonstrative thon, a live regional word meaning "that one over there," a relative of yon and unrelated to Converse's coinage.
entries.see also: thonself, e, they, they (generic), he (generic), one (generic), yon

entries.meaning: The reflexive of thon: the same person, when that person is both subject and object of the clause.
examples: Each applicant must sign the form thonself.
Thon poured thonself a cup and sat down by the window.
The witness contradicted thonself twice in the space of a page.
Anyone living by thonself out there needs a generator.
The author thonself has said the ending was an accident. (intensive)
The modern equivalents: each applicant must sign the form themself; e poured emself a cup.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on self, exactly as in himself and herself; the plural thonselves was proposed but is not attested in use
entries.русский: неологизм, эквивалента в русском нет — возвратное к thon, «сам себя» без указания пола
entries.register: coined and now obsolete; it appeared in the same dictionaries that carried thon
entries.type: reflexive and intensive pronoun, coined — the reflexive of thon
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. No plural in practice.
entries.refers to: the same person thon refers to, and only when that person is already the subject of the same clause — the ordinary requirement of every English reflexive.
entries.agreement: none of its own; the clause's verb agrees with thon, which is singular (thon washes thonself, never ✗thon wash).
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] thonself (reflexive object) · [preposition] thonself (by thonself, to thonself) · [subject] thonself [verb] (intensive: the author thonself said so)
entries.contrast: thonself is built on the object form thon, following the third-person pattern of himself and themselves rather than the first- and second-person pattern of myself and yourself — which is a small piece of evidence that Converse was thinking carefully, since thon is both subject and object and either analogy was available. The modern counterparts are themself (the singular reflexive of singular they, now recognized by Merriam-Webster and used widely) and emself, the reflexive of the Spivak set. All three do the same job: give a gender-neutral singular a reflexive of its own, which English otherwise lacks.
entries.see also: thon, e, themself, themselves, oneself, reflexive formation

entries.meaning: That person and their family or usual companions. The Southern associative plural, built out of an ordinary coordination that has stopped needing an antecedent.
examples: Mama'n'em are coming over after church. (regional; standard Mama and the rest of the family)
We ran into Ruthie and them at the county fair.
Tell Bob'n'em to bring a cooler and some chairs.
Aunt Della and them have had that place on the lake since the sixties.
I stayed over at my cousin and them's for most of a week. (the possessive on the whole phrase)
Standard: We ran into Ruthie and her family at the fair.
entries.pronunciation note: the reduced form is /nɛm/ · NEM, written 'nem or 'n'em, and it fuses onto the name in front of it: Mama and them → Mama'n'em /ˈmɑmənɛm/, Bob and them → Bob'n'em /ˈbɑbnɛm/. The th of them drops entirely, which is the ordinary weak form /əm/ carried one step further
entries.русский: и его родня, и все свои — диал. (Юг США), разг.: Mama'n'em «мама и её домашние»
entries.case: none of its own; the whole phrase takes whatever case its position calls for (Mama'n'em are coming / we visited Mama'n'em)
entries.register: informal and spoken; Southern American English, African American English, and the South Midland, with a parallel and dem in Hawaiian Creole English and and them in Cajun and Gulf Coast speech
entries.type: associative plural — a postposed phrase that attaches to a personal name or kin term and turns it into "that person and the people who go with them"
entries.person / number: third person plural, always — even though the named person is singular, the phrase as a whole is plural.
entries.refers to: the person named plus their usual people — family, household, in-laws, the friends they arrive with. Human only. The crucial point is that them here has no antecedent: nobody has said who "they" are, and nobody needs to, because the construction means "and the rest of that person's crowd." Guessing the exact membership is the listener's job and rarely matters.
entries.agreement: plural verb: Mama'n'em are coming, Bob and them were already there. ✗Mama'n'em is coming is wrong even in the dialect that produces the phrase.
entries.pattern: [personal name or kin term] and them (Ruthie and them, Aunt Della and them) · [name]'n'em (the reduced spelling) · my cousin and them · as object of a preposition (over at Grandma'n'em's — with the possessive on the end of the whole phrase)
entries.contrast: ordinary English coordination — Bob and them meaning "Bob and those particular people over there" — needs them to point at somebody already identified. The associative and them does not, and that is the whole difference: I ran into Ruthie and them is perfectly informative to a Southern listener who has never met anyone in Ruthie's family. The standard equivalents are all longer: Ruthie and her family, Ruthie and her people, Ruthie's crowd, Ruthie and the rest of them. English is unusual in not having a grammatical associative plural; many languages mark one with an affix, and Southern American English has simply built its own out of the material at hand — the same instinct that produced y'all and you'uns. Note the possessive, which goes on the very end: we stayed at Mama'n'em's, never ✗Mama's'n'em.
entries.see also: them'uns, we'uns, you'uns, y'all, them (dialectal demonstrative), them, 'em

entries.meaning: His, hers, ours, theirs. The rest of the Appalachian -n possessives, whose second-person member is yourn.
examples: Is this coat hisn or yourn? (nonstandard; standard his or yours)
Hern is the one with the dent in the fender. (nonstandard; standard hers)
We keep ourn in the shed and they keep theirn in the barn. (nonstandard; standard ours, theirs)
That old dog of theirn has been in my garden again. (nonstandard, double genitive)
He parked right next to hisn and never said a word. (nonstandard, after a preposition)
Standard: Is this coat his or yours? — Hers is the one with the dent.
entries.pronunciation note: ourn is also /ɑrn/; one syllable each; the -n is a plain consonant, never a separate -en syllable, and the h of hisn and hern drops in connected speech (/ɪzn/, /ɚn/)
entries.русский: его, её, наше, их — прост., диал. (Аппалачи); нелитературные his, hers, ours, theirs
entries.case: possessive, independent — they stand alone and never precede a noun (✗hisn truck; the determiner is his)
entries.register: nonstandard; Appalachian, the Southern Midland, the Ozarks, and older rural speech generally, and a stock marker of that speech in fiction from Twain onward
entries.type: possessive pronouns; nonstandard and regional
entries.person / number: hisn third person singular masculine, hern third person singular feminine, ourn first person plural, theirn third person plural. yourn is the second-person member of the same set, and mine — which already ended in -n — is shared with standard English.
entries.refers to: whatever belongs to the person or people already named. The possessor is human in ordinary use; the thing possessed may be anything at all, singular or plural, count or mass.
entries.agreement: as a subject complement, none of its own; as a subject, the verb agrees with what the pronoun stands for, not with the pronoun's form — hisn is the red one (one truck), theirn are in the barn (several).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] is hisn · hern as subject (hern's the one with the dent) · [verb] theirn (they keep theirn inside) · of ourn (a neighbor of ourn, the double genitive) · [preposition] hisn (next to hisn)
entries.contrast: the standard forms are his, hers, ours, and theirs, and those are the ones to write. What is worth seeing is that these are not sloppy versions of the standard words — they are a rival paradigm, and a regular one. Standard English generalized the -s of his across the whole set (yours, hers, ours, theirs); these dialects generalized the -n of mine and thine instead (yourn, hern, ourn, theirn), a change that happened in the dialects of northern and western England and crossed to Appalachia with their speakers. Two systems, opposite starting points, each internally consistent — which is why hisn is instantly parsable to people who would never say it. None of them takes an apostrophe, because nothing has been contracted away: ✗his'n, ✗her'n, ✗their'n add a mark for a letter that was never there, and ✗hisn's doubles the possessive. And do not mix the systems: ✗hisn book is wrong twice, since these forms cannot stand in front of a noun at all.
entries.see also: yourn, mines, thine, them (dialectal demonstrative), hisn, hern, ourn, yourn, theirn, hers, theirs, mine

entries.ipa: /ˌhɪz oʊn ˈsɛlf/, /ˌhɚ oʊn ˈsɛlf/, /ˌðɛr oʊn ˈsɛlvz/
entries.meaning: Himself, herself, themselves — with own wedged in for emphasis. Nonstandard, and heard across the South and the Midland.
examples: He built the whole porch hisownself, in one August. (nonstandard; standard himself)
She drove all the way to Memphis by herownself. (nonstandard; standard by herself)
The preacher hisownself came out to the house. (nonstandard, intensive)
They painted the barn theirownselves rather than wait on the co-op. (nonstandard)
He never could look after hisownself, not even as a grown man. (nonstandard)
Standard: He built the whole porch himself; she drove to Memphis all by herself.
entries.pronunciation note: main stress on self, secondary on own; the h drops in connected speech, giving /ɪzoʊnˈsɛlf/ and /ɚoʊnˈsɛlf/, exactly as it does in hisself
entries.русский: он сам лично, она сама лично — прост., диал.; усиленное himself, herself
entries.register: nonstandard; Southern, South Midland, Appalachian, and older rural speech, and African American English; a stock marker of that speech in fiction from Twain and Harris through Faulkner
entries.type: emphatic reflexive and intensive pronouns; nonstandard and regional
entries.person / number: hisownself third person singular masculine, herownself third person singular feminine, theirownselves third person plural. The first- and second-person members are usually written as separate words (my own self, your own self) and are much less marked.
entries.refers to: the same antecedent himself, herself, and themselves refer to — a person already the subject of the same clause — with added emphasis: not merely "he did it" but "he did it and nobody helped."
entries.agreement: none of their own; the clause's verb agrees with its subject.
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] hisownself (reflexive object) · by hisownself / all by herownself (the commonest slot, meaning "alone, unaided") · [subject] hisownself [verb] (intensive: the preacher hisownself said it) · theirownselves after a plural subject
entries.contrast: the standard forms are himself, herself, and themselves, and for the extra emphasis standard English says his very own self, all by himself, or he himself. What makes these forms interesting is that they are doubly regularized: hisself already rebuilds the reflexive on the possessive (his + self) instead of the object form, and hisownself then wedges in the intensifier own, which standard English allows in the first and second person (my own self, your own self are both ordinary English) but blocks in the third. Theirownselves goes further still and marks the plural twice, on their and on selves. All of them are logical, all are common in speech across a wide swath of the country, and all will be marked wrong in writing.
entries.see also: hisself, theirselves, ourself, thyself, himself, herself, themselves, reflexive formation

entries.meaning: Himself. The regularized reflexive — logical, widespread in speech, and nonstandard in writing.
examples: He fixed the transmission hisself. (nonstandard; standard himself)
He was setting out there by hisself all afternoon. (nonstandard)
The man never gave hisself any credit. (nonstandard)
He hisself admitted he'd been wrong. (nonstandard, intensive)
Don't worry about him — he can look after hisself. (nonstandard)
He talked hisself right out of the job. (nonstandard)
entries.pronunciation note: commonly /ɪzˈsɛlf/ with the h dropped in connected speech
entries.русский: себя, сам — прост., диал.; нелитературная форма himself
entries.register: nonstandard; regionally ordinary in Southern, Appalachian, and rural vernacular English and in African American English, but marked as an error in all writing and in standardized testing
entries.type: reflexive and intensive pronoun; nonstandard
entries.person / number: third person singular masculine.
entries.refers to: a single male antecedent that is already the subject of the same clause — exactly what himself refers to.
entries.agreement: none of its own.
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] hisself · [preposition] hisself (by hisself, to hisself) · [subject] hisself [verb] (intensive: he hisself said it)
entries.contrast: the standard form is himself, and that is the one to use. What is worth understanding is that hisself is the regular form and himself the irregular one: English builds first- and second-person reflexives on the possessive (myself, yourself, ourselves, thyself) and third-person reflexives on the object pronoun (himself, themselves) — with herself sitting on the fence, since her is both the possessive and the object form of she, which is part of why a paradigm this mixed keeps getting regularized. Hisself and theirselves simply extend the majority pattern across the whole paradigm, which is why children produce them without ever hearing them. Logic does not help here: they have been nonstandard for three centuries and will be marked wrong every time.
entries.see also: theirselves, ourself, thyself, himself, hisself (reflexive), reflexive formation

entries.meaning: It. The Old English form of it with its h still attached, kept in Appalachian and Ozark speech under stress.
examples: Hit was the coldest winter anybody in the county could remember. (regional; standard it)
Hit's a long way to the head of that hollow, and hit's farther coming back.
Give hit here before you drop it. (the stressed and unstressed forms in one sentence, which is the dialect's actual rule)
Hit don't make a particle of difference now.
Hit ain't the years, it's the miles.
Hit rained every day of that trip. (the dummy subject of weather)
Standard: It was the coldest winter anybody could remember.
entries.pronunciation note: stressed only — and the weak form is modern it /ɪt/, which is the whole history of the word in one line: the h survives under stress and drops everywhere else, so the same speaker says Hit's a long way and I don't like it in the same breath
entries.русский: оно, это — устар. и диал.; старая форма it, где h сохранилось под ударением
entries.case: none in the dialect: the same form serves as subject and object (hit is cold, give hit here), and the possessive is ordinary its — Old English used his for it, which is why the King James Bible has his where a modern text has its
entries.register: archaic (standard English down to about 1600, and normal in Chaucer and in the King James Bible) and regional (Appalachian, the Ozarks, and older Southern Highland speech, where it survives in stressed position); heavily stigmatized outside those regions
entries.type: personal pronoun, archaic and dialectal — the older form of it
entries.person / number: third person singular, neuter. There is no plural — that is them or standard they.
entries.refers to: everything modern it refers to: a thing, an animal, a situation, the weather, and the empty dummy subject (hit's raining, hit's a shame). It can also carry a whole clause as its referent (hit don't matter what he said). Never a person, except as it can be (hit's the baby).
entries.agreement: singular verb: hit is, hit was, hit has. Where the dialect that keeps hit also has its own verb concord — hit don't matter, hit ain't — that is a property of the dialect's verbs, not of the pronoun, and the two should not be filed together.
entries.pattern: hit [singular verb] (stressed subject at the head of a clause, where the h survives) · hit's [complement] (hit's a shame, hit's cold) · hit don't / hit ain't · [verb] hit (object, though the unstressed it is commoner here) · hit as dummy subject of weather and time
entries.contrast: standard it is hit with the h worn off. Old English had hit, Middle English kept it, and standard English lost the h in unstressed position and then generalized the h-less form to every position. Appalachian and Ozark speech kept the older distribution instead: h under stress, no h elsewhere. That makes hit a conservative feature and not a corruption — the same relationship the h-dropping of ordinary connected speech has to him and her, where every American says /ˈtɛlɚ/ for tell her without noticing. Compare hisself, which is likewise more regular than the standard form it replaces. Do not confuse the pronoun with the verb hit, and do not write it in any register where you would not write them (dialectal demonstrative).
entries.see also: hisself, ou, them (dialectal demonstrative), this'n, that'n, we'uns, it, it (weather, time, and distance)

entries.meaning: The subject pronoun I pushed into an object slot inside a coordinated phrase — the classic hypercorrection.
examples: ✗ Between you and I, the numbers don't add up. → between you and me
✗ He gave the tickets to my brother and I. → to my brother and me
✗ Thanks for inviting my wife and I to the ceremony. → my wife and me
✗ This is just for Marcus and I to sort out. → for Marcus and me
✗ There has always been an understanding between she and I. → between her and me
Correct: The manager spoke with Priya and me for an hour. (deletion test: spoke with me)
entries.pronunciation note: the subject pronoun I has no weak form — which is part of why speakers reach for it when they want to sound careful
entries.русский: «я» вместо «меня» — гиперкоррекция: between you and I вместо me; ошибка
entries.case: subject (in a position that requires the object case)
entries.register: nonstandard, and specifically a hypercorrection — an error produced by trying to avoid an error
entries.type: personal pronoun, subject form, used wrongly in an object slot
entries.person / number: first person singular.
entries.refers to: the speaker. The problem is never the reference; it is the case.
entries.agreement: none — as an object, it triggers no agreement at all, which is exactly why nothing in the sentence flags the mistake.
entries.pattern: the error appears only inside coordination: [preposition] [noun/pronoun] and I (✗between you and I, ✗for my wife and I) · [verb] [noun] and I (✗he invited Bob and I) · it essentially never occurs alone (nobody says ✗he invited I)
entries.contrast: the object form is me, and the fix is the deletion test: remove the other person and listen. ✗Between you and I → ✗between I → between you and me. ✗He gave it to my wife and I → ✗to I → to my wife and me. ✗Thanks for inviting my husband and I → inviting me. This error is now more common in educated American speech than the me error it is overcorrecting for, precisely because so many speakers were taught in childhood that me and him went was wrong and drew the wrong conclusion — that me is always the vulgar choice. It is not: me is simply the object form, and after a preposition or a verb it is the only correct form. Honesty requires two footnotes. Shakespeare wrote all debts are cleared between you and I (The Merchant of Venice), so the construction is old; and between you and I is now so frequent that some linguists treat coordinated pronouns as a special case. Neither will save you: every American editor, teacher, and standardized test marks it wrong.
entries.see also: me (nonstandard as subject), I, me, after a preposition, always the object case

entries.meaning: The object pronoun me used as a subject inside a coordinated phrase — the most common nonstandard pronoun form in American speech.
examples: ✗ Me and Jim went down to the lake. → Jim and I went down to the lake
✗ Me and my sister split the cost. → My sister and I split the cost
✗ Him and me were the last two out of the building. → He and I were the last two out
✗ Me and her have known each other since third grade. → She and I have known each other
Correct and standard: Who's there? — It's me.
Correct and standard: She got there before me, and she's faster than me anyway.
entries.pronunciation note: unstressed /mi/; in fast speech me and him runs to /mi ən ɪm/
entries.русский: «меня» вместо «я» — прост.; me and him went, обычно в устной речи
entries.case: object (in a position that requires the subject case)
entries.register: nonstandard in writing; extremely common in ordinary American speech at every social level, especially in children's speech
entries.type: personal pronoun, object form, used in a subject slot
entries.person / number: first person singular.
entries.refers to: the speaker.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the coordinated subject as a whole, which is plural: Me and him were late — the agreement is not the problem; the case is.
entries.pattern: the error appears only in coordination and only at the front of a clause: me and [noun/pronoun] [verb] (✗me and Jim went) · [noun] and me [verb] (✗Jim and me went) · it never happens alone (nobody says ✗me went)
entries.contrast: the subject form is I, and the deletion test settles it instantly: ✗Me and Jim went to the game → ✗Me went → I and Jim went → politely reordered, Jim and I went to the game. Two things are worth being honest about. First, this is genuinely nonstandard and will be corrected by teachers and editors, so it is worth training out of your writing. Second, several near neighbors that sound similar are perfectly standard and should not be overcorrected: It's me — standard American English in speech and in edited writing, and the normal form after be; It is I is not an error either, but it is stiff enough to sound like a costume, and correcting anyone into it is worse than leaving them alone. Likewise Me too, Who wants coffee? — Me, Me neither, and He's taller than me (standard in American English alongside the more formal than I am). The genuine error is narrow: the object form standing as the subject of a finite verb. Overcorrecting past it produces the opposite mistake, I in object position.
entries.see also: I (hypercorrect in object position), me, I, methinks, case follows function

entries.meaning: Myself. The ordinary weak pronunciation of myself, written down — an Irish English marker rather than an American form.
examples: I'll see to it meself and be done with it. (intensive)
I cut meself on the tin, and it bled for an hour. (reflexive)
I was sitting by meself at the back of the hall the whole evening.
Sure, I wasn't meself at all that week.
It was meself that told him, and I'd tell him again tomorrow. (the Irish English cleft, where standard English wants I)
I kept the news to meself until the papers were signed.
Standard American: I'll see to it myself; I cut myself on the tin.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on self; also /məˈsɛlf/ with a plain schwa. The first syllable is the weak my /mɪ/ or /mə/, never the full /maɪ/ — which is the entire point of the spelling: meself writes down the ordinary unstressed pronunciation of myself
entries.русский: себя, сам — диал. (ирл. и др.); запись безударного произношения myself
entries.register: dialectal; Irish English above all, and Newfoundland, older Northern English, and Scots. In American writing it is almost always a novelist's marker for an Irish or Irish-American voice rather than a feature of any American dialect
entries.type: reflexive and intensive pronoun — a dialectal and eye-dialect spelling of myself
entries.person / number: first person singular. The plural is ourselves — there is no ✗ usselves in the same dialects.
entries.refers to: the speaker, and, as a reflexive, only when the speaker is already the subject of the same clause (I cut meself).
