As an intensive it refers to the speaker for emphasis (I saw it meself), and in the Irish English cleft it stands where standard English wants a plain I (it was meself that told him).
entries.agreement: none of its own; the clause's verb agrees with its subject, which for the reflexive use is I (I was sitting by meself).
entries.pattern: [verb] meself (reflexive object: I cut meself) · [preposition] meself (by meself, to meself) · I [verb] meself (intensive: I'll do it meself) · be meself (I wasn't meself that day) · it was meself that [verb] (the Irish English cleft)
entries.contrast: the standard form is myself, and the two are the same word: myself is my + self, and meself is what that becomes when the possessive reduces to /mə/ — which happens in every variety of English, standard American included. Nearly every American who says myself at speed is saying something close to meself; what makes it dialectal is writing it down. So do not read it as a case error on the pattern of ✗ me and him went: it is a spelling of the weak form, not an object pronoun doing a subject's job, and the deletion test has nothing to catch here. It is also unlike hisself and theirselves, which really are different formations — those replace an object form with a possessive one, while meself was built on the possessive all along. What is genuinely syntactic in Irish English is the cleft — it was meself that told him, where standard English wants it was I who told him or I told him — and that is a difference in grammar, not in spelling.
entries.see also: hisself, theirselves, hisownself, herownself, theirownselves, ourself, thyself, myself, reflexive formation

entries.meaning: Mine. The regularized first-person possessive pronoun — logical, widespread in speech, and nonstandard in writing.
examples: That jacket on the chair is mines. (nonstandard; standard mine)
Mines is the one with the cracked screen. (nonstandard, as subject)
A friend of mines works over at the plant. (nonstandard, double genitive — the commonest context)
She parked right next to mines. (nonstandard, after a preposition)
They took hers and they took mines too. (nonstandard, as the object of a verb)
Standard: That jacket is mine, and a friend of mine has the other one. — and, with the contraction, Mine's the blue one.
entries.pronunciation note: one syllable, rhyming with lines; identical in sound to the plural noun mines and to the contraction mine's (= mine is)
entries.русский: мой, моё — прост.; нелитературная форма mine: that's mines
entries.case: possessive, independent — it stands alone and never precedes a noun (✗mines car; the determiner is my)
entries.register: nonstandard; a regular feature of African American English and of Chicano English, common in working-class speech generally, and produced by children of every background before school trains it out
entries.type: possessive pronoun; nonstandard
entries.person / number: first person singular. Invariant for the number of the thing possessed: that book is mines, those books are mines.
entries.refers to: whatever belongs to the speaker. The possessor is always the speaker; the thing possessed may be anything at all, count or mass, singular or plural.
entries.agreement: as a subject complement, none of its own; as a subject, the verb agrees with what mines stands for, not with the -s on the pronoun — mines is the blue one (one car), mines are on the table (several keys). The -s is a possessive marker, not a plural, and reading it as one is the commonest way people mis-hear the form.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] is mines · mines as subject (mines is over there) · of mines (a friend of mines, the double genitive — the commonest context of all) · [preposition] mines (next to mines) · [verb] mines (they took mines)
entries.contrast: the standard form is mine, and that is the one to write. What makes mines interesting is that it is a regularization running the opposite way from hisn, hern, ourn, theirn. Standard English generalized the -s of his across nearly the whole independent paradigm — yours, hers, ours, theirs — and then left mine behind as the one holdout; mines simply finishes the job, which is why it is so easy to produce and so hard to argue with on logical grounds. The -n dialects went the other way and generalized mine's own -n instead (yourn, hern, ourn, theirn). Three systems, one paradigm, and only the middle one gets past an editor. Like every possessive pronoun, it never takes an apostrophe: ✗mine's is not a spelling of this word but the contraction of mine is (Mine's the blue one), and that contraction is perfectly standard — which is part of why the spoken forms are so easily confused.
entries.see also: hisn, hern, ourn, theirn, yourn, thine, mine, hers, theirs, my

entries.meaning: Nothing; nobody — negated twice. The negative pronouns as they appear in negative concord, where the second negative reinforces the first instead of canceling it.
examples: I didn't do nothing wrong. (nonstandard; standard I didn't do anything wrong or I did nothing wrong)
He don't know nobody on that side of town. (nonstandard; standard doesn't know anybody)
Nobody never said a word about the money. (nonstandard as subject; standard Nobody ever said)
Ain't nobody home. (vernacular, with the auxiliary fronted; standard Nobody is home)
She ain't got nothing to prove to nobody. (nonstandard, marked three times over)
Standard: I didn't see anything, and I told nobody about it. (each negative marked once)
entries.pronunciation note: the d of nobody taps to [ɾ]; in negative concord the sentence keeps one falling contour with the main stress on the pronoun — I didn't do nothing
entries.русский: ничего, никто — прост.; двойное отрицание: I didn't do nothing «я ничего не делал»
entries.register: nonstandard in Standard American English, marked wrong in all edited writing and on every standardized test — and at the same time completely systematic and rule-governed in African American English and in Southern, Appalachian, and working-class urban vernacular English nationwide. There is no single region to name because there is no single region: negative concord is the majority pattern across the world's Englishes, it was ordinary in Chaucer and Shakespeare, and Standard English is the outlier that dropped it
entries.type: indefinite pronouns used inside negative concord, the construction usually called the double negative
entries.person / number: third person singular, both of them. Nobody and no one are human; nothing is non-human.
entries.refers to: no person (nobody, no one) and no thing (nothing). The reference does not change when the negative is doubled: I didn't see nothing means I saw nothing, never I saw something.
entries.agreement: singular verb, with or without the second negative: nobody knows, nothing works, no one is coming, nobody never said a word. Doubling the negation does nothing to agreement, so ✗nobody know is a separate error, not part of this pattern. Compare none, which is the one negative pronoun that takes either number — none of them is and none of them are are both standard, with the plural the ordinary default — while nobody and nothing are singular, always.
entries.pattern: [negated verb] + nothing/nobody (I didn't say nothing, he don't know nobody) · nobody/nothing + [negated verb] (nobody never called) · ain't nobody / ain't nothing + [predicate], with the auxiliary fronted (Ain't nobody home) · three or more markings in one clause (I ain't never told nobody nothing)
entries.contrast: Standard English marks the negative once, and it offers two ways to do it: negate the verb and use the nonassertive form (I didn't see anything), or leave the verb positive and let the pronoun carry the negation (I saw nothing). Choose one; using both is what gets marked. The schoolroom argument that "two negatives make a positive" is imported from logic and has never described English — I didn't see nothing has never once been understood as I saw something by any listener. The second negative is emphasis, and what it signals socially is which variety the speaker is using, which is exactly why it is worth recognizing, worth respecting in the varieties that own it, and worth keeping out of a cover letter. One lookalike is genuinely standard and does cancel: not uncommon, not unlike, not without merit, where a negative prefix under a negated verb yields a deliberately hedged positive. Another is not a double negative at all: I don't know nothing about it is concord, but I don't know anything about it is the standard equivalent, and I know nothing about it is its more formal twin.
entries.see also: nothing (negative concord), ain't nobody, nobody, nothing, none, no

entries.meaning: The singular reflexive of a plural-form we: the royal and editorial reflexive, and a modern nonstandard collective one.
examples: "Ourself will mingle with society, and play the humble host." (Macbeth — the royal we)
We have considered the petition and will rule upon it ourself. (ceremonial)
In this column we have never allowed ourself the luxury of a prediction. (editorial we)
✗ As a company, we should ask ourself whether this is who we want to be. → ourselves
✗ We have to be honest with ourself about the numbers. → ourselves
Standard: We gave ourselves an extra day to finish the audit.

senses.head: The royal or editorial reflexive (archaic, ceremonial)
body: With a we that names one person by convention — a monarch, a pope, a judge speaking for the bench, an editorial page. Correct within that convention and nowhere else.

senses.head: The collective reflexive (modern, nonstandard)
body: With a we that names a group treated as a single body: as a nation, we must ask ourself what we have become. Spreading, but an editor will change it to ourselves.
examples: "Ourself will mingle with society, and play the humble host." (Macbeth — the royal we)
We have considered the petition and will rule upon it ourself. (ceremonial)
In this column we have never allowed ourself the luxury of a prediction. (editorial we)
✗ As a company, we should ask ourself whether this is who we want to be. → ourselves
✗ We have to be honest with ourself about the numbers. → ourselves
Standard: We gave ourselves an extra day to finish the audit.

entries.pronunciation note: also /aʊrˈsɛlf/; stress on self
entries.русский: мы сами (об одном лице) — устар., «королевское мы»; в совр. речи нелитературно
entries.register: archaic and ceremonial (the royal or editorial we); nonstandard in present-day general use
entries.type: reflexive pronoun; archaic in the royal use, nonstandard in the modern one
entries.person / number: first person; plural in form, singular in reference — that mismatch is the whole point of the word.
entries.refers to: a we that names one person: a monarch using the royal plural, an editor using the editorial we, or, in the modern nonstandard use, a we that names a collective treated as one body (as a nation, we must ask ourself).
entries.agreement: none of its own; the clause takes the plural verb that we requires (we ourself have decided, never ✗we ourself has).
entries.pattern: we [verb] ourself · we ourself [verb] (intensive) · [preposition] ourself (by ourself)
entries.contrast: the standard modern reflexive for we is ourselves, full stop: we gave ourselves an extra day. Ourself is right only where we refers to one person by convention — a king, a pope, an editorial page — and even there it is a period effect. The modern collective use (we need to ask ourself what kind of company we want to be) is a real and spreading pattern, but it is not yet standard and an editor will change it to ourselves. The exact parallel is themself, the singular reflexive of singular they (someone locked themself out), which unlike ourself is now accepted in much edited American prose alongside themselves — the two words are at very different points on the same road.
entries.see also: theirselves, hisself, oneself, ourselves, themself, we (generic)

entries.meaning: Themselves. The regularized plural reflexive: common in speech, nonstandard in writing.
examples: They built the whole deck theirselves. (nonstandard; standard themselves)
The kids were out there playing by theirselves all afternoon. (nonstandard)
They got theirselves into this mess. (nonstandard)
They theirselves never said a word about it. (nonstandard, intensive)
Folks around here mostly keep to theirselves. (nonstandard)
Standard: They talked themselves into buying the bigger truck.
entries.pronunciation note: the singular variant theirself is /ðɛrˈsɛlf/
entries.русский: себя, сами — прост., диал.; нелитературная форма themselves
entries.register: nonstandard; regionally ordinary in Southern, Appalachian, and rural vernacular English and in African American English; marked wrong in all writing
entries.type: reflexive and intensive pronoun; nonstandard
entries.person / number: third person plural (the variant theirself is third person singular, used with singular they).
entries.refers to: a plural antecedent already serving as the subject of the same clause — exactly what themselves refers to.
entries.agreement: none of its own.
entries.pattern: [plural subject] [verb] theirselves · [preposition] theirselves (by theirselves) · [subject] theirselves [verb] (intensive)
entries.contrast: the standard form is themselves. Like hisself, theirselves is built on the possessive (their + selves), which is the pattern of myself, yourself, ourselves, and yourselves — so it is the regular form, and it is still nonstandard. Keep it apart from themself, which is a different matter entirely: themself is the singular reflexive of singular they (whoever left this should claim themself), it is built on the standard object base them, and it is increasingly accepted in edited American prose. Note what is and is not in dispute there: singular they is standard American English — recognized by Chicago, the AP stylebook, APA, MLA, and Merriam-Webster, for an unknown or unspecified person (someone left their coat) and for a person who uses it — and the only live question is which reflexive to build on it, themself or themselves. Theirself — possessive base, singular — is not a candidate in either camp, and is nonstandard like its plural.
entries.see also: hisself, ourself, themselves, themself, reflexive formation

entries.meaning: Those. The object pronoun them used as a demonstrative pronoun — nonstandard, but preserved for everyone in two famous sayings.
examples: Them's the breaks. (frozen; general American, and the way most Americans meet this form)
Them's fighting words, mister. (frozen)
Them are the ones I was telling you about. (nonstandard; standard those)
I'll take them right there, the ones on the bottom shelf. (nonstandard as a pointing pronoun)
Them were good years, before the mill closed. (nonstandard)
Standard: Those are the ones I was telling you about.

senses.head: Demonstrative pronoun (nonstandard, regional)
body: Standing alone for those, in subject or object position: Them are the ones I want, I'll take them right there. Rural, Southern, Appalachian, and older working-class speech.

senses.head: Frozen them's (general American)
body: In them's the breaks and them's fighting words, with a singular verb, used by millions of speakers who would never produce sense 1. These are quotations of the dialect rather than the dialect itself.
examples: Them's the breaks. (frozen; general American, and the way most Americans meet this form)
Them's fighting words, mister. (frozen)
Them are the ones I was telling you about. (nonstandard; standard those)
I'll take them right there, the ones on the bottom shelf. (nonstandard as a pointing pronoun)
Them were good years, before the mill closed. (nonstandard)
Standard: Those are the ones I was telling you about.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /ðəm/ → /əm/, so give me them apples comes out /ˈɡɪmi əm ˈæpəlz/. The weak form is a clue to the word's origin: this is the ordinary object pronoun doing a new job, weak form and all.
entries.русский: те, эти — прост., диал.; them apples вместо those apples
entries.case: the object form, used in both subject and object slots
entries.register: nonstandard; widespread in rural, Southern, Appalachian, and older working-class speech nationwide, and in African American English
entries.type: demonstrative pronoun; nonstandard
entries.person / number: third person plural. There is no singular counterpart — them covers only what standard English calls those.
entries.refers to: plural things or people already identified or physically present — the same job standard English gives to those. It points; it does not merely refer back.
entries.agreement: plural verb in ordinary use — them are the ones I want, them were good years. The one systematic exception is the frozen phrase them's, with a singular verb, in sayings like them's the breaks and them's fighting words.
entries.pattern: them [plural verb] (them are mine) · [verb] them (I'll take them over there) · them's [noun phrase] (frozen: them's the breaks) · them there (double-marked emphatic)
entries.contrast: the standard demonstrative pronoun is those: those are mine, those were good years. The nonstandard them is the personal object pronoun recruited into demonstrative work, which is why it keeps the weak form /əm/ that no true demonstrative has — this, that, these, and those are pointing words and carry stress. Two frozen phrases have carried it into general American English, where speakers who would never say them apples still say them's the breaks and them's fighting words without a second thought; those are quotations of the dialect, not the dialect itself. Note the split with the determiner: them apples, with a noun following, is the determiner use and is covered in the determiner dictionary; the entry you are reading is the pronoun standing alone. The emphatic them there doubles the pointing and is covered there as well.
entries.see also: yourn, hisself, those, them (demonstrative pronoun), yonder, them (determiner)

entries.meaning: Those who. The fused relative of the King James Bible and of Southern and Appalachian speech.
examples: "For them that honour me I will honour." (1 Samuel 2:30, King James Version)
Them that work get paid; them that don't, don't. (regional; standard those who)
Give the seed to them that will plant it, not to them that will sell it. (object of a preposition)
Them that has, gets — that has always been the way of it around here. (with the dialect's own -s inside the clause)
She had no patience with them as talked and never did a thing about it. (the as variant)
Them what built the place never got paid for it. (the what variant)
Standard: Those who work get paid; give the seed to those who will plant it.
entries.pronunciation note: the first word takes the ordinary weak form /ðəm/ → /əm/, so the phrase comes out /əm ˈðæt/ and, at conversational speed, close to /mˈðæt/ — the th of them disappears entirely, exactly as it does in give 'em
entries.русский: те, кто — прост., диал.; сращение «те» и «которые»: them that knows
entries.variants: them as (them as knows), the same construction with the older relative as, Northern English and its American descendants; them what (them what has, gets), the third variant and the most heavily stigmatized of the three
entries.case: none — the phrase serves as subject and as object alike
entries.register: archaic in general English — it is the King James Bible's ordinary phrasing — and nonstandard and regional in modern American speech: Southern, Appalachian, African American English, and older rural speech nationwide
entries.type: fused relative pronoun phrase — the demonstrative them as head plus the relative that, together meaning "those who"
entries.person / number: third person plural. Older English had the matching singulars he that and him that (him that overcometh), and those are archaic rather than dialectal; modern dialect keeps only the plural.
entries.refers to: the people who do or are whatever the relative clause says — human, plural, and always characterized by the clause rather than named. It never refers to a thing (for things, them that gives way to the ones that), and never to a clause.
entries.agreement: plural verb after the phrase as a whole: them that wait are blessed, ✗ them that wait is. The verb inside the relative clause follows the dialect's own concord instead — standard English gives it a plural (them that wait), and much regional speech gives it the -s (them that waits, them that has). Both are recorded, and the -s is a feature of the dialect's verb system rather than a slip.
entries.pattern: them that [verb] (subject: them that work get paid) · [verb] them that [clause] (object: give it to them that need it) · [preposition] them that · them that has, gets (the proverb) · them as / them what (the variants)
entries.contrast: the standard form is those who — or, for things, those that and the ones that. Three things are worth keeping straight. The them here is the demonstrative them of them (dialectal demonstrative), not the object pronoun, which is why it can head a subject at all; that is the same them as in them apples. The construction is archaic before it is dialectal — the King James Bible uses them that freely (for them that honour me I will honour), and readers who would call it an error in speech read it every Sunday without blinking. And put a noun after them and the dictionary line has been crossed: them people that came has them modifying people, which is a determiner and belongs to the determiner dictionary.
entries.see also: them (dialectal demonstrative), them'uns, this'n, that'n, a body, such a one, those, that, them, them (determiner)

entries.meaning: They; them; those people. The Appalachian them ones, the far-side mate of we'uns.
examples: Them'uns are coming up the road right now. (nonstandard; standard they or those people)
We'uns will take the near field and them'uns can have the far one. (the matched pair)
He never had any use for them'uns up at the mine office. (object of a preposition)
Them'uns over yonder have been fishing that hole since daylight.
Ask them'uns whether they mean to stay for supper.
Standard: They're coming up the road; we'll take the near field and they can have the far one.
entries.pronunciation note: often /ˈðɛmz/ at speed in some communities, and the th weakens to /ð/ or drops as it does in every form of them; also spelled them uns, themuns, and them'ns
entries.русский: они, те люди — диал., разг.; Аппалачи, из them ones
entries.case: none for most speakers — the same form serves as subject and object (them'uns are late / go with them'uns)
entries.register: informal and spoken; Appalachian, the South Midland, and the Ozarks; old-fashioned and receding, and stigmatized outside the region
entries.type: third-person plural pronoun; regional
entries.person / number: third person plural.
entries.refers to: the other group — the people who are not the speaker's people. Human in ordinary use, and it very often carries a faint edge of distance or opposition, which is why it so naturally answers we'uns in the same breath: we'uns draws the line and them'uns names who is on the far side of it.
entries.agreement: plural verb: them'uns are, them'uns were, do them'uns know. Never ✗them'uns is.
entries.pattern: them'uns [plural verb] · [verb] them'uns · [preposition] them'uns (with them'uns, for them'uns) · them'uns over yonder (with a pointing adverb) · we'uns and them'uns (the paired contrast)
entries.contrast: the standard forms are they and them, or, when the pointing is the point, those people. Them'uns is them ones, built exactly as we'uns is we ones and you'uns is you ones, and the three are one Scots-Irish-descended paradigm that came into Appalachia together. The singular members of that paradigm are this'n and that'n, where one has worn down to a syllabic -n rather than -uns. Note where them'uns sits relative to them (dialectal demonstrative): plain them for those is far more widespread and can be heard nationwide, while them'uns is narrowly regional and much rarer. And note that them'uns takes an apostrophe because a vowel really has been lost from ones — unlike hisn and yourn, where nothing was contracted and the apostrophe is an error.
entries.see also: we'uns, you'uns, y'uns, this'n, that'n, them (dialectal demonstrative), they, them, those

entries.meaning: This one; that one. The Appalachian and Southern reductions of the demonstrative pronouns.
examples: I'll take that'n right there, the one with the red handle. (nonstandard; standard that one)
This'n here is broke, but that'n still runs. (nonstandard, the pair in contrast)
That'n was the good year; every one since has been dry.
Which of the pups do you want — this'n or the one asleep by the stove?
She kept this'n and gave that'n to her sister. (both as objects)
Standard: I'll take that one right there; this one is broken, but that one still runs.
entries.pronunciation note: two syllables each, with a syllabic /n̩/ carrying the second — there is no vowel left in it at all; the t of that'n taps to [ɾ] between vowels in that'n over there; the plurals are these'ns /ˈðizn̩z/ and them'uns
entries.русский: этот, тот — диал., разг.; стяжения this one и that one, мн. ч. these'ns
entries.case: none — the same form serves as subject and object
entries.register: informal and spoken; Appalachian, Southern, South Midland, and Ozark speech, and a standard marker of it in fiction and country songwriting
entries.type: demonstrative pronouns; regional and nonstandard — reduced forms of this one and that one
entries.person / number: third person singular. The plurals are these'ns and them'uns, and there is no possessive.
entries.refers to: one thing or person being pointed at or picked out of a set — this'n for the near one, that'n for the far one, on exactly the same axis as standard this one and that one. Things far more often than people, and always with something else available to contrast it with.
entries.agreement: singular verb: this'n is broke, that'n was the good one, ✗that'n are.
entries.pattern: this'n / that'n [singular verb] · [verb] that'n (I'll take that'n) · this'n here / that'n yonder (double-marked with a pointing adverb) · this'n or that'n · that'n of yourn
entries.contrast: the standard forms are this one and that one, and the reduction is regular: one loses everything but its n, which then becomes the second syllable on its own. That makes the apostrophe honest — a vowel really has been lost — unlike the -n possessives hisn and yourn, where nothing was ever contracted and the apostrophe is a mistake. Two boundaries are worth marking. Put a noun after the demonstrative and you have a determiner, not a pronoun: that there truck and them apples belong to the determiner dictionary. And keep that'n apart from t'other, which also means "the other one" but specifically picks the second of two, where that'n simply points.
entries.see also: them'uns, t'other, them (dialectal demonstrative), we'uns, this, that, that there, one, that there (determiner)

entries.meaning: The other one — the second of two. An archaic pronoun kept alive in Southern and Appalachian speech, and a fossil of a four-hundred-year-old misdivision.
examples: One of them wanted to sell and t'other wanted to hold on another year. (nonstandard; standard the other)
Take this rope and give me t'other.
It was one or t'other — there was no third choice on the ballot.
This'n runs and t'other has been up on blocks since the spring.
The two brothers never agreed: what one built, t'other tore down.
Standard: One wanted to sell and the other wanted to hold on.
entries.pronunciation note: two syllables, stress on the first, voiced th; also spelled tother and t'othern, and the older spelling without the apostrophe is the historically correct one, since nothing was ever cut out of it
entries.русский: другой, второй — устар. и диал.; «тот другой», из the other
entries.case: none — the same form serves as subject and object
entries.register: archaic in general English and regional in American speech; Appalachian, Southern, and older rural usage, and common in British dialect writing and in Twain
entries.type: indefinite and demonstrative pronoun, archaic and dialectal — "the other one"
entries.person / number: third person singular; the plural is t'others. No possessive.
entries.refers to: the second of two already identified — the one that is not the one just mentioned. It needs a set of exactly two to work in; with three or more, English wants the others or the rest.
entries.agreement: singular verb: t'other is broke, t'other was late. The plural t'others takes a plural verb.
entries.pattern: one … and t'other (the frozen pairing: one or t'other of them) · this one or t'other · [verb] t'other · t'other of the two · the determiner use, t'other day / t'other night, which belongs to the determiner dictionary
entries.contrast: the standard form is the other, and the history is the best part of this entry. Middle English wrote that other; the final t of that got re-analyzed as the start of the next word, giving the tother, and t'other is what that left behind. The same misdivision — a metanalysis — gave English a newt from an ewt, a nickname from an ekename, and an apron from a napron, and it explains why the apostrophe is misleading: the t is not a contracted the, it is the tail of that. Two limits. T'other means the second of two; for one of many, write another or the others. And t'other standing in front of a noun (t'other day, t'other night) is a determiner, covered as t'other in the determiner dictionary; the entry you are reading is the pronoun standing alone.
entries.see also: this'n, that'n, them'uns, the same, other, others, another, t'other (determiner)

entries.meaning: We; us — the Appalachian we ones, the first-person mate of you'uns.
examples: We'uns are going down to the church supper. (nonstandard; standard we)
You'uns take the truck and we'uns will walk. (nonstandard; the matched pair, one clause each)
He never had much use for we'uns. (nonstandard as the object of a preposition; standard us)
We'uns didn't get a drop of rain all summer. (nonstandard)
Come on down and eat with us'uns. (the object variant)
Standard: We're going down to the church supper, and you can walk with us.
entries.pronunciation note: often /winz/ at conversational speed; the object variant us'uns is /ˈʌsənz/ · USS-unz
entries.русский: мы — диал., разг.; Аппалачи, из we ones; объектный вариант us'uns
entries.case: none for most speakers — the same form serves as subject and object (we'uns are going, come with we'uns) — though some speakers keep us'uns for the object and we'uns for the subject, preserving the standard split
entries.register: informal and spoken; Appalachian and Southern Midland, old-fashioned and receding even at home; stigmatized everywhere else, and the single most reliable dialect marker a novelist can hang on a mountain character
entries.type: first-person plural pronoun; regional
entries.variants: us'uns (the object form) and its reduced spelling us'ns /ˈʌsn̩z/ · USS-nz, along with we'ns and the apostrophe-free weuns and usuns. They are one word in several spellings, not separate pronouns; the plural mate is them'uns
entries.person / number: first person plural.
entries.refers to: the speaker together with the speaker's own group — family, household, neighbors, side of the ridge. Human only. Its work is to draw a line between my people and yours, which is why it so often turns up in the same breath as you'uns.
entries.agreement: plural verb: we'uns are, we'uns were, do we'uns need, we'uns have. Never ✗we'uns is.
entries.pattern: we'uns [plural verb] · [verb] we'uns · [preposition] we'uns / us'uns (with we'uns, for us'uns) · we'uns' [noun] (possessive, rare in writing) · we'uns and you'uns (the paired contrast)
entries.contrast: we'uns is we ones, built exactly as you'uns is built from you ones, and the two are matched halves of one Scots-Irish-descended system that the settlers of Appalachia brought with them. But they are not doing the same job, and that is the interesting part. You'uns fills a genuine hole — standard English has no plural you — which is why it and its relatives (y'all, youse, yinz) have thrived and spread. We'uns fills nothing: we is already unambiguously plural, so the form adds no distinction the standard pronoun lacks, and it has faded faster and further as a result. Nobody is spreading we'uns nationally the way y'all has spread. The standard forms are we (subject) and us (object).
entries.see also: you'uns, y'uns, yinz, yourn, hisn, hern, ourn, theirn, we, us

entries.meaning: Yours. The Appalachian and Southern Midland possessive pronoun, built on the old -n pattern of mine and thine. --- ← The grammar of pronouns · All categories
examples: That truck out front is yourn, ain't it? (nonstandard; standard yours)
Is this coat yourn or hisn? (nonstandard)
Yourn is the one with the blue handle. (nonstandard)
A cousin of yourn stopped by the store this morning. (nonstandard)
We keep ourn in the shed and they keep theirn in the barn. (nonstandard)
Standard: That truck out front is yours, isn't it?
entries.pronunciation note: also /jɔrn/, rhyming with born
entries.русский: твой, ваш — прост., диал.; нелитературная форма yours
entries.register: nonstandard; Appalachian, Southern Midland, and older rural speech; a literary marker of that speech in fiction
entries.type: possessive pronoun; nonstandard and regional
entries.person / number: second person, singular or plural alike — it does not distinguish number, any more than standard yours does.
entries.refers to: what belongs to the person or people addressed. The possessor is the addressee; the thing possessed may be anything.
entries.agreement: as a subject complement, none; as a subject, the verb agrees with what yourn stands for (yourn is the blue one, yourn are in the truck).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] is yourn · yourn as subject (yourn's the one on the left) · of yourn (a cousin of yourn) · parallel forms: hisn, hern, ourn, theirn
entries.contrast: the standard form is yours, and the whole family is nonstandard: hisn for his, hern for hers, ourn for ours, theirn for theirs. The pattern is an old and perfectly regular one — these forms were built by analogy with mine and thine, the two possessive pronouns that already ended in -n, and the analogy simply spread to the rest of the paradigm in the dialects of northern and western England before crossing to Appalachia. Standard English went the other way and generalized -s instead (yours, hers, ours, theirs), so the two systems are mirror images, each regular in its own terms. Note that mine is shared by both — and that a third set of speakers finishes the standard pattern instead, saying mines. None of these forms ever takes an apostrophe: ✗your'n and ✗yourn's are wrong twice over.
entries.see also: hisn, hern, ourn, theirn, mines, thine, them (dialectal demonstrative), hisn, hern, ourn, yourn, theirn, yours, mine
